featuredDrafts.title: The Prevalence of Dementia Diagnosis and Delivery of Appropriate Dementia Care in Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study aimed to assess the recorded prevalence of a dementia diagnosis and the receipt of appropriate dementia care among current Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients of Aboriginal and Community Controlled Health Services (ACCHS) aged 45 and over, as documented in medical records. ACCHSs are Australian primary healthcare organisations that are initiated, governed and operated by local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. A manual audit of medical records was undertaken by a staff member from each participating ACCHS to identify current clients with a documented diagnosis of dementia and examine their receipt of key elements of dementia-related care. Across 9 ACCHSs located in New South Wales, a total of 70 clients with a recorded diagnosis of dementia were identified (1.2% recorded prevalence rate). The majority of clients with a dementia diagnosis had documented receipt of elements of appropriate dementia care including an active chronic disease management plan (61%), annual health assessment (56%), referral to aged care services (69%), and assessment of one or more dementia-related risks (94%). However, less than half of clients had a documented cognitive assessment within the last 12 months (41%) or completed any advance planning documentation (37%). Clients with a dementia diagnosis received a mean of 3.6 out of 6 assessed elements of best practice dementia care. As with primary care nationally and internationally, ACCHSs require co-designed support strategies to enhance their processes for dementia diagnosis and documentation and to build upon their delivery of best-practice dementia care. Priority dementia care areas for older clients with a confirmed dementia diagnosis include the evaluation of dementia-related risks such as elder abuse and driving safety, and the implementation of advance care planning including discussion or completion of relevant legal documents. featuredDrafts.title: What do young adults think about informal care for older adults?: Testing and validation of a public caregiver stigma scale in Canada
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Young adults are the caregivers of tomorrow. However, it remains unclear what stereotypes about informal caregiving for older adults they have learned. This study aimed to test and validate a first of its kind scale to measure public caregiver stigma as perceived among young adults without prior care experiences. Research Design and  Participants aged 18 to 35 years, collected from the community (sample 1) and university students (sample 2) in Canada answered a self-reported online survey on public caregiver stigma (Public Caregiver Stigma Scale, Warmth-Competence-Scale) and their sociodemographic . Exploratory (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor analyses (CFA) were conducted, and the resulting scale was tested for content and concurrent validity and reliability.  : The EFA performed on sample 1 resulted in a two-factor model with correlated factors that was confirmed by a CFA in sample 2, demonstrating excellent model fit. Content and concurrent validity were supported by the study’s findings and internal consistency of the two scales varied between acceptable and good. Young adults showed moderately high positive and negative public caregiver stigma, which were associated with their sociodemographic characteristics.  The study confirmed a new quantitative measure of public caregiver stigma targeting unpaid caregiving for older adults, reflecting negative (e.g., isolation, invisibility) and positive (e.g., admiration) stereotypes, emotional, and behavioral reactions. In addition to new insights into younger adults’ perspectives of care, it provides a promising new instrument to investigate society’s expectations of informal caregiving for the aging population.

featuredDrafts.title: Chair-Rise Difficulty as a Functional Correlate in the Longitudinal Association Between Loneliness and Incident Osteoarthritis in Older Adults
featuredDrafts.abstract: To examine whether chair-rise difficulty functions as a functional mediator in the association between loneliness/social isolation and incident osteoarthritis (OA).  Data from 6,232 adults ≥50 in 12 European countries (SHARE waves 7–9, 2017–2022). Social isolation and loneliness were exposures; depression, physical inactivity, and chair-rise difficulty were mediators; OA onset was the outcome. Structural equation modeling tested mediation, adjusting for covariates.  No direct associations were found; both exposures had significant indirect effects via depression and functional decline. Chair-rise difficulty was the strongest mediator (β = 0.74, p  Loneliness and social isolation were indirectly linked to incident OA via psychological, behavioral, and functional mechanisms. Chair-rise difficulty is a functional intermediary linking psychosocial distress to physical vulnerability and increased OA incidence, not a direct cause of joint-degeneration.

featuredDrafts.title: Greenspace Exposure During Everyday Mobility and Working Memory in Older Adults: Momentary Benefits Amid Stressors
featuredDrafts.abstract: Introduction. While residential greenspace has been linked to better cognitive function in older adults, it remains unclear whether short-term greenspace exposure during everyday mobility can provide immediate cognitive benefits. Stress may play a critical role in this process, as it reflects a mismatch between environmental demands and personal resources and may signal an increased need for restoration. . This ambulatory assessment study examined the association between greenspace exposure and cognition in daily life, as well as the moderating role of stress. Over a two-week period, 123 older adults (aged 65–89 years) wore a GPS device that continuously recorded their mobility trajectories and carried a smartphone to complete repeated working memory tasks and experience sampling assessments of stressors approximately every two hours (seven times per day). . Multilevel models showed that, at the within-person level, greater-than-usual greenspace exposure in the past two hours was associated with higher-than-usual momentary working memory performance when stressor occurrence was reported, compared to moments when stressors were not reported. At the between-person level, individuals with higher overall greenspace exposure showed better working memory performance. . These findings suggest that the cognitive benefits of greenspace exposure are context-dependent, emerging when stressors were recently present and when the need for restoration may be high. More broadly, our findings point to a dynamic, needs-based process in which everyday mobility through natural environments may support cognitive health among older adults.

featuredDrafts.title: Network Analysis of Depressive Symptoms Among Chinese Older Adults Across Different Intergenerational Support Patterns
featuredDrafts.abstract: Intergenerational support plays a crucial role in mental health in later life, yet both the heterogeneity of support patterns and the symptom-level interplay among depressive symptoms remain underexplored.  Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS 2020, N = 7,444), Latent Class Analysis (LCA) identified intergenerational support patterns. Network analysis and the Network Comparison Test (NCT) were utilized to estimate and compare depressive symptom networks (CESD-10) across subgroups.  Three patterns emerged: Distant-Supportive (55.9%), Proximate-Interactive (24.2%), and Traditional Co-resident (19.9%). While “sadness” and “being bothered” were universal core symptoms, NCT revealed distinct structural disparities. The Proximate-Interactive group exhibited a uniquely strong “bothered–fearful” connection. The Distant-Supportive group showed pronounced “effort–cannot get going” pathways, whereas the Traditional Co-resident group displayed a stronger “bothered–trouble focusing” link.  Intergenerational support patterns are not only associated with overall depression severity but also with differences in the network topology of depressive symptoms. Differentiated interventions tailored to specific family structures are essential for geriatric mental health.

featuredDrafts.title: Smart wearable device ownership and depressive symptoms among older adults in China: a longitudinal fixed-effects analysis
featuredDrafts.abstract: Smart wearable devices are increasingly incorporated into later-life health management, but longitudinal evidence concerning device ownership and depressive symptoms remains limited.  This study examined the within-person association between smart wearable device ownership and depressive symptoms among older adults in China, alongside concurrent psychosocial and behavioral characteristics and variation across digital and sociodemographic contexts.  Data were drawn from the 2018, 2020, and 2023 waves of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey. The baseline analytical sample comprised 30,255 person-year observations from 16,752 respondents. Two-way fixed-effects models were estimated using 22,536 observations from 9,033 repeatedly observed respondents, including 902 ownership switchers. Depressive symptoms were measured using a reverse-coded nine-item CES-D score. Additional analyses examined health perception, social adaptation, leisure participation, mobile phone proficiency, sociodemographic heterogeneity, sample selection, and attrition.  Smart wristband or smartwatch ownership was positively associated with the reverse-coded CES-D score within individuals ( β = 0.719, 95% CI [0.414, 1.024]), indicating fewer depressive symptoms during waves in which ownership was reported. The association remained positive across multiple sensitivity analyses. Ownership also covaried positively with health perception, social adaptation, and leisure participation, although their contemporaneous measurement precluded causal mediation claims. Contemporaneous analyses showed a more favorable ownership association at higher levels of self-rated mobile phone proficiency (linear interaction β = 1.890, p .001), whereas prior-proficiency analyses produced weaker evidence. Heterogeneity was statistically supported for hukou origin, but not for gender, age, or education after multiplicity adjustment.  Smart wearable device ownership was positively associated with fewer depressive symptoms within individuals, but the findings do not establish a causal effect. Digital capabilities and institutional context appear important for understanding heterogeneity in the ownership–depressive-symptom association. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

featuredDrafts.title: Age trajectories of informal caregiving for older people in England: Testing the healthy caregiver hypothesis
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  This study investigates how health status shapes the age trajectories of informal caregiving for spouses and older parents in England. Research Design and  The data came from five waves (2012–2023) of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). We analysed 41,997 person-wave observations from 12,420 individuals aged 50+. We derived a latent health construct via hierarchical confirmatory factor analysis, integrating functional, mental, physical, and cognitive domains. Dynamic random-effects models were employed to examine the influence of prior health on consequent caregiving, and initial condition adjustment was made to correct estimation bias.  Among those with a spouse, parents, or parents-in-law, healthier individuals demonstrated steeper increases in caregiving probability over time, while those in poor health showed flatter or declining caregiving trajectories. For spousal caregiving, better health was associated with a lower likelihood of caregiving at age 50, but this relationship turned positive from age 70 onwards. For parental caregiving, better health was associated with a higher likelihood of caregiving from age 53 onwards.  Overall the research findings are consistent with the healthy caregiver hypothesis, particularly in later life. Good health facilitates the provision of informal care, whereas poor health compromises caregiving capability and constitutes a barrier to taking on a caregiving role. A healthier older population not only means lower care needs but also has greater capacity to provide care.

featuredDrafts.title: Feasibility of a multidimensional interdisciplinary rehabilitation program for people with dementia and their informal primary caregivers – a randomized pilot trial with a caregiver focus
featuredDrafts.abstract: To improve the situation of informal caregivers, both supportive efforts for caregiver and rehabilitation for the person with dementia, may be needed. This randomized controlled pilot trial evaluated, among caregivers, the feasibility of a person-centred multidimensional interdisciplinary rehabilitation program for community-dwelling people with dementia that incorporated an education and support intervention for informal caregivers.  Informal caregivers were randomized alongside the person with dementia to an intervention group (n=36) or usual care (n=31). Multiprofessional team rehabilitation for individuals with dementia and support for caregivers, were offered for one 20-week and two 4-week follow-up periods after 5 and 14 months. Caregivers were offered assessments, participation in group sessions, and individual support. After the last group session, scheduled during the last four weeks of the 20-week period, a survey was distributed. Attendance at group sessions and uptake of individual support were recorded. Blinded assessments of caregiver burden (Caregiver Burden Scale, CBS), depressive symptoms (Geriatric Depression Scale 15-item version, GDS) and health-related quality of life (Short Form 36–Health Survey, SF-36), were performed at baseline and after 5, 12, 24, and 36 months.  Thirty-seven participants (56%) were spouses and 26 (39%) were adult children. Participation rate in assessments of outcomes at 36 months was 100% and 87% for intervention and control group in GDS and SF-36, respectively, and 69% and 61% for CBS, respectively. Missing data were primarily due to mortality. All caregivers in the intervention group (n=36) were assessed, and all received individual interventions by team staff. Twenty-three caregivers attended group sessions, and 21 completed a survey after the last session. Twenty (95%) caregivers reported increased knowledge about supporting the person with dementia, and 19 (90%) improved coping strategies. No significant differences were observed between groups in depressive symptoms or caregiver burden, yet differences in favour of the control group were seen in subscales of health-related quality of life at 24 and 36 months.  The program, combining rehabilitation for the person with dementia with caregiver support, seems feasible regarding caregivers’ participation in the intervention and study evaluation, and thus further evaluation in an adequately powered randomized controlled trial seems relevant. A future definitive trial should evaluate continuous support over a longer period adapted to the caregiver and refine assessment procedures, including conducting assessments during ongoing interventions to provide greater insights into rehabilitation and caregiver-support effects. Trial registration The study protocol is published online 04/11/2015 at http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN59155421.

featuredDrafts.title: Latent profile analysis of digital health literacy among digital device-using older adults with coronary heart disease: a cross-sectional study
featuredDrafts.abstract: Our study aimed to analyze the latent profiles of digital health literacy among community-dwelling older adults with clinically diagnosed coronary heart disease (CHD) who can use digital devices, and to explore factors associated with different profiles.  This cross-sectional survey was conducted among community-dwelling older adults with clinically diagnosed CHD who can use digital devices in Qingdao, from October 2024 to December 2024. Data were collected using a Demographic and Clinical questionnaire, the Older Digital Health Literacy Scale, and the Online Health Information Seeking Behavior Scale. We performed latent profile analysis to identify the latent profile of older adults with CHD. And we used chi-square and multinomial logistic regression analysis to explore associated factors.  A total of 371 older coronary heart disease patients completed the questionnaire. The digital health literacy score was (39.31 ± 7.27) points. Statistical fit indices (LMR and BLRT) supported a three-class solution ( p low literacy type ( n = 96, 26.3%), middle literacy type ( n = 188, 50.5%), and high literacy type ( n = 87, 23.2%). Place of residence, monthly household income, living arrangements, duration of coronary heart disease, frequency of using digital devices for health, and online health information seeking were significant associated with the different latent profiles ( p  Three distinct latent profiles of digital health literacy were identified among older adults with CHD, each exhibiting significant differences in characteristics. Based on the identified profiles, tailored interventions may differ in focus: basic digital skill training for the low literacy group, guided and confidence-enhancing strategies for the middle literacy group, and advanced engagement optimization for the high literacy group. Higher levels of digital health literacy were associated with greater potential capacity for disease self-management. Notably, the findings in this study should be interpreted in light of the cross-sectional design and exclusion of non-digital-device users. Trial registration Clinical trial number: not applicable. This study didn’t report any  of a health care intervention on human participants.

featuredDrafts.title: Balance on the Brain: Multimodal exercise programme evaluating physical performance, falls, quality of life and cognition for people with mild cognitive impairment-randomised controlled trial
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  The aim of this study was to evaluate whether a balance-focused multimodal exercise programme improves balance and reduces falls for people with mild cognitive impairment. Research Design and  A single-blind randomised controlled trial (n = 128, before withdrawals), with 6-month intervention, followed by 6-month maintenance period. The intervention, Balance on the Brain, consisted of three exercise programmes: walking, Balance Yourself and Clock Yourself.  Data from 126 adults with mild cognitive impairment were included in the study (median age = 76, 63% female). The study did not meet the required sample size to be fully powered for either falls or balance primary outcomes. Therefore, the lack of significant between-group differences for the primary outcomes of falls or balance at 6 and 12-months remains inconclusive, due to insufficient power. Fifty-nine percent (n = 38) of intervention participants were identified as adherers. Adherers’ balance improved significantly compared to low-adherers/controls at 6 and 12-months and intervention adherers fell less than low-adherers/controls, although the difference was not significant. However, the adherers data were exploratory and need to be used with caution.  Balance on the Brain was underpowered and as such the non-significant primary balance and falls outcomes should be interpreted as inconclusive for people living with mild cognitive impairment in the community. Those who adhered demonstrated improved balance, and reduced falls compared to low-adherers/controls, however these data should be interpreted as exploratory and with caution.

featuredDrafts.title: Spending time helping others and well-being of givers: Age differences in immediate and long-term effects on well-being
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: The extant literature suggests that spending time helping others is associated with both beneficial and detrimental effects on givers’ emotional experiences. To reconcile these findings, the current study examined the daily- and monthly-level associations between spending time helping others and well-being. We predicted that spending time helping others would be associated with lower hedonic well-being at the daily level but higher eudaimonic well-being at the monthly level. We further hypothesized that age would moderate these associations. Method We used data from the main survey and the National Study of Daily Experiences (NSDE) in MIDUS 3 (N=865) and MIDUS Refresher 1 (N=612). Participants reported their daily and monthly time spent helping others. Measures included hedonic well-being (negative affect and positive affect) and eudaimonic well-being (social and psychological well-being).  At the daily level, our sample of adults experienced mixed emotional consequences on days when they spent more time helping others, reporting both higher negative and positive affect. Age moderation showed young and middle-aged adults experienced more negative affect. At the monthly level, spending time helping others was associated with higher social and psychological well-being. This association was significantly stronger among older adults than middle-aged adults in Refresher 1. Monthly spending time helping others was not associated with hedonic well-being. Discussion These findings suggest that spending time helping others can be both taxing and enjoyable in the short term while contributing to eudaimonic benefits over the long term. Older age may reduce costs and enhance benefits of spending time helping others.

featuredDrafts.title: Emergent Connections: A Community-Based Model for Advancing Social Connection Among Immigrant Older Adults with Disabilities
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Social isolation is an urgent public health concern, especially for older immigrants who face heightened barriers to social participation due to disability, structural health inequities, and limited access to culturally and linguistically appropriate services. This study presents a programmatic model that explains how social connection and sustained participation can be fostered through accessible, culturally responsive, and participatory design. Research Design and  This community-engaged case study examines a national virtual program serving Spanish-speaking older adults, many of whom have sensory disabilities and chronic illnesses. A thematic and comparative analysis was conducted using qualitative interviews with ten older adults with vision impairment, program documents, and consultation with program leadership. This led to the identification of a programmatic model, the emergent connections platform.  The emergent connections platform strengthens loosely connected social networks among older adults who share cultural and lived experiences through three pillars. The first is cultural, linguistic, and physically accessible infrastructure. Second, shared governance cultivates member leadership and program co-creation. Third, a flexible structure allows for evolution in response to member needs and innovations. These pillars collectively create pathways for individuals to engage, lead, and strengthen their communities.  Advancing a more inclusive democracy requires sustained investment in accessible, community-led initiatives that support the leadership and innovation of marginalized older adults. This calls for moving towards models that position older adults as co-creators of programs and services. Doing so cultivates social connection through leadership, reciprocity, and a sense of belonging within a broader social fabric.

featuredDrafts.title: Determinants of Self-Care Practices Among Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Caregiver burden significantly impedes self-care, often resulting in poor health and increased vulnerability to chronic illness. Despite these risks, the underlying factors influencing caregivers’ self-care remain understudied. This qualitative descriptive study explored the context of caregiver self-care and identified perceived barriers and facilitators to practicing self-care. Research Design and  We conducted four focus groups with 14 caregivers primarily responsible for providing in-home care to older adults (≥ 65 years) with chronic illnesses. Focus groups were audio-recorded and transcribed. A hierarchical coding system was developed and refined using the focus group guide and preliminary transcript review. Coded transcripts were analyzed using an iterative inductive-deductive thematic approach based on established theories.  Caregivers’ multi-dimensional definitions of self-care shaped their perceived barriers and facilitators. Three core determinants of self-care behaviors were identified: capability (caregivers’ psychological and physical health, and behavioral regulation); motivation (caregiver identity, emotions, and perceived control); and opportunity (social and environmental influences and resources). Caregivers recognized that self-care deficits negatively affect their clinical, behavioral, and psychosocial outcomes. These  informed the development of a conceptual framework for caregiver self-care.  Findings underscore the importance of integrating caregivers’ own perceptions of self-care into support models. Interventions should transition toward personalized approaches that address both intrinsic psychological drivers and extrinsic environmental constraints. The framework derived from this study provides a theory-driven roadmap that informs future interventions, ensuring support systems align with caregivers’ unique needs and contexts to foster better self-care and ultimately enhance their health outcomes.

featuredDrafts.title: Lifetime family caregiving for older U.S. adults by men and women, 2011 and 2023
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Prior research finds that women spend more years than men caring for older relatives and friends (“lifetime family caregiving”) in the United States. This study examines whether these amounts have changed in recent years (2023 vs. 2011) and how recent estimates differ for men and women by relationship to the care recipient and type of care provided.  We update and expand previously published estimates, drawing upon the National Study of Caregiving (n=1,972 in 2011; n=6,500 in 2021-2023) and the Current Population Survey. We use a demographic technique to calculate years of remaining life men and women ages 20+ would provide family caregiving to an older adult if current age-specific rates held.  In 2023, lifetime family caregiving for an older adult was nearly three years longer for women relative to men: 7.1 (95%CI: 6.2,8.0) vs. 4.2 (95%CI: 3.7,4.7) (p Discussion Our  indicate lifetime family caregiving has increased for women. Gaps in lifetime family caregiving for men and women may grow further as late-life care needs increase and the percentage of older adults without close kin continues to rise.

featuredDrafts.title: Drafting the next chapter: A scoping review of academic retirement planning
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Interest in retirement planning among university faculty has grown in recent years as more academics approach traditional retirement age. This scoping review examines the current literature on retirement planning among higher education faculty by examining study characteristics; participant characteristics; theoretical frameworks employed; factors influencing retirement planning; and the quality of the included studies. Research Design and  A comprehensive search across Medline, Embase, APA PsycInfo, AgeLine, ERIC, Education Source, Business Source Premier, Sociological Abstracts, International Bibliography of the Social Sciences, JSTOR, and Web of Science Core Collection yielded an initial dataset of 8,906 unique articles. Following full-text assessment, 44 studies met the inclusion criteria.  Five factors prevailed across this literature as key mechanisms in academic retirement planning, including: 1) financial security; 2) health factors; 3) age and/or institutional policies; 4) work, family, and lifestyle factors; and 5) professional identity. Participant characteristics such as age, gender, stage of retirement, and other characteristics of the academic environment were reported inconsistently across the literature; only 14 of the studies mentioned a theoretical framework.  This is the first scoping review of academic retirement with a focus on planning that includes a range of . While health and financial security remain central to retirement planning broadly, the studies in this review suggest that professional identity plays a distinct role in shaping how academics approach retirement planning. Implications include the need for longitudinal designs to capture how faculty transitions, shifting professional identities, and planning behaviors evolve dynamically over time.

featuredDrafts.title: Practice Effects on Repeated Self-Administered Digital Cognitive Assessments in Cognitively Intact Older Adults from the Framingham Heart Study: Longitudinal Observational Study
featuredDrafts.abstract: Remote, self-administered digital assessments provide scalable approaches for monitoring cognition in older adults. Practice effects (PEs), once viewed as measurement noise, are increasingly recognized as potential markers of cognitive decline. As disease-modifying therapies for neurodegenerative conditions emerge, longitudinal digital assessments may capture subtle cognitive changes. Although the majority of PE studies have focused on memory tasks, it is critical to determine whether PEs occur in other domains. Clarifying the potential presence of PEs across multiple time points on the Food and Drug Administration–cleared Defense Automated Neurocognitive Assessment (DANA) platform remains critical for determining whether PEs can serve as a measure of cognitive decline longitudinally.  This study aimed to examine whether PEs occur and whether demographics moderate them across quarterly self-administrations of digital cognitive tasks spanning different cognitive domains in cognitively intact older adults.  Cognitively intact older adults from the Framingham Heart Study self-administered DANA tasks at baseline and every 3 months for 1 year (4 assessments: T1-T4). Tasks included Simple Reaction Time (SRT), Go/No-Go (GNG), and Code Substitution (CS). These tasks varied in complexity, from simple motor responding (SRT) to inhibitory control (GNG) and associative learning with working memory demands (CS). The primary outcome was Cognitive Efficiency, a derived measure of speed and accuracy, which are also recorded as secondary measures. PEs were quantified using linear mixed-effects models, and the change in mean score across time points was expressed in pooled SD units as Cohen d .  A total of 717 participants completed all 4 time points (mean age 64.1, SD 9.5 years; n=469, 65.4% female participants; n=481, 67.1% college-educated). PEs were observed on all tasks, with small effects on CS ( d =0.43) and GNG ( d =0.32) and a below-threshold effect on SRT ( d =0.16). Demographics influenced baseline performance: older age predicted lower baseline scores on all tasks, females scored lower on SRT and GNG, and higher education predicted better performance on all tasks. Age was the only demographic moderator of PEs, with smaller improvements on CS among participants aged 65 years or older (B=−0.39; P  Quarterly self-administered digital cognitive assessments elicited measurable PEs across processing speed, inhibitory control, and visual scanning, with stronger effects on more complex tasks. Demographics influenced baseline performance, while age moderated PEs on the most demanding task. These findings provide baseline data against which PEs in clinical populations can be compared in future work, complementing prior evidence on other cognitive instruments.

featuredDrafts.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness in Young Adulthood and Depressive Symptoms Later in Life Among Swedish Men
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study investigated whether cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) in young adulthood is associated with depressive symptoms several decades later and if later-life physical activity and self-rated health mediate this association.  The sample comprised 690 Swedish men completing a CRF test at age 18 and self-reported depressive symptoms around age 61. Unadjusted and adjusted logistic and linear regression models and Bayesian mediation analyses were estimated.  Medium and high CRF at age 18, compared with low CRF, were associated with lower odds of clinically significant depressive symptoms in late adulthood. The odds ratios of clinically significant depressive symptoms were 0.329 (95% CI [0.157, 0.687]) for men with medium and 0.383 (95% CI [0.157, 0.939]) for men with high CRF compared with those with low CRF. No credible mediated associations were observed.  These findings suggest that promoting fitness early in life may represent a useful preventive strategy for mental health resilience across the life course.

featuredDrafts.title: Outdoor cycling competence and balance control in older adults – cross-sectional analysis of the BiPerAge trial
featuredDrafts.abstract: Although cycling offers numerous health benefits, age-related functional decline can increase the risk of accidents. Identifying balance components linked to outdoor cycling competence could inform targeted assessment and training. We aimed to exploratorily investigate the association between outdoor cycling competence and static, dynamic, and reactive balance control in older adults.  In this exploratory cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from a two-center randomized controlled trial, 116 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 years with ≥ 3 errors on a standardized outdoor cycling course completed a balance test battery: Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), including gait speed, Modified Balance Error Scoring System (MBESS) and Four Square Step Test (FSST). Cycling-specific trunk balance was assessed with the Perturbation Stationary Bicycle Robotics (PerStBiRo) system, which delivers unannounced angular-tilt perturbations during stationary cycling. We derived mediolateral (ML) trunk sway during unperturbed cycling (UPC) and trunk time-to-peak angle (s) and trunk sway (°) during perturbed cycling (PC). Spearman correlations and multivariable models adjusted for age, sex and country were used to examine associations with the number of errors in the standardized outdoor cycling course.  Participants (mean age 74.0 ± 5.4 years; 53% women) made 13.1 ± 8.0 errors on the outdoor cycling course. In bivariate analyses, more outdoor cycling errors were weakly associated with more total errors on the MBESS (r s = 0.213, p = 0.022), slower gait speed (r s = -0.203, p = 0.029), greater ML trunk sway during UPC (r s = 0.246, p = 0.009), shorter trunk time-to-peak angle (r s = -0.289, p = 0.002) and lower trunk sway in PC (r s = -0.295, p = 0.002). In multivariable analyses, longer FSST time (B = 1.28 [95% CI 0.39, 2.17], p = 0.005) and greater trunk sway during UPC (B = 2.68 [0.60, 4.77], p = 0.012) were independently associated with more cycling errors.  This study shows weak associations between outdoor cycling competence and dynamic balance control during both UPC and FSST. Low trunk sway during UPC on the PerStBiRo is weakly associated with better outdoor cycling competence. These findings could be further evaluated in future studies aiming to improve outdoor cycling competence. Trial registration This is a retrospective analysis of BiPerAge study data registered at clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06453473 (initial submission: 11/06/2024), link: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06453473 .

featuredDrafts.title: Motivations, Barriers, and the Potential of AI in Physical Activity Apps for US Older Adults: Interview Study
featuredDrafts.abstract: The older adult population is increasing rapidly and experiences a multitude of chronic conditions affecting quality of life. Physical activity and reduced sedentary behavior reduce adverse health conditions and help preserve functional independence and cognitive abilities, but the older adult age group has much lower levels of physical activity than recommended compared with other population demographics.  The study aimed to understand older adults’ motivations toward health and physical activity and the role of technology in achieving their health and physical activity goals and to explore the attitudes toward the use of generative AI in health apps.  This study was qualitative and based on hour-long interviews with 20 older adults living in the United States. To elicit specific design preferences, participants were presented with visual probes of AI-generated avatars. The interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis, and the coding process drew on reflexive and grounded theory techniques.  Older adults primarily wished to maintain functional independence, both physical and cognitive, prioritizing baseline maintenance rather than continuous optimization. They reported satisfaction with levels of physical activity, adjusting them to chronic conditions and injuries. They were active through everyday functions of living as well as structured exercise programs with many participants using wearable devices and smartphones to help monitor their activity. They reported being motivated by social accountability and gamification, although some found the latter condescending or anxiety-inducing. Accessibility issues were mentioned frequently, including problems with touchscreens, limited viewing, difficulty navigating interfaces with clutter, complex multitouch processes for undertaking actions, and steep learning curves. Computers were preferred for certain tasks over mobile phones due to easier viewability, keyboard access, and greater security features. Personalization was highly desired in health apps. There was a willingness to use more health technology, including generative AI, and they were willing to consider AI in both motivational and informational roles in apps as long as it was personalized. AI embodiment preferences varied widely but with an emphasis on relatability. However, there was marked skepticism toward data privacy, concerns about the loss of independence and self-efficacy, and doubts about AI’s accuracy.  Older adults are primarily motivated by sustaining functional independence, although accessibility barriers in current health apps remain. Participants were open to AI for physical activity support, but expectations varied. They viewed AI as a passive “tool,” a directive “coach,” or a relational “companion.” Considerable variation in preferences for gamification and visual design suggested that future apps require greater modularity. As skepticism over data privacy and AI accuracy remains high, greater transparency and explainability might be needed to engender trust.

featuredDrafts.title: Perceptions of Dementia Prevention on YouTube: A Thematic Analysis of Viewer Comments
featuredDrafts.abstract: Dementia prevention is receiving increasing attention considering the surge in number of dementia incidence worldwide. Although there are modifiable risk factors, the public remains largely unaware of dementia prevention. Many individuals turn to online platforms such as YouTube for health-related information, where content can shape beliefs, attitudes, and decision-making. However, little is known about how people interpret and discuss dementia prevention in these digital spaces. This study aimed to explore how dementia prevention is perceived by the public, as reflected in user generated comments posted on YouTube videos related to dementia prevention. A qualitative thematic analysis was conducted by examining comments from YouTube videos identified through Google Advanced Search. Twenty-six videos were selected based on predefined criteria, and comments were extracted and cleaned prior to analysis. Engagement metrics, including views, likes, and replies, were also examined to understand how users interacted with the content. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-step thematic approach. A total of 7314 comments were retrieved from 26 videos. Following data cleaning and removal of ineligible comments, 2034 comments were included for final analysis. Thematic analysis revealed three themes: (i) fear and perceived vulnerability to dementia; (ii) perceptions of dementia risk factors; and (iii) trust and credibility of dementia prevention information. These themes revealed fear, modifiable vs non-modifiable risk factors, and both public reliance on and distrust of scientific evidence. YouTube provides an important platform for public discussion about dementia prevention. Although it offers opportunities to increase awareness, viewer comments reflected inconsistent understandings and conflicting beliefs about dementia prevention, highlighting the need for clear, evidence-based communication to improve public understanding.

featuredDrafts.title: Understandings of Ageism and Healthcare in the COVID-19 Pandemic
featuredDrafts.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
featuredDrafts.abstract: Ageism is widespread and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, with resource shortages contributing to healthcare guidelines that systematically deprioritised older adults. Whilst the ethical considerations of these guidelines are well documented, perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare allocation remain underexplored. This study examined younger and older adults’ perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare during COVID-19 through a social identity approach. Using a story completion method, 22 older and 41 younger adult participants completed a story about a younger or older COVID-19 patient and doctors allocating the last available ventilator. Using thematic analysis, three themes were developed: (1) age determines health, (2) age determines the value of life, and (3) age determines acceptance of death.  support the need for policies protecting against the influence of ageism in healthcare systems and emphasise the need to understand how internalised ageism may influence perceptions and health behaviours of older patients.

featuredDrafts.title: Association Between a Hybrid Video-Guided Multicomponent Exercise Program With Staff Assistance and Free-Living Gait in Older Adults With Knee and Low Back Pain: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
featuredDrafts.abstract: Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as  indicators of mobility.  In this study, we aimed to examine the effects of a 12-week hybrid exercise-based program on daily-life walking characteristics.  A total of 59 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥65 years) with mild to moderate knee and/or low back pain were randomized to either a hybrid exercise group or an educational control group. Daily-life walking was monitored using an ankle sensor. Daily observation data were collected within 2 planned 7-day windows. Primary parameters included activity volume and gait characteristics. Statistical analyses were conducted based on a modified intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models, with a per-protocol set used for sensitivity analyses.  The mixed-effects analysis based on the modified intention-to-treat principle (n=52 participants; 696 observations) suggested an effect of the intervention on improving walking quality, particularly step length (β=2.39 cm; P =.04; Hedges g =0.493), with a smaller effect with borderline statistical significance observed on improving walking speed (β=0.05 m/s; P =.06; Hedges g =0.496). Cadence, daily distance, daily steps, active energy expenditure, and accumulated 3 or more metabolic equivalent of task activities showed no clear difference between the groups. In the per-protocol sensitivity analysis (n=44), the same directional pattern of improvement was observed for step length (β=1.95 cm; P =.13; Hedges g =0.365) and walking speed (β=0.04 m/s; P =.14; Hedges g =0.368); however, the estimates were imprecise.  A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.

featuredDrafts.title: Socioeconomic Differences in the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Episodic Memory Trajectories in Midlife and Old Age
featuredDrafts.abstract: : Episodic memory trajectories vary substantially between individuals in the second half of life: some maintain high levels of performance into their 80s, whereas others experience marked declines as early as their 50s. Identifying factors that help explain this heterogeneity is critical for understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on the resource substitution hypothesis and the Openness–Fluid–Crystallized–Intelligence (OFCI) model, this preregistered study examined whether the Big Five personality traits and their interactions with socioeconomic status (SES) predict individual differences in episodic memory trajectories, testing also potential non-linear associations. We expected higher openness and lower neuroticism to be associated with better memory levels and slower decline, with stronger effects at lower levels of SES. : We analyzed data from 57,947 individuals aged 50 and older (M = 67.78, SD = 9.03) who participated in at least two waves (7, 8, or 9) of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Multilevel growth models were used to estimate associations between personality and episodic memory levels and 5-year change, and whether SES (i.e., education, income, and wealth) moderated these associations. : Consistent with the OFCI model and the resource substitution hypothesis, higher openness was associated with better episodic memory levels, particularly among individuals with lower wealth. Higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness were linked to poorer episodic memory levels, but only among less wealthy individuals. Higher extraversion was associated with better memory levels overall, and individuals at the extremes of extraversion exhibited somewhat flatter declines compared to those with moderate levels. Except for extraversion, there was little evidence for non-linear associations or for associations with 5-year change in episodic memory. : Our findings underscore the relevance of wealth as an important socioeconomic resource for cognitive health beyond income and education, particularly in old age, when income is typically reduced. Overall, the  support modest concurrent associations between personality, SES, and episodic memory levels, but provide hardly any evidence for longitudinal effects. More frequent and longer-term longitudinal assessments are needed to clarify potential effects on cognitive aging.

featuredDrafts.title: Being sensed, scored, and “connected”: a social-gerontological critique of artificial intelligence-driven loneliness detection for older adults in Taiwan
featuredDrafts.abstract: Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) that continuously infers emotion promises to change how care systems identify older adults at risk of loneliness. We use AI-driven loneliness detection to mean systems that infer loneliness, or a proxy for it, from sensed data rather than from a person’s answer, rendering the inference as a score or category used in care; they range from facial and vocal emotion recognition to behavioral risk prediction from everyday activity data. Engineering feasibility, more than any social-gerontological understanding of loneliness, has driven this agenda, and little attention has gone to how older adults in different cultural contexts wish to be known and supported. Because such detection is not yet in routine use in Taiwan, this Forum article adopts an anticipatory-governance stance, examining before deployment a trajectory that policy makes plausible. Anchored in Taiwan’s ageing society and long-term care system, it argues that culturally responsive design should begin with older adults’ own meanings, relational obligations, and expectations of privacy and autonomy, not with the sensors. It identifies three tensions for social gerontology: the reframing of a relational experience as an individual biometric deficit; the risk that algorithms read culturally patterned emotional restraint as noise; and the slippage from care toward surveillance once risk indices enter routine care workflows. Taking seriously the case for technological augmentation of scarce care resources, the article proposes principles for a socially accountable approach and a research agenda on how older adults negotiate being sensed, scored, and “connected.”

featuredDrafts.title: A culturally and linguistically tailored web-based decision aid for dementia care decision-making among Chinese American family caregivers: Feasibility and preliminary effects
featuredDrafts.abstract: and  Chinese American family caregivers face cultural and logistical barriers to accessing dementia care services. This study evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, usability, and preliminary signals of benefit of a culturally and linguistically tailored, web-based decision aid for dementia care decision-making. Research Design and  This study used a two-phase design comprising usability and acceptability testing followed by a single-arm pre-post evaluation to assess the feasibility, acceptability, and usability of the decision aid among Chinese American family caregivers (N=74) who had provided care to a family member with dementia or dementia-related symptoms and to report preliminary outcomes on changes in dementia care knowledge and decisional conflict.  The decision aid demonstrated high acceptability and usability. All participants rated the length and informational content as appropriate, and the tool was perceived as easy to use, informative, and helpful for decision-making. Consistent with predefined progression criteria, significant improvements were observed in dementia care knowledge, particularly in home and long-term care. Decisional conflict was significantly reduced, reflecting greater understanding of care options, clearer perceptions of benefits and risks, and increased confidence in decision-making.  Decision-related outcomes improved following exposure, indicating greater clarity and confidence in decision-making. Findings suggest that this culturally and linguistically tailored decision aid met early-phase progression criteria for acceptability, usability, and improvement in proximal outcomes, supporting its advancement to the next phase of testing. Future research should evaluate behavioral and longer-term outcomes, all of which will be important for subsequent controlled trials.

featuredDrafts.title: Educational attainment, secondary school features, and midlife cognitive functioning: understanding the associations between education and cognitive domains
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study aimed to examine the associations between educational characteristics and cognitive functioning among U.S. early midlife adults and to assess how biological sex modifies these associations.  Using data on up to 9,420 participants from Waves I–VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), we assessed the association between education (degree attained and secondary school features) and cognitive functioning (working memory, episodic memory, executive function, processing speed, and language/fluency) at midlife (ages 39 to 51 years) with linear regression. We adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics, measures of adolescent cognition (baseline Add Health Picture Vocabulary Test), and social origins to minimize confounding of the exposure-outcome relationship. We further examined the interaction between degree attained and secondary school features and these associations stratified by biological sex. Weights for the complex Add Health sampling design were applied to ensure nationally representative .  Higher educational attainment was consistently associated with better midlife cognition, as measured by the composite TestMyBrain cognition score. Associations generally followed dose-response patterns by degree attained. In contrast, school feature measures were largely not associated with midlife cognition, and effect sizes were inconsistent when present. Sex-stratified analyses revealed similar patterns across sexes, though associations between education and some working memory and language measures were stronger among men, while associations with some episodic memory measures were stronger among women. Discussion Educational attainment is strongly associated with cognitive functioning in midlife, after adjustment for adolescent cognitive performance and social origins.

featuredDrafts.title: Immigration arrests and midlife cognitive health in the United States
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Intensified immigration enforcement is a salient feature of contemporary U.S. sociopolitical environments with implications for healthy aging. This study examines whether immigration arrest rates are associated with working memory in early midlife and whether associations vary across ethnoracial groups.  Using longitudinal data from The National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, we assessed associations between county-level Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest rates and working memory measured via backward digit span recall at Wave VI. ICE rates were operationalized as the average number of arrests per 1,000 foreign-born adults in the prior year and linked to respondents’ county of residence at Wave V. Poisson regression models estimated associations across ethnoracial groups, with stratified analyses among Latinx and Asian respondents. Sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation assessed robustness to missing data.  Latinx respondents residing in counties with higher ICE arrest rates exhibited significantly lower backward digit span recall relative to White respondents. No such associations were observed among Black or Asian respondents. The association was observed among U.S.-born Latinx respondents, and there was no evidence of nativity differences, but statistical power to detect those differences was limited. Sensitivity analyses produced similar . Discussion Findings suggest that immigration enforcement environments may be unevenly related to cognitive functioning across ethnoracial groups and that these associations may extend to U.S.-born members of racialized communities. By establishing a midlife cognitive benchmark, this study provides a foundation for future research on the relationship between immigration enforcement contexts and cognitive aging trajectories.

featuredDrafts.title: Family and neighborhood environments in adolescence and subsequent mortality
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study examined family and neighborhood conditions in adolescence and subsequent mortality over 29 years for a cohort of individuals recently reaching middle age.  We employed a nationally representative sample of adolescents (N = 18,921) from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health). Survey and linked contextual data from Wave I (1994–1995) offered information on conditions in adolescence (ages 12–19), and the Add Health Mortality Outcomes Surveillance Study (Add Health MOSS) provided mortality follow-up through the end of 2023.  Cox proportional hazard models revealed that adolescents in lower socioeconomic status (SES) families and neighborhoods with greater concentrated disadvantage had increased all-cause mortality from adolescence through midlife. These family and neighborhood measures were attenuated when accounting for one another and were further diminished when controlling for individual-level factors reflecting adolescent development, particularly cognitive skills and educational expectations. Neighborhood disadvantage showed stronger  for external causes, whereas low parental education displayed a more robust relationship with internal causes of death. Discussion The findings support the long arm of childhood perspective in highlighting the importance of adolescent conditions for subsequent mortality up to midlife. The association between neighborhood concentrated disadvantage and mortality points to residential context as an important early life exposure for further research. Family SES, neighborhood disadvantage, and individual aptitude and motivation together influence the risk of death in adulthood. Our study contributes to a better understanding of individual, family, and neighborhood contexts in adolescence, which can ultimately improve aging and lengthen lives.

featuredDrafts.title: Residential context and cognitive aging: Differences by urbanicity across the retirement transition
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: Cognitive aging is shaped by biological and social processes that unfold across the life course and the contexts in which they occur. Retirement may coincide with faster cognitive decline. Because cognitively supportive resources differ across places, this study assesses whether residential context (urban, suburban, rural/ex-urban) moderates cognitive trajectories before and after retirement.  Data were drawn from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study (2000-2020; n = 3,675). We estimated within-person change in cognition before and after retirement and included interaction terms to test modification by residential context. To reduce compositional differences across contexts, we applied inverse probability of treatment weighting and estimated piecewise linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes.  Cognitive decline was observed before and after retirement, with faster decline following retirement. Post-retirement decline was steepest in rural areas (-0.194 points/year), followed by suburban (-0.184) and urban (-0.164) settings. Pairwise contrasts indicated steeper post-retirement decline in rural than urban areas (β = -0.031 points/year), or 0.31 points over 10 years; urban-suburban differences were small.  were similar after combining urban and suburban respondents. Discussion Retirement may represent a turning point during which geographic inequalities in cognitive aging widen. Faster post-retirement decline in rural contexts may reflect reduced access to social, environmental, and institutional resources, but these pathways were not directly tested and should be interpreted as plausible explanations. Findings point to the potential importance of place-based strategies to mitigate spatial disparities in cognitive aging among retirees.

featuredDrafts.title: Race/ethnicity, completed parity, and women’s later-life health in the Health and Retirement Study
featuredDrafts.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
featuredDrafts.abstract: This study examines associations between completed parity, including childlessness (zero parity), and a range of medical conditions (individually and cumulatively) and self-rated health, including differences associated with race/ethnicity-related factors.  We conduct correlational and multivariable regression analyses using a historical HRS/AHEAD sample of ever-married, non-Hispanic Black and White women born between 1920 and 1941. Multivariable models adjust for early-life-course social determinants of health, including contextual birthplace exposure to Jim Crow-era structural racial inequalities. We focus on childlessness/zero parity by using zero-inflated count regression  that statistically identify women with zero probability of having had a live birth (a latent “always-zero” group).  Black women had three times the odds of “always-zero” group membership and, if not in that group, an expected parity 11% higher than White women. In correlational analyses, the predicted probability of “always-zero” group membership (Predicted Infecundity Probability or PIP)—rather than reported childlessness status—and high parity were associated with high-fatality medical conditions and self-rated fair/poor health. In multivariable models, PIP and high parity were positively associated with number of conditions, while PIP and number of conditions were positively associated with self-rated fair/poor health. Net of parity, consistent with weathering, younger Black women had a higher-than-expected number of medical conditions relative to all women. Discussion In the context of historical structural racial inequality, race/ethnicity-related differences in childlessness and high parity were strongly associated with later-life, post-reproductive health disparities. Women’s number of births was associated with the accumulation of medical conditions in a U-shaped pattern.

archiveRecords.title: Epigenetic aging in people with HIV across the life course: a systematic review and meta-analysis
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Epigenetic aging algorithms are emerging tools for understanding the biological effects of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A growing body of literature has applied DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks in people living with HIV (PWH) across the life course, examining epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) in relation to HIV infection, antiretroviral therapy (ART), comorbidities, and clinical biomarkers (e.g., viral load, CD4 T-cell counts). This systematic review (Prospero: CRD420251126874) summarizes and synthesizes the current evidence on epigenetic aging in PWH across the life course and identifies critical knowledge gaps for future research. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Medline through June 26, 2026. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and assessed studies for risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We created a narrative synthesis of  and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA. Fifty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. More than half (n = 33) examined EAA in PWH compared to an uninfected control population. We identified heterogeneity in study populations and design, biospecimens profiled, platforms used for DNA methylation analysis, and epigenetic clocks employed. Only 6 studies included participants younger than 18 years and no studies focused exclusively on individuals over 65 years. Only 10 studies examined longitudinal changes in EAA. Thirty-seven papers evaluated associations between EAA and comorbidities. A meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA across 14 studies found a mean difference of 3.41 years (95%CI 2.22, 4.60) in PWH relative to controls. Current evidence supports accelerated EAA among PWH but highlights substantial methodological heterogeneity and important knowledge gaps. Longitudinal studies of EAA in PWH are needed in populations under 18 and over 65, to clarify the effects of ART, clinical biomarkers, and age-related comorbidities, and determine the clinical utility of epigenetic aging biomarkers.

archiveRecords.title: Developing a self-management support intervention for older adults living with osteoarthritis and multiple long-term conditions
archiveRecords.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects over half of people over the age of 65, and many live with other multiple long-term conditions (MLTC). Existing self-management interventions for OA do not adequately address the complexities of MLTC and there is a lack of holistic and coordinated provision across health services.  To develop a personalised self-management support intervention for adults aged 65 + with knee and/ or hip OA living with MLTC, receiving care in the NHS.  We used a six-step intervention mapping approach supplemented by co-design activities. Thirty adults (28 living with OA and MLTCs and two carers) participated in consultations and workshops, contributing their lived experiences and preferences to shape the intervention’s development and implementation.  The emerging intervention was informed by nine core principles to address the physical, emotional, and psychological symptoms associated with the interplay between OA and MLTC. The intervention aimed to enhance individuals’ knowledge, confidence, and self-management capabilities to interact with health and care professionals and support informed decision making about their health and care. The intervention comprised (1) personalised coaching delivered by trained healthcare professionals to reflect self-management support in the context of living with OA and MLTCs supported by (2) a co-designed ‘Living well with Joint Pain’ handbook. A fidelity checklist was developed to evaluate whether the intervention underpinned by the nine core principles was delivered as intended in subsequent effectiveness evaluations.  The clinical and cost effectiveness of the intervention will now be evaluated in a randomised controlled trial comparing it to treatment as usual across the UK.

archiveRecords.title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships.  This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender.  A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI.  DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116).  DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.

archiveRecords.title: Development and Evaluation of a Transportation Planning e-Tool for Older Adults: Co-Design Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults often face challenges using digital transportation planning tools to engage in meaningful activities. In Sherbrooke, a Canadian city located in the province of Québec, hilly terrain, bus-based mobility, and varied digital literacy among older adults highlight the need for accessible transportation planning technologies. Despite the growing demand for accessible and inclusive technologies, interfaces are often not tailored to the specific needs and preferences of older adults, making them difficult to use. Addressing this gap is essential to support the mobility and social participation of older adults in their communities.  This study aimed to enhance older adults’ experience with a transportation planning e-tool—called Mobilainés—by co-designing its interface and evaluating its usability and user experience in line with their needs and preferences.  Using a participatory design approach, the study encompassed both development and evaluation phases, integrating qualitative and quantitative . In the development phase, heuristic evaluation, along with the Mobilaînés mock-up, was performed to identify the percentage of compatibility with age-friendly usability design principles and guidelines. Fourteen co-design workshops with the steering committee and research team informed persona development and core functionalities, while 3 workshops with older adults refined the mock-ups. For the evaluation phase, 2 laboratory usability tests (simulated context) and 1 in-field test (real-world context) were conducted with 5, 7, and 4 older adults, respectively. Data were collected using a combination of  performance metrics recorded in real time by a computer and subjective user feedback, gathered using the System Usability Scale, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology questionnaires, and focus group discussions. For the in-field testing, user experience data were obtained via the User Experience Questionnaire and semistructured interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative data were analyzed thematically.  The participatory design and iterative evaluation process identified key design decisions for age-friendly transportation planning, including step-by-step navigation, simplified task flow, clear feedback, visual clarity, and personalization. In the final laboratory usability test, the Mobilaînés e-tool showed 84% compatibility with age-friendly guidelines, a 97% task completion rate, and System Usability Scale and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology scores corresponding to very good usability. In-field User Experience Questionnaire  and interviews suggested that participants perceived the e-tool as reliable, easy to use, and accurate, despite the lack of real-time data.  Participatory design and iterative usability testing revealed that older adults’ experience with Mobilainés transportation planning e-tools is improved. These design learnings contributed to improved usability and confidence in real-world travel planning, offering practical guidance for the development of age-friendly digital transportation tools. Future research should explore collaborative and technological strategies to support its adoption and sustained use, particularly among older adults with limited digital literacy.

archiveRecords.title: The rigor in qualitative research framework: A practical guide to evaluating qualitative studies
archiveRecords.abstract: Qualitative research is central to understanding aging-related experiences, yet expectations for rigor are often unclear and inconsistently applied across studies. Here, we introduce the Rigor in Qualitative Research Framework, developed through a structured review of qualitative quality frameworks and reporting guidance and application to qualitative articles published in Innovation in Aging. We identified ten domains of qualitative rigor that reflect core areas across qualitative approaches: methodological coherence, relevance and contribution, contextual sensitivity and transferability, researcher reflexivity and positioning, participant/data-item selection and composition, ethical and relational integrity, data generation quality and richness, analytic rigor and transparency, interpretive credibility and evidence linkage, and reporting clarity, coherence, and usability. We then examined how these domains are described and operationalized in 39 published qualitative studies from 2020-2025 in Innovation in Aging, identifying exemplars in how rigor is enacted in practice. Findings suggest that existing frameworks provide broad coverage of key domains but differ in scope, emphasis, and level of guidance; qualitative studies thus vary in how clearly and consistently these domains are articulated. In response, our proposed framework integrates these domains into a structure supporting both evaluation and application, while remaining flexible to different epistemological and methodological traditions. The Rigor in Qualitative Research Framework is intended to guide study design, analysis, and reporting, and to support more consistent evaluation during peer review, providing a practical reference point for qualitative research across applied health and gerontology.

archiveRecords.title: Effect of customized 3D-printed hip protectors on user compliance in older adults in care homes: protocol for a cluster randomized controlled trial
archiveRecords.abstract: Hip fractures are a major health concern among older adults, particularly in residential care homes where the risk of falls and fall-related injuries is substantially higher than those in community settings. Hip protectors have been shown to reduce the risk of hip fracture when worn during a fall; however, poor user compliance limits their effectiveness. Conventional hip protectors are often uncomfortable and poorly fitted, which discourages regular use. Customized hip protectors produced through 3D printing technology may improve comfort and fit, potentially enhancing adherence. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of customized 3D-printed hip protectors in improving user compliance and reducing fall-related hip injuries among older adults in care homes.  This study is a 12-month, two-arm cluster randomized controlled trial conducted in residential care homes in Hong Kong. Thirty care homes will be randomly allocated to either the intervention group or the control group, with approximately 10 participants recruited from each home (total n = 300). Participants in the intervention group will receive customized 3D-printed hip protectors in the size that best fits their body size and pelvic shape, while those in the control group will receive conventional hip protectors. All participants will be encouraged to wear hip protectors for 12 months. The primary outcomes include acceptance rate, adherence rate (day and night), percentage of protected falls, and percentage of protected residents. Secondary outcomes include incidence of hip injury, adverse effects related to hip protector use, costs of using hip protectors, and perceived benefits reported by older adults and care staff. Quantitative data will be analysed using regression models and generalized estimating equations to account for clustering, while qualitative interview data will be analysed using thematic analysis. Discussion This trial will determine whether customized 3D-printed hip protectors improve acceptance of and adherence to hip protectors among older adults in care homes, compared with conventional hip protectors. If they do, the findings could support the use of customized hip protection as part of fall-injury prevention in residential care. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry: ChiCTR2500111563. Registered on 3 November 2025.

archiveRecords.title: Stressful life events and hip fracture risk in older Chinese adults: a prospective cohort study
archiveRecords.abstract: Stressful life events (SLEs) are established precursors to adverse geriatric outcomes; however, their association with hip fracture risk and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study evaluated the association between SLEs and incident hip fracture among Chinese older adults, specifically examining depressive symptoms as a potential intermediary pathway.  In this prospective cohort study, we utilized data from 3,706 participants (aged ≥ 65 years) from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020). SLEs were quantified across five key adulthood domains. Incident hip fractures were ascertained through standardized self-reports. Time-to-event outcomes were analyzed using multivariable Cox regression and exploratory mediation analysis for depressive symptoms.  Over a 9-year follow-up, 218 (5.9%) participants sustained a hip fracture. Cumulative SLEs exhibited a dose-dependent association with fracture risk (HR = 1.32; 95% CI: 1.13–1.54 per additional event). Compared with no SLEs, adjusted HRs were 1.57 (95% CI: 1.07–2.31) for one event and 2.14 (95% CI: 1.43–3.20) for ≥ 2 events. In an exploratory mediation analysis, depressive symptoms accounted for 11.4% of the association.  Cumulative SLEs are associated with hip fracture risk in a dose-dependent manner among older Chinese adults, with depressive symptoms potentially serving as an intermediary pathway. These findings support the consideration of integrating psychosocial assessments into fracture prevention strategies. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

Survey-weighted regressions were used to estimate independent associations of OBS with GOLD BioAge and Accelerated GOLD BioAge.
