archiveRecords.title: Association between inappropriate medications and comprehensive geriatric assessment outcomes: a cross-sectional study using PRISCUS, STOPP, and Beers criteria
archiveRecords.abstract: Aim Different criteria were developed to identify drugs with a negative benefit/risk ratio in older adults, so-called potentially inappropriate medication (PIM). We investigated the correlation between the number of PIMs identified using PRISCUS 2.0, STOPP version 3, and Beers criteria and the functional and nutritional status of Turkish geriatric patients, as assessed by comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) tools.  This retrospective cross-sectional analysis was conducted in geriatric outpatients over the past 10 months. Data were collected on age, clinical conditions, medication, and CGA test . To identify independent factors associated with PIM use and to adjust for potential confounding, logistic regression analyses were performed. PIM use was analysed as a binary outcome (no PIM versus at least one PIM), and no imputation was performed. Two logistic regression models were fitted in 362 patients with complete data, without (Model 1) and with (Model 2) the number of drugs.  Among 397 participants, 58.7% ( n = 233) of patients received at least one PIM when combining all three criteria (PIM-ALL). Multivariable analyses showed that the number of medications and functional status (Katz Activities of Daily Living) were most strongly associated with PIM use. In the fully adjusted model (Model 2, n = 362), each additional medication was associated with 55% higher odds of PIM use (OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.40–1.73), while a higher Katz ADL score was associated with lower odds (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.60–0.87).  There is relevant variability among PIM tools and in their association with CGA test . Advanced, systematic, and easily implementable methodologies are required to address these shortcomings. Clinical trial registration This study does not involve a clinical trial and thus was not registered.

archiveRecords.title: Supporting Diversity in Health and Aging Research and Education: Recommendations from a Multidisciplinary Gerontological Symposium
archiveRecords.abstract: Increasing attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) have left many researchers and educators in aging scrambling on how best to navigate this political landscape in their research and teaching. In response, the Gerontological Society of America (GSA)’s Public Policy Advisory Panel convened a multidisciplinary panel discussion of experts from the six GSA member groups and three advisory panels in November 2025 to discuss the current state of the research and education, particularly as it relates to diversity in health and aging; current efforts by researchers and educators to adapt and respond to these efforts; and future actionable recommendations on how to continue to support DEI principles in all phases of health and aging research and education. Several common themes emerged across disciplines (collaboration, education, mentorship, and research) that led to four key recommendations: (1) cultivate authentic community relationships and collaboration; (2) intentionally engage historically excluded populations; (3) innovate; and (4) invoke national and state professional and competency standards. Ultimately, this multidisciplinary convening and its ensuing recommendations provide gerontological researchers and educators with both context and guidance for navigating recent attacks on DEI and contribute to a broader conversation on this important topic.

archiveRecords.title: Caring across borders: ageing and digital technology in transnational families
archiveRecords.abstract: and  The rise of transnational families has generated new care arrangements in which migrant children use digital technologies to support ageing parents across borders. While the functional role of digital technologies in facilitating remote care is well documented, their relational and culturally embedded dimensions remain less understood. This review synthesises recent evidence on how digital technologies shape transnational caregiving. Research Design and  Eight electronic sources were systematically searched for studies on transnational families, ageing, digital technology (including artificial intelligence—AI), and care, published between 2020 and 2025. Eligible studies were extracted, coded, and analysed using thematic analysis.  Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the analysis. Five themes were identified: 1) adoption and challenges for transnational ICT-mediated care; 2) ambivalence towards digital intimacy; 3) emotional labour and strategic concealment in transnational family care; 4) cultural norms and moral hierarchies of digital care; 5) structural inequalities in transnational care. Digital technologies both foster connection and amplify separation, serving as symbolic markers of family devotion and tools for managing information across generations. Rather than democratising care, technologies often reinforce existing global North–South, gendered, and class-based inequalities.  Digital technologies both sustain and transform transnational care, yet digitally mediated care remains relational and structurally constrained. Stronger digital inclusion and coordinated cross-border care infrastructures are needed to support ageing transnational families, while avoiding the reproduction of existing social, gendered, and global inequalities, and enabling older adults to age with dignity, connection, and security.

archiveRecords.title: A randomized controlled trial, process and economic evaluation, comparing multimodal care intervention to standard care for older adults in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Germany: study protocol of the intensified interprofessional outpatient therapy for geriatric patients (InATheGer) model
archiveRecords.abstract: Geriatric patients with multimorbidity and functional impairments represent a rapidly growing population that requires coordinated outpatient care to maintain independence and quality of life. In Germany, particularly in rural regions, outpatient care is primarily delivered by family doctors and general practitioners within a fragmented system that often lacks sufficient interdisciplinary collaboration. This fragmentation limits access to comprehensive, continuous care. Multimodal, interprofessional interventions that integrate medical, therapeutic, and psychosocial support may improve functional outcomes and reduce hospitalizations in these populations. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of a structured, multimodal, and interprofessional coordinated outpatient care model for geriatric patients.  This multicenter randomized controlled trial will enroll 540 geriatric patients aged 70 years and older across three regional outpatient centers (intervention centers) in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania (MV), Germany. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to receive either standard care or the Intensified Interprofessional Outpatient Therapy for Geriatric Patients (InATheGer) intervention. The intervention group will participate in a 14-week interprofessional outpatient program, comprising 20 therapy days with multimodal therapy sessions coordinated by a trained care manager (“InA-Manager”). Assessments will be conducted at baseline (before randomization), 18 weeks, and 31 weeks post-baseline. The primary outcome measure is the improvement in mobility and functional independence 18 weeks post-baseline, measured by an adapted Functional Independence Measure (FIM). Secondary outcomes include change in quality of life (EQ-5D-5 L), medication use, healthcare utilization, and costs. A qualitative process evaluation will complement the trial to explore implementation and contextual factors. Discussion If the InATheGer model demonstrates clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, it will provide policymakers and healthcare stakeholders with evidence to inform the development and scaling of coordinated, interprofessional outpatient care for geriatric patients. Broad implementation of this model within routine geriatric outpatient care could enhance functional independence and quality of life among ageing populations while improving healthcare system efficiency. Trial registration German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS) registration number DRKS00036229. Prospectively registered on 08 April 2025.

archiveRecords.title: Prevalence of frailty syndrome among patients with severe aortic stenosis qualified for TAVI
archiveRecords.abstract: Frailty syndrome is a common comorbidity in elderly patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS), significantly influencing outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Early identification of frailty and its determinants is essential for optimizing care and improving quality of life.  This cross-sectional, observational study included 113 Polish patients qualified for TAVI between January and September 2024. Frailty was assessed using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI). Quality of life, mental health, and social support were evaluated with TASQ, HADS, and MSPSS questionnaires. Logistic regression was used to identify predictors of frailty.  Frailty syndrome was present in 82.3% of patients. Higher frailty levels were associated with worse NYHA class, unhealthy lifestyle, and increased emotional burden. Depression and anxiety were significantly correlated with frailty, especially its psychological domain. Logistic regression revealed that NYHA class, emotional impact (TASQ), and unhealthy lifestyle were independent predictors of frailty. Social support negatively correlated with social frailty scores, suggesting a protective effect.  Frailty is highly prevalent among patients with severe AS undergoing TAVI. Comprehensive preprocedural assessment should include physical, emotional, and social factors. Targeted interventions - particularly prehabilitation and psychosocial support - may help address modifiable components of frailty in this population. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

archiveRecords.title: Integrating Perceived Psychosocial Outcomes Into the Assessment of Telecare Acceptability Among Slovenian Informal Caregivers of Older People: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
archiveRecords.abstract: While telecare has considerable potential to improve home care services, benefit older adults, and support informal caregivers, its adoption remains limited. There is also a notable gap in empirical research on the factors that influence informal caregivers’ behavioral intention to use telecare. In particular, existing theoretical acceptance models are insufficiently comprehensive, as they do not specifically address informal caregivers of older adults and have largely overlooked the psychosocial outcomes of engaging with telecare.  This study examined the behavioral intention of Slovenian informal caregivers of older adults to use telecare, focusing on the preuse stage of technology acceptance, by integrating the perceived psychosocial outcomes of telecare engagement (peace of mind, reduced anxiety, sense of safety, and perceived connectedness with the care recipient) into the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model.  The study applied nested ordinary least squares regression analysis to survey data collected in 2021 in Slovenia from informal caregivers of older adults, all of whom were aged 40 years or older. Of 612 respondents in the dataset, 558 were retained after excluding current or former users of care-related assistive technologies; the regression analyses were based on the 526 participants with complete data on all model variables.  The regression analysis used 3 nested models to examine predictors of the intention of informal caregivers of older adults to use telecare. The first model, which included only  variables (burden of care, financial coping, and caregiver sociodemographic characteristics), had limited explanatory power ( R ²=0.03), with financial coping as the only significant predictor (β=−0.14, P =.005). Adding UTAUT predictors significantly improved the model’s fit ( R ²=0.49). Performance expectancy (β=0.52, P P =.005), and social influence (β=0.21, P R ²=0.54); this additional factor also showed the strongest association (β=0.41, P  In this cross-sectional sample, perceived psychosocial outcomes were the predictors most strongly associated with behavioral intention in the extended UTAUT model, indicating that they may be important factors in understanding telecare acceptability among informal caregivers. The findings suggest that developers, policymakers, and health and social care providers should consider not only functional aspects of telecare but also the psychosocial needs of informal caregivers. As the study measured self-reported intention at the preuse stage rather than actual use, longitudinal and behavioral research is needed to establish whether these associations translate into telecare adoption.

archiveRecords.title: Multilingual Dementia Training for Paid Caregivers: A RE-AIM Mixed-Methods Evaluation
archiveRecords.abstract: and  This study evaluated the IHSS+ ADRD Training Project, a multilingual intervention for caregivers serving individuals living with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) through California’s In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) program, using the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) framework. Research Design and  A quasi-experimental, mixed- evaluation was conducted from July 2019 to June 2024 across Alameda and Los Angeles counties. By applying the RE-AIM framework, Reach and Effectiveness dimensions were assessed through surveys completed by 488 caregivers in English (n = 297), Spanish (n = 102), and Chinese (n = 89) at pre-training, post-training, and 3-month follow-up. Caregivers were diverse among English speakers (38% Black/African American, 23% Hispanic/Latino, and 20% Asian), averaged 49.9 years old, and were predominantly women (88%). Quantitative measures assessed dementia knowledge, self-efficacy, distress, and depression. Qualitative interviews with stakeholders (n = 11) and open-ended caregiver survey responses explored Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance dimensions  RE-AIM findings demonstrated: Reach across diverse caregiver populations in multilingual formats; Effectiveness with significant improvements in dementia knowledge and self-efficacy sustained at 3-month follow-up, plus 88-99% satisfaction; Adoption facilitated by union partnership; Implementation successfully transitioned to virtual delivery during COVID-19 despite technology barriers; and Maintenance supported by increased caregiver confidence, self-care awareness, and stress management skills, though sustainability required ongoing funding.  Language-concordant training produced meaningful, sustained improvements across a diverse paid caregiver workforce, demonstrating its value as an equity strategy in home care workforce development. While virtual delivery was feasible and cost-effective, long-term success depends on securing dedicated funding and reliable technology infrastructure.

archiveRecords.title: Patterns of Social Participation Among Community-Dwelling People With Dementia in Japan: Individual and Neighborhood Correlates
archiveRecords.abstract: Social participation supports quality of life among people with dementia, yet participation patterns and their correlates remain poorly understood.  To identify patterns of leisure activities, community group participation, and social contact and their individual and neighborhood correlates.  We analyzed cross-sectional data from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study–Home Care linked with Long-Term Care Insurance records ( n = 1,604; aged ≥65 years with dementia). Fourteen participation-related indicators were analyzed using latent class analysis. Correlates were examined using bias-adjusted multinomial logistic regression adjusted for sex and age.  Three classes were identified: Broad (10.1%), Relationship-based (21.9%), and Limited (68.0%). Compared with Limited participation, both other classes were associated with younger age, living alone, greater functional independence, lower dementia severity, and more favorable perceived walkability and availability of parks or walking paths.  Findings suggest that participation support should consider individual characteristics and perceived characteristics of the neighborhood physical environment.

archiveRecords.title: Levels of Digital Engagement Among Older Adults in South Korea: A Latent Profile Analysis and Implications for Digital Inclusion
archiveRecords.abstract: Digital inequality among older adults involves within-group differences in the levels of digital engagement across multiple everyday-life domains.  This study identified levels of digital engagement among Korean adults aged 65 and older and examined factors associated with profile membership.  Using data from the 2022 Digital Divide Survey, latent profile analysis was conducted, followed by multinomial logistic regression using a manual three-step approach.  Three engagement profiles emerged: low (46.2%), moderate (46.3%), and high engagement (7.5%). Gender, residential area, digital device self-efficacy, and digital attitudes were significantly associated with profile membership, whereas household income was not significantly associated with profile membership. These findings indicate differences in levels of digital engagement among older adults and highlight associations with selected sociodemographic, individual, and contextual factors.

archiveRecords.title: Providers’ Perspective on Barriers and Solutions to Adult Day Services Provision in Ohio
archiveRecords.abstract: Adult day services (ADS) are essential home- and community-based supports, yet providers continue to face significant post-COVID operational and engagement challenges. Limited state-level evidence constrains efforts to strengthen ADS capacity.  To identify barriers experienced by ADS providers in Ohio and provider-driven solutions to sustain and strengthen services in the post-COVID environment.  A sequential mixed- design integrated pre-survey focus groups ( n = 17), a statewide provider survey ( n = 28), and post-survey focus groups ( n = 11). Descriptive statistics and thematic analysis were used to synthesize findings.  Two themes emerged: (1) Participants, Family, and Community Engagement, characterized by limited public awareness, caregiver hesitation, and unstable referral pathways; and (2) Operational Challenges and Limited Resources, including financial strain, staffing shortages, transportation barriers, administrative burden, and facility limitations. Providers identified solutions such as statewide education, workforce development, shared transportation models, and regulatory streamlining.

archiveRecords.title: Longitudinal Association Between Prefrailty/Frailty and HIV-associated Neurocognitive Disorder (HAND): a Mexican Prospective Study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Geriatric syndromes such as frailty may be more prevalent and occur earlier in people aging with HIV, negatively impacting outcomes like cognition. Cross-sectional data show strong associations between pre-frailty/frailty and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND). However, prospective studies suggest baseline HAND increases frailty risk, while pre-frailty/frailty do not predict HAND onset. We aimed to investigate longitudinal association between baseline frailty and HAND category progression. Longitudinal analysis of 194 participants aged ≥50 years from Mexico City referral center. Two standardized geriatric assessments performed at least one year apart. HAND defined using Antinori criteria, frailty by Fried phenotype. Inverse probability weighted Cox models adjusted for confounders from directed acyclic graph (age, educational level, detectable viral load, diabetes, stroke, ischemic heart disease) determined association between frailty and HAND progression. Median age 55 (53–61) years; 167 (86%) men; median follow-up 2.3 (1.6–3.1) years. Baseline: 129 (66.4%) robust, 62 (31.9%) pre-frail, 3 (1.5%) frail. No longitudinal association between pre-frailty/frailty and HAND progression was observed in this cohort (32 progression events; adjusted HR = 0.63, 95% CI 0.27–1.48; p = 0.29). No evidence of a prospective association between prefrailty/frailty and HAND category progression was observed in this cohort; most participants remained cognitively stable. To our knowledge, this is the first study describing HAND trajectories and their relationship with prefrailty/frailty in older adults with HIV in Mexico and Latin America.

archiveRecords.title: Naturalistic Driving Engineered Trajectories Forecast Future Cognitive Decline
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Early population-based screening for Alzheimer’s disease remains limited by the scalability and accessibility of conventional biomarker testing. We tested whether passive naturalistic driving changes predict progression from cognitively normal status to sustained mild cognitive impairment.  Season-adjusted monthly driving data from 298 older adults, including 25 progressors, were summarized into within-person trajectory features capturing drift and instability in cornering and destination diversity relative to a six-month baseline. A GEE logistic regression was evaluated under leave-one-out cross-validation with a paired-consecutive flagging rule. Landmark survival analyses at 12 and 24 months assessed prognostic value. Five held-out clinical subgroups (n = 82 evaluable), plasma pTau217, MoCA trajectories, and depression scores provided independent post hoc validation.  The model detected 19/25 progressors (AUC=0.752, 95%CI: 0.627–0.863; 76% sensitivity; 75% specificity) with an 18-month median lead time before sustained CDR conversion. Adding static baseline driving features reduced discrimination (AUC=0.702), supporting that within-person driving change, not absolute level, carries a predictive signal. Driving markers stratified risk at 12 months (HR = 6.02, 95%CI: 2.35–15.41) and 24 months (HR = 13.38, 95%CI: 3.03–59.04). Signals converged or were directionally consistent with higher pTau217 among detected progressors and clinically ambiguous single-endpoint cases, whereas flagged stable participants showed MoCA decline without pTau217 enrichment. Depressive symptoms did not explain the driving signal (Spearman rho=0.05, p=0.53). The sustained conversion rate (12.3/1,000 person-years) matched epidemiological expectations. Discussion Scalable driving-trajectory features can detect preclinical functional decline with clinically meaningful lead time, without demographic, genetic, or cognitive data, and may serve as an  neurobehavioral screening tool.

archiveRecords.title: Caregiver-provider relationship quality and health outcomes in family caregivers of people living with dementia
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Family caregivers of individuals with Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) work with healthcare providers to ensure effective care coordination on behalf of the care recipient. However, challenges within the caregiver-healthcare provider relationship are common and may contribute to poor caregiver health outcomes. This study examined the impact of perceived quality of the relationship between family caregivers and healthcare providers and the caregivers’ daily mental health symptom burden (depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress).  The study included 228 family caregivers who lived with and provided unpaid care to a family member with dementia. Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM) were developed to assess whether the caregiver-provider relationship was associated with caregiver daily depressive symptoms, daily anxiety, and daily stress.  Of 228 caregivers, 82% were female, 84% were spouses or partners of the care recipient, and 9% of caregivers were classified as living in poverty. Caregivers who rated their providers’ affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) more positively reported lower daily depressive symptoms (β= -0.06, p = .001) and anxiety symptoms (β= -0.07, p Discussion Findings from the study suggest that healthcare provider affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) may be a protective factor, especially against depressive symptoms and anxiety, and offer an avenue for future interventions. Integrating caregiver-provider relationship-informed practices into routine dementia care may help foster emotionally responsive, person- and family-centered care.

archiveRecords.title: Anticipated Gerontechnology Needs in Later Life: eHealth Literacy, Adult Children’s Support, and Age-Group Variation in Urban China
archiveRecords.abstract: Gerontechnology supports ageing in place, but older adults’ anticipated needs before adoption remain understudied.  We examined anticipated gerontechnology needs among community-dwelling older adults in urban China.  A cross-sectional Shanghai survey ( N = 869, aged 60+) used multi-group path analysis to examine safety-monitoring, health-management, and daily-life-convenience needs against eHealth literacy, three types of adult-child support, self-rated health, and sociodemographic factors across three age bands.  eHealth literacy was positively associated with safety monitoring ( b = .126, p = .002), health management ( b = .140, p b = .158, p b = −.175, p = .004) and daily-life convenience ( b = −.145, p = .019), but not safety monitoring. Emotional support to daily-life convenience differed across age bands (omnibus p = .004), but no within-band coefficient was significant.

archiveRecords.title: Turnover of Housekeeping, Dietary, Laundry, and Maintenance Staff in Nursing Homes
archiveRecords.abstract: Turnover among non-nursing staff such as housekeeping, dietary, laundry, and maintenance workers is a growing concern in nursing homes. To our knowledge, only Iowa collects systematic data on turnover for these roles. Because these workers are essential to daily services for older adults, understanding their turnover trends is critical.  We used turnover data from all Iowa nursing homes from 2009 to 2022 to summarize annual turnover rates and examine trends over time, stratified by profit status, rurality, and overall quality.  The sample included 421 nursing homes with 5,130 facility-year observations. Turnover increased over time for all staff types; in 2022, turnover rates were 88.1% for housekeeping, 87.8% for dietary, 53.9% for laundry, and 43.6% for maintenance. Turnover was higher in for-profit, urban, and lower-quality facilities.  Non-nursing staff turnover in nursing homes is extremely high. Broader data collection is needed to evaluate its impact on quality.

archiveRecords.title: Grounded in Experience: Designing the Financial Empowerment Scale Through Community Dialogues
archiveRecords.abstract: Financial fraud and exploitation (FFE) are associated with billions of dollars lost annually and have significant adverse effects on older adults.  Given the challenges and complexities of FFE identification and response, this study aimed to identify domains associated with elder FFE risk from a multidisciplinary perspective.  This qualitative study interviewed experts within the field through six qualitative focus groups conducted in 2024. A thematic analysis approach was used to identify themes.  Five domains were identified encompassing intersecting factors associated with elder FFE: cognitive health, individual behaviors, social health, financial well-being, and health and environment considerations. These findings demonstrate nuanced FFE risk considerations and the need to approach assessment models from a multidisciplinary, accessible perspective to enhance financial empowerment in older adulthood. Findings will be used to inform development of a financial tool to assess potential risk for FFE among older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Comorbid Psychopathology of Insomnia: A Validity Study of the Insomnia Severity Index Among Older Adults
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: The Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) is a brief screening tool that assesses the presence and severity of insomnia symptoms. Although widely validated, its psychometric properties remain understudied in older adults, a population at increased risk for insomnia due to age-related changes in sleep architecture and quality. This study assessed the concurrent and factorial validity of the ISI among community-dwelling older adults ( N = 250) who completed the ISI and measures of comorbid symptoms: Brief Geriatric Suicide Ideation Scale, Michigan Alcohol Screening Test-Geriatric Version, Geriatric Depression Scale-15, and Geriatric Anxiety Scale. Bivariate correlations supported concurrent validity, with insomnia positively associated with anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, and alcohol misuse. Anxiety was the strongest correlate and the only unique predictor of ISI scores in multivariate analyses. Exploratory factor analysis revealed a one-factor solution. Findings support the concurrent validity and factor structure of the ISI and highlight comorbidity with other mental health symptoms among older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Mentoring Undergraduates in Aging and Disparities Research: Hopkins USTAR
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: The Johns Hopkins Undergraduate Summer Training and Research Program (Hopkins USTAR) was a 2-year program funded by the National Institute on Aging R25 Advancing Diversity in Aging Research through Undergraduate Education. Hopkins USTAR was designed to provide undergraduate students primarily from underrepresented backgrounds in biomedical and behavioral science with interdisciplinary research training in aging and health disparities research. From 2023 to 2025, a total of 15 undergraduate students participated in faculty-mentored research projects, professional development, research education, and national research conferences. Program evaluation  included pre- and post-program surveys and interviews.  suggest that the Hopkins USTAR program significantly increased aspects of participants’ research self-efficacy and strengthened perceived science identity. Despite the early termination of Hopkins USTAR, the program's short-term outcomes indicate modest success in fostering positive feelings about science and preparing participants for graduate school. Continued follow-up to assess long-term program outcomes will be important to measure impact.

archiveRecords.title: Abdominal ultrasound mitigates neurodegenerative pathology and alters specific gut microbial taxa in senescence-accelerated mice
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Age-related changes in gut microbiota composition have been implicated in brain aging and cognitive decline, acting through the gut-brain axis on amyloid accumulation, tau pathology, synapse damage, and glial activation. Live microbial approaches such as probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation address this mechanism, but they still suffer from low efficacy and unknown safety issues. We tested whether abdominal ultrasound, an approach that does not involve microbes, can alleviate age-related neurodegeneration in the senescence-accelerated mouse strain SAMP8. We treated 6-month-old male SAMP8 mice for 1 month. We then assessed behavior, neuropathology, and synaptic proteins, and quantified four pre-specified fecal bacterial taxa. Ultrasound preserved neuronal survival in the hippocampal CA3, decreased amyloid-β load in the cortex and CA3, decreased tau hyperphosphorylation in all three regions, reduced Iba-1 and GFAP immunoreactive areas, and increased synaptophysin and cortical PSD-95. Neuronal survival in the cortex and CA1 did not differ significantly from sham-treated SAMP8 mice. In the gut microbiota, ultrasound significantly reduced the enriched taxon Tyzzerella, whereas the changes in Lactobacillus, Akkermansia and Atopobiaceae were large in magnitude but not statistically significant. In an exploratory analysis, four of 64 microbiota–neuropathology associations survived correction for multiple testing. Neither object recognition memory nor spatial memory differed significantly between treated and sham-treated SAMP8 mice. Abdominal ultrasound applied to the periphery therefore reduced age-associated neuropathology in the brain, accompanied by changes in specific gut microbial taxa whose causal contribution remains untested.

archiveRecords.title: Frailty trajectories and hip fracture risk in older Chinese adults: a prospective cohort study with competing risk analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: Frailty is associated with hip fractures in older adults. However, frailty is a dynamic process, longitudinal trajectories may provide complementary descriptive insights. The exploratory association between frailty trajectories and hip fracture risk remains uncertain, particularly in older Chinese adults.  We analyzed longitudinal data from 3,868 community-dwelling Chinese adults aged ≥ 65 years in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Frailty was assessed using the CHARLS modified frailty index (CMFI). Latent class mixed models were used descriptively to characterize frailty trajectories. The primary risk analysis used baseline CMFI, measured before follow-up, to evaluate associations with incident hip fractures using cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray models. Restricted cubic splines were employed to explore nonlinear relationships. Associations between frailty trajectory class and hip fracture were also examined as exploratory analyses.  During a median follow-up of 7.2 years, 225 incident hip fractures occurred. Two frailty trajectory patterns were identified descriptively: slow-rising and fast-rising. The primary finding was that each 0.1-unit increase in baseline CMFI was associated with a 32% higher risk (HR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.19–1.46), and this association persisted after accounting for the competing risk of death (SHR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.07–1.31). A non-linear relationship was observed, suggesting a possible attenuation of the association at higher frailty levels. The associations were generally consistent across the subgroups. In exploratory analyses, the fast-rising trajectory was associated with a higher hazard of hip fracture (HR = 2.39, 95% CI: 1.77–3.23; SHR = 2.05, 95% CI: 1.49–2.84).  Higher baseline frailty was independently associated with a higher risk of hip fracture. The fast-rising trajectory showed a higher hazard in descriptive analyses but requires time-varying validation. Dynamic frailty monitoring may aid risk stratification, pending future time-varying and external validation.

archiveRecords.title: Development of an exploratory preoperative laboratory-based score for 24-month mortality after major lower extremity amputation in geriatric diabetic foot patients
archiveRecords.abstract: Major lower extremity amputation for diabetic foot complications is associated with substantial mortality, particularly in older adults. We evaluated whether routinely available preoperative laboratory parameters provide prognostic information for 24-month mortality and developed an exploratory laboratory-based risk score.  This retrospective cohort study included 72 patients aged ≥ 65 years who underwent transtibial or transfemoral amputation for diabetic foot complications between January 2021 and June 2023 at a tertiary referral center. Vital status was ascertained through July 31, 2025. Associations with 24-month all-cause mortality were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression. A 3-point score was derived from laboratory predictors using receiver operating characteristic analysis and Youden-index-based thresholds. Model discrimination and calibration were assessed, and bootstrap optimism correction was applied to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. The proposed score was additionally compared with the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI), and Hemoglobin–Albumin–Lymphocyte–Platelet (HALP) score.  Thirty-nine patients (54.2%) died within 24 months. Kaplan–Meier-estimated 24-month survival was 45.8% (95% CI 34.1–56.8%). In multivariable Cox analysis, higher hemoglobin (adjusted HR 1.302, 95% CI 1.041–1.628; p = 0.021), lower platelet count (adjusted HR 0.9966, 95% CI 0.9939–0.9994; p = 0.017), and lower albumin (adjusted HR 0.868, 95% CI 0.813–0.927; p 10.3 g/dL, platelet count p  A simple score based on albumin, hemoglobin, and platelet count showed promising prognostic discrimination for 24-month mortality after major amputation in this geriatric diabetic foot cohort. Quantitative ischemia severity and standardized neuropathy and frailty assessments were unavailable, and the score was derived and evaluated in the same derivation cohort, while bootstrap optimism correction was limited to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. It should therefore be regarded as exploratory, should not replace comprehensive clinical and vascular assessment, and requires external validation before clinical use.

archiveRecords.title: Impact of malnutrition and protein-enriched oral nutrition on early recovery after fragility fractures in older adults: the NuTra trial
archiveRecords.abstract: Malnutrition is highly prevalent in geriatric trauma patients and is associated with impaired recovery, complications, and reduced likelihood of returning home. Nonetheless, the impact of a targeted protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay on patient outcome and rehabilitation remains to be investigated. Materials and  This single-center randomized controlled study enrolled patients ≥ 70 years with fragility fractures admitted to a Level I trauma center. Nutritional status was assessed using the Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 and Mini Nutritional Assessment. Patients screened positive in ≥ 1 tool were classified as being at nutritional risk and randomized to a protein-enriched diet (Group A) or standard diet (Group B); patients with negative screening served as observational reference group without nutritional risk (Group C). The intervention targeted 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protein. Primary outcomes were in-hospital medical complications, surgical site infections and functional mobility at discharge. Secondary outcomes included length of stay, discharge destination, and in-hospital mortality. Multinomial logistic regression assessed independent associations with discharge destination.  Of the 218 patients (mean age 81.8 ± 6.9 years; 72.0% female), 100 (45.9%) screened positive for being at nutritional risk and were randomized to intervention (A, n = 46) or control (B, n = 54), while 118 (54.1%) patients without nutritional risk served as reference group (C). Patients at nutritional risk showed higher comorbidity burdens, higher ASA classes, and greater frailty than group C. Medical complications occurred in 45.0% of patients, with no significant differences between groups. Serum albumin decreased and CRP increased during hospitalization, without differences among the groups. Patients in reference group C were more often independently mobile and discharged home, whereas all patients at nutritional risk more frequently required institutional care. In multivariable analysis, a higher age-adjusted CCI was independently associated with discharge destination, whereas no independent effect of the nutritional intervention was observed.  In this geriatric trauma cohort, being at nutritional risk was closely linked to frailty and multimorbidity. A protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay did not translate into measurable short-term benefits regarding complications, functional mobility, length of stay or discharge destination. Nutritional risk should therefore be considered within the broader context of overall vulnerability, and nutritional care may need to be embedded in comprehensive longitudinal rehabilitation strategies extending beyond the acute in-hospital phase. Trial registration The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on 12 May 2026 (NCT07582575).

archiveRecords.title: From chronic disease burden to cognitive decline: a systematic review of multimorbidity in older adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Multimorbidity is common in older adults and has been associated with adverse cognitive outcomes. However, findings remain heterogeneous because of differences in multimorbidity definitions, cognitive measures, and study designs. This review aimed to synthesize evidence on the association between multimorbidity and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years.  Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and gray literature sources were searched up to August 2026. Observational studies examining multimorbidity, defined as ≥ 2 chronic conditions, and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years were included. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists, and findings were synthesized narratively.  Seventeen studies met the eligibility criteria. Overall, greater multimorbidity burden was generally associated with poorer cognitive outcomes, while several specific multimorbidity patterns, particularly cardiometabolic and cardiovascular patterns, were associated with cognitive impairment, cognitive decline, or dementia. However, some studies reported null or domain-specific associations. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across multimorbidity definitions, cognitive assessments, study designs, populations, and confounding adjustment.  Multimorbidity may be associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in older adults, but the strength and consistency of the evidence vary across studies. Interpretation is limited by methodological heterogeneity, potential risk of bias, and the observational nature of the evidence. More standardized prospective studies are needed to clarify these associations.

archiveRecords.title: Activity diversity and psychological richness across midlife and older adulthood
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Psychological richness, a dimension of well-being characterized by novelty, complexity, and perspective change, is theoretically grounded in varied and unusual experiences. This study examined whether daily activity diversity was associated with psychological richness in two cohorts of midlife and older adults from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study.  Daily reports were drawn from two cohorts of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study: MIDUS 2 (M2; N = 1,834) and the MIDUS Refresher (MR; N = 730). Daily activity diversity was quantified with Shannon entropy, capturing both the breadth and evenness of participants' daily activities.  Lower activity diversity was associated with higher psychological richness in both cohorts (M2: β = −0.07, p Discussion These findings suggest that broader activity repertoires do not necessarily correspond to greater psychological richness and that psychologically rich lives may coexist with relatively narrow patterns of daily engagement.

archiveRecords.title: Crossing the Digital Divide: Understanding Older Adults’ Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Qualitative Study
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence is redefining the relationship between older adults and digital technologies. Existing studies have largely explained the digital divide among older adults through traditional digital media such as smartphones and mobile payment, while insufficient attention has been paid to how conversational artificial intelligence changes older adults’ entry thresholds, sustained-use motivations, and risk-judgment mechanisms. This study adopts a multimethod qualitative design, with semistructured interviews as the primary method and digital scenario-based tasks as a complementary method. From January to February 2026, the study was conducted in Chedun Town and Xinqiao Town, Songjiang District, Shanghai, with 40 participants aged 60 and above who had internet-use experience and showed a pronounced tendency toward high-frequency smartphone use. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Interview transcripts, task-observation records, screenshots of AI conversations, and field notes were triangulated; an initial coding manual, double review, and consensus discussion were used to enhance analytic credibility. The study finds that generative artificial intelligence shifts the technological threshold from procedural operation to need articulation and result evaluation, enabling some older adults to compensate for limitations in traditional interface operation through life experience and language-expression skills. Older adults’ sustained use is not driven simply by efficiency, but is closely related to emotional anchoring in later life, experience organization, relationship maintenance, and concrete task handling. Community support, peer learning, and intergenerational assistance constitute important mediating mechanisms through which older adults move from initial experimentation to stable use. Whether older adults truly cross the digital divide depends on whether they can develop the capacities of source verification, contextual delimitation, and boundary judgment. Based on these findings, the study proposes a “conditional crossing” mechanism for older adults’ acceptance of AI technologies and argues that age-friendly governance should move beyond interface simplification toward capability enhancement and risk support.

archiveRecords.title: Navigating a new era of disease-modifying therapy: experiences, treatment preferences, and unmet expectations of family caregivers of Alzheimer’s patients receiving lecanemab in China
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction As one of the newest disease-modifying therapies for early Alzheimer’s disease, lecanemab has attracted widespread research interest in various clinical settings around the world. However, there is currently insufficient understanding of patients’ and family caregivers’ real-world treatment experiences.  This study employed an exploratory qualitative research design and conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with family caregivers of patients with early AD who are currently receiving lecanemab treatment.  Three themes emerged: (1) Experiences and Attitudes Toward Lecanemab Treatment; (2) The Multiple Practical Challenges of Treatment Costs, Informed Decision-Making, and Efficacy Assessment; (3) Strategies for Future Improvements. Discussion Given the current state of healthcare in China, families of Alzheimer’s patients still have high hopes for lecanemab treatment. Although some patients report that it has slowed the rate of cognitive decline, factors such as high costs and significant side effects make treatment decisions extremely complex. Impact These findings provide valuable real-world insights into the use of Lecanemab in Chinese Alzheimer’s patients, thereby informing and improving the design of future clinical studies. Reporting method This study adhered to the COREQ guideline. Public contributions No paper or public contribution. Clinical trial number not applicable.

archiveRecords.title: Sources of enjoyment in life and frailty among community-dwelling older adults: cross-sectional and longitudinal associations
archiveRecords.abstract: Although greater life enjoyment is associated with a lower risk of frailty, little is known about the association between sources of life enjoyment and frailty. This study investigated the associations between the variety and types of sources of enjoyment in life (“enjoyment sources”) and frailty among community-dwelling older adults.  Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted using data from a community-based cohort study in Japan. In 2020, questionnaires were mailed to 4,996 randomly selected adults aged ≥65 years, and 2,764 responded. Follow-up questionnaires were sent to 1,635 consenting participants in 2023, with 904 responses obtained. Frailty was assessed using a 5-item self-report questionnaire at baseline and follow-up. Enjoyment sources were assessed through yes/no and open-ended questions at baseline and categorized using content analysis. The number of identified categories was counted, and participants were classified into no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups.  The cross-sectional analysis included 2,361 participants, and the prevalence of frailty was 26.6%, 16.7%, and 11.3% in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. Cross-sectional analyses showed that a greater variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of both prefrailty and frailty. In the 3-year longitudinal analysis, 688 participants were included. Among them, incident frailty occurred in 20.2%, 11.1%, and 10.0% of participants in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. The variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of incident frailty in both crude and basic adjusted models. The odds ratios for the single-source and multiple-source groups were similar. Exploratory analysis of the 10 most frequently reported enjoyment sources showed that books, sports, friends, foods, and singing/playing musical instruments showed inverse trends with frailty, whereas media consumption showed a positive trend with frailty in unadjusted cross-sectional trend tests. Discussion Having one or more enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of frailty among community-dwelling older adults in both cross-sectional and 3-year longitudinal analyses. The exploratory analysis also suggested that the associations between specific types of enjoyment sources and frailty may differ. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

archiveRecords.title: Age-associated differences in lower-extremity muscle mass, force, and power in older adults: a cross-sectional analysis of sex differences
archiveRecords.abstract: The decline in musculoskeletal function with aging is a key contributor to mobility impairments and loss of independence. While sarcopenia and dynapenia are well described, recent evidence highlights muscle power as a more sensitive indicator of functional deterioration. Aims This study aimed to compare age-associated differences in muscle mass, force, and lower-limb muscle power in older adults over different assessment , while accounting for sex-related differences.  Three hundred nineteen community-dwelling adults aged 60–97 years were assessed for muscle mass (DXA-derived lean mass, appendicular skeletal muscle mass index), muscle force (handgrip force, knee extension maximal isometric contraction), muscle moments and angular velocity (isokinetic dynamometry), and lower-limb muscle power (isokinetic testing and sit-to-stand power). Associations with age and sex were examined using regression models and ANOVA.  Lower-limb muscle power showed a stronger negative association with age than muscle force or mass (β = − 0.433 vs. − 0.303 and − 0.119, respectively; p  Lower-limb muscle power appeared more sensitive to age-associated differences than muscle force or mass, supporting its role as a key biomarker of neuromuscular aging. This study also highlights that sex may contribute to variability in age-associated patterns of muscle power, raising questions about the universality of its definition that warrant further confirmation. These findings emphasize the clinical importance of including power assessments in strategies to preserve independence in older adults. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05343286, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05343286 .

archiveRecords.title: Diagnostic performance of calculated serum osmolarity versus clinical impression for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients
archiveRecords.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and agreement of calculated serum osmolarity for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients, using clinical impression of dehydration as the reference standard, and to examine glucose levels across concordant and discordant classification groups. Design and setting This prospective, observational study was conducted in a geriatric acute care unit. Participants The study included 455 older hospitalized patients with a mean age of 82.2 ± 6.8 years and 70% were female. Measurements Clinical impression of dehydration (dehydration vs. no dehydration [normal hydration + hyperhydration]) was judged and recorded by the attending physician within 24 h of admission. Calculated serum osmolarity was derived from routine laboratory values and classified as high (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) or normal (  Clinically, 23% of patients were classified as dehydrated. High calculated osmolarity occurred in 38%. Using the ≥ 295 mOsmol/l cut-off, sensitivity was 48.6% and specificity 65.1%; positive and negative predictive values were 29.7% and 80.7%, respectively, and accuracy was 61.3%. Agreement beyond chance was poor (κ = 0.112). Mean glucose was higher in osmolarity-positive groups, including false positives (all p  In older hospitalized patients, calculated serum osmolarity (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) showed limited agreement with clinical dehydration assessment with frequent osmolarity-positive classifications in clinically non-dehydrated patients. These findings support cautious clinical interpretation of calculated osmolarity in acute care, particularly when glucose is elevated.

archiveRecords.title: Probable sarcopenia, depressive symptoms, and nutritional status as independent predictors of dysphagia risk in community-dwelling older adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Dysphagia is a critical geriatric syndrome associated with an increased risk of aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and mortality in older adults. The aim of this study was to evaluate the associations between Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) parameters and dysphagia risk (Eating Assessment Tool-10 (EAT-10) ≥ 3) in community-dwelling older adults.  This cross-sectional study included 468 community-dwelling older adults presenting to a geriatric outpatient clinic. Participants with severe cognitive impairment, Parkinson’s disease, those residing in a nursing home, and those with an acute medical condition were excluded from the study. Dysphagia risk was assessed using the EAT-10; probable sarcopenia was defined according to the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2019 (EWGSOP2) criteria; depressive symptoms were evaluated with the Geriatric Depression Scale-15 (GDS-15); and nutritional status was assessed using the Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form (MNA-SF). Independent risk factors were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.  In the final multivariate regression model, the presence of probable sarcopenia (OR = 2.654, 95% CI: 1.184–5.947, p = 0.018) and higher GDS-15 scores (OR = 1.155, 95% CI: 1.063–1.255, p = 0.001) were independently and significantly associated with dysphagia risk. In contrast, a one-point increase in the MNA-SF score (indicating better nutritional status), when treated as a continuous variable, was an independent protective factor against dysphagia risk (OR = 0.684, 95% CI: 0.521–0.897, p = 0.006).  In community-dwelling older adults, probable sarcopenia and depressive symptoms significantly increase the dysphagia risk, whereas good nutritional status plays a protective role. Prior to the development of dysphagia and its associated complications, optimizing muscle strength, mood, and nutritional status in outpatient settings is of importance for maintaining swallowing safety.

archiveRecords.title: Osteoporosis in the Oldest Old - From Diagnosis to Treatment: A Narrative Review
archiveRecords.abstract: Osteoporosis and fragility fractures are major causes of disability, loss of independence, institutionalization, and mortality in the oldest old. Despite their exceptionally high fracture risk, adults aged ≥80 years remain underrepresented in randomized controlled trials. Diagnosis and treatment are complicated by the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, sarcopenia, frailty, multimorbidity, cognitive and functional impairment, and competing mortality. Summary: This narrative review discusses the diagnosis, fracture-risk assessment, non-pharmacological management, and pharmacological treatment of osteoporosis in the oldest old. Bone mineral density (BMD) remains central to osteoporosis diagnosis but incompletely characterizes fracture risk at advanced age. Previous and particularly recent fractures, prevalent vertebral fractures, falls, physical performance, nutritional status, and frailty provide complementary information. Interpretation of the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool FRAX® requires particular consideration in the oldest old because competing mortality may cause 10-year fracture probabilities to plateau or decline despite increasing age-specific fracture incidence; FRAXplus® incorporates additional risk modifiers, including falls and the number and recency of previous fractures. Non-pharmacological interventions addressing nutrition, muscle function, balance, and falls complement bone-directed pharmacotherapy. Available evidence does not indicate that chronological age itself attenuates the efficacy of osteoporosis pharmacotherapy, although direct randomized fracture-endpoint evidence in adults aged ≥80 years remains limited. Risedronate and, historically, strontium ranelate provide some of the clearest fracture data specifically in this age group, whereas evidence for most other therapies derives from older-subgroup analyses, skeletal efficacy studies, observational data, or extrapolation from pivotal trials. At advanced age, renal function, cognition, mobility, adherence, caregiver support, and continuity of care increasingly influence the translation of efficacy into clinical effectiveness. Key Messages: Fracture risk in the oldest old reflects the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, frailty, sarcopenia, and functional reserve. Available evidence supports preservation of pharmacological antifracture efficacy with advancing age, but direct evidence in octogenarians and particularly nonagenarians remains scarce. Treatment feasibility and continuity of care become increasingly relevant at advanced age. Greater representation of the oldest old in clinical trials is needed, with particular attention to fracture outcomes, treatment sequencing, time to benefit, and outcomes relevant to independence and quality of life.

archiveRecords.title: Beyond BMI: The Role of Abdominal Obesity in Hypertension Risk Among Adults Aged 45 Years and Older in India
archiveRecords.abstract: Hypertension is highly prevalent among adults aged 45 years and older in India, yet limited evidence exists on the combined associations of waist circumference (WC) and body mass index (BMI) with hypertension. This study examined their independent and joint associations with hypertension using Wave 1 (2017–18) of the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) among 59,658 adults aged 45 years and older. Hypertension was defined as measured blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations across combined WC–BMI categories. Overall hypertension prevalence was 31.3%. Individuals with normal BMI but large WC had higher odds of hypertension (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 1.37; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.19–1.58). Obese individuals with large WC had the highest odds (AOR = 1.77; 95% CI: 1.45–2.17). Both central and general obesity were independently associated with hypertension. Routine WC assessment alongside BMI may improve identification of high-risk individuals in India’s middle-aged and older population.

archiveRecords.title: Incentives for Access: Changes in Admissions and Care Delivery for Metastatic Cancer Patients in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities, After the Patient-Driven Payment Model
archiveRecords.abstract: Cancer patients experience suboptimal care in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs). Medicare’s Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) incentivized SNFs to admit complex patients, potentially promoting admissions without appropriate changes in care delivery.  To evaluate changes in SNF admissions, rehabilitation therapy volume, and chemotherapy/radiation around admission or discharge, following PDPM and COVID-19.  Adjusted interrupted time series examining 1,125,782 hospital stays from metastatic cancer patients, using 100% Traditional Medicare claims (2018–2021).  PDPM was associated with increased SNF admissions (0.47 pp/month; 95% CI: [0.17, 0.76]) and an immediate reduction in therapy volume (−24.95 minutes per day, 95% CI: [−26.40, −23.48]). Chemotherapy use remained low, but increased by 21% at PDPM implementation, without subsequent slope change (RR: 1.21; 95% CI: [1.01, 1.46]); radiation was unchanged. COVID-19 reversed admission gains. SNF admissions for metastatic cancer patients increased without sustained changes in cancer-relevant care delivery, warranting investigation of health outcomes and outcome-driven policy.

archiveRecords.title: Local RAGE Inhibition Attenuates Early Diabetic Retinal Pathology in Streptozotocin-Induced Rats
archiveRecords.abstract: Introduction Diabetic retinopathy, which occurs during extended periods of chronic hyperglycemia, is one of the main causes of vision loss. The receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) plays a central role in inflammatory and angiogenic signaling, both of which contribute to the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, but its therapeutic targeting in ocular disease has been insufficiently explored.  We evaluated topical RAGE229, a small-molecule RAGE inhibitor, and an intravitreally administered anti-RAGE antibody in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model. At day 84, treatment effects were assessed using masked fundoscopic scoring, RT-qPCR, immunohistochemistry, and histological morphometry. Treated eyes were evaluated against both route-matched diabetic vehicle-control groups and paired contralateral vehicle-treated eyes.  Both interventions reduced fundoscopic pathology and retinal Vegfa and Nfkb1 expression, whereas Ager showed only a non-significant downward trend. NF-κB p65 immunoreactivity was reduced by both treatments, while a significant reduction in VEGF-A immunoreactivity was detected only in the paired anti-RAGE antibody analysis. Morphometric analysis indicated attenuation of diabetes-associated retinal thinning with both interventions. Neither intervention altered systemic glycemic control. Although both interventions demonstrated similar overall anatomical protection, anti-RAGE antibody treatment showed more consistent effects across protein-level and structural endpoints.  These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that local RAGE-targeted treatment may attenuate vascular, molecular, and structural manifestations of early experimental diabetic retinopathy without detectable changes in systemic glycemia. Further preclinical studies should evaluate ocular exposure, direct target engagement, functional visual outcomes, and reproducibility in larger cohorts.

archiveRecords.title: Gaps Between Self-Reported and Documented Use of a Health Care Service Portal Among Older Adults: Cross-Sectional Survey and Retrospective Electronic Data Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Health care systems increasingly offer services to citizens through online portals, which have been found to be associated with patient satisfaction and better management of health concerns. Few studies have compared self-reported use with objectively documented portal use, especially among older adults.  This study aimed to examine differences between documented and self-reported health portal use, and their associations with  variables and digital health literacy (DHL) among older adults.  A cross-sectional telephone survey was conducted among 600 participants aged 60 years and older, who were sampled from a registry of members of a national health maintenance organization (HMO). The participants reported their use of the HMO’s portal, their DHL, and demographic and  variables. Participants’ use of the portal was retrospectively retrieved from the HMO’s administrative database.  A large gap between self-reported use and documented use of the health portal was found: for example, while only 8.1% (46/566) reported not using the portal, the HMO’s records indicated that 62% (372/600) did not make use of the portal. However, a positive correlation was found between self-reported use and documented use ( r =0.22; P r =0.41; P r =0.56; P P =.02) and ethnicity (β=−0.22; P r =0.09; P= .04), was not significantly associated with documented use in this analysis (β=0.02; P =.97).  The findings indicate that users tend to overestimate their health portal use. Interpretations vary from measurement issues, such as social desirability bias regarding digital functioning or the perception that assisted use also constitutes usage, to signaling their identity as engaged digital health consumers. Future studies on digital health use should also include measures of electronically documented use and not only self-reported use.

archiveRecords.title: Multi-Domain Intrinsic Capacity Decline and Fall History Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Rural Taiwan: Implications for ICOPE-Based Community Screening
archiveRecords.abstract: While WHO ICOPE screening is routine, the association between multi-domain intrinsic capacity (IC) decline and falls remains understudied in community-based gerontology practice.  This study analysed 775 rural older adults (mean age 79.4) with ≥1 IC abnormality using multivariable logistic regression and dose–response analysis to evaluate fall risk.  Nutrition (aOR = 5.10), mobility (aOR = 2.60), depression (aOR = 2.34), and vision (aOR = 2.21) impairments were independently associated with falls. Fall rates rose monotonically from 4.6% (one domain) to 29.1% (≥4 domains; p trend  An IC impairment count of ≥3, or specific clusters (nutrition, mobility, depression), provides practical triage criteria for community-based fall-prevention. These findings facilitate person-centred risk stratification and resource allocation within integrated care systems for super-aging societies.

archiveRecords.title: Toward Standardization of Intrinsic Capacity Assessment: A Methodological Comparison of the Responsiveness of Composite Scoring Methods
archiveRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used as an intervention outcome; however, IC composites lack a standardized scoring method, hindering comparisons across trials. To determine whether the scoring method influenced the detection of intervention effects, we applied multiple composite scoring approaches to the same data and compared their responsiveness to a 12-week exercise intervention in older adults at risk of mild cognitive impairment. : Pre- and post-intervention IC data were obtained from 59 community-dwelling older adults assigned to resistance training (n=34) or stretching and flexibility (n=25). The five-domain IC composite was computed repeatedly using alternative scoring approaches: z-score (concurrent and baseline-anchored variants), percentage of maximum possible (POMP), binary classification (0/1), and a three-category ordinal scale. Responsiveness was quantified using the standardized response mean (SRM). : Responsiveness ranged from negligible to large for identical data, indicating that the intervention effect depended on the scoring method. The ordinal and POMP composites were the most responsive (SRM 0.74–0.88 and 0.50–0.76). Within the z-score composite, responsiveness depended entirely on the standardization anchor: the concurrent specification was insensitive (SRM ≈ 0), whereas baseline-anchoring showed moderate responsiveness (0.62–0.71). The binary scoring was the least sensitive, showing a ceiling effect. : Ordinal three-category scoring was the most responsive, suggesting that approaches combining a fixed reference with a category-based structure are well suited for detecting change in IC. This finding requires confirmation against external criteria for IC, such as its predictive validity for adverse health outcomes, along with domain weighting and instrument selection.

archiveRecords.title: Structural Vulnerability and the Pandemic: Widening Gaps in Nursing Home Antipsychotic Prescribing
archiveRecords.abstract: To assess whether national reductions in antipsychotic prescribing in U.S. nursing homes were shared equitably or masked widening gaps between top and bottom performers, we examined distributional trends across facilities from 2013 to 2023 using national facility-level data (CMS Provider Data Catalog; LTCFocus). We modeled long-stay antipsychotic measure performance using linear quantile mixed regression, assessed mobility across performance quartiles with transition matrices, and evaluated facility characteristics associated with trajectories. From 2013 to 2019, prescribing fell across all quantiles, with the steepest reductions among the worst performers, narrowing gaps with the best. After 2020, progress diverged: lower-performing facilities experienced sharp setbacks while top performers maintained gains. Mobility analyses showed entrenched disadvantage, with bottom-quartile facilities disproportionately likely to remain there. Higher Medicaid share predicted decline, whereas higher star ratings predicted improvement. The pandemic reversed earlier equity gains, amplifying structural disparities and exposing unequal capacity to sustain improvement.

archiveRecords.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
archiveRecords.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

archiveRecords.title: Social Engagement Programs of Area Agencies on Aging: Understanding Efforts to Reduce Social Isolation and Loneliness Among Older Adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Social isolation and loneliness in later life are major public health concerns associated with increased morbidity and premature mortality. Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) constitute the primary local infrastructure for aging services in the US.  To describe social engagement program types and partnership structures among AAAs and to examine rural–non-rural differences.  We analyzed data from the 2025 National Survey of AAAs (n = 449). Descriptive statistics summarized program and partnership prevalence; item-level Pearson chi-square tests with Bonferroni adjustments compared rural and non-rural agencies.  Most AAAs offered multiple social engagement programs; volunteer engagement (66.0%), arts and creative activities (62.2%), visiting/calling programs (57.7%), and technology engagement (55.5%) were common. Non-rural AAAs were more likely to offer visiting/calling, technology-based activities, and memory cafes, while rural AAAs were more likely to partner with public health units. Rural–non-rural differences suggest context-specific influences of resources and infrastructure on program availability.

archiveRecords.title: Intrinsic capacity among Hispanic older adults in the United States: Sociodemographic correlates and subgroup analyses
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used to conceptualize healthy aging. However, evidence on socio-demographic correlates in IC among Hispanic older adults in the United States remains limited. Research Design and  We analyzed data from a nationally sampled cohort from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, including Hispanic adults aged ≥60 years. IC was constructed from five domains. Multiple linear regression models examined associations between socio-demographic factors and IC, with stratified analyses by gender, community of residence, and place of birth.  The sample included 749 participants (60.08% female; 89.05% urban residents; 63.02% foreign-born), with a mean IC score of 6.49 (SD = 1.67). In the overall sample, being male, married/partnered, having a household income above $28,034, and being physically active were positively associated with IC, whereas having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC (all p  Physical activity and chronic disease burden were important correlates of IC among Hispanic older adults, with some subgroup-specific patterns observed across gender, residential community, and place of birth. These findings highlight the importance of considering demographic and contextual factors when promoting healthy aging among Hispanic older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Ambivalent return: Older adults’ homecoming after wartime displacement
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Little is known about how older adults experience their return home after wartime displacement, particularly when home and community are altered or remain insecure. This longitudinal qualitative study examined continuity and change across the displacement–return transition.  Twelve participants (aged 65–92), previously interviewed during displacement (T1), were re-interviewed after returning home (T2) using a qualitative descriptive approach with thematic analysis.  Three themes emerged: (1) the unsettled return, involving altered security, unfamiliarity within the home, and disrupted community life; (2) continuity of social relationships and activities after return; and (3) shifts in life perspective and self-perception. These themes describe the shared dimensions of post-return experience, whereas the complementary diachronic analysis examined how these dimensions changed and combined across T1 and T2. A diachronic analysis identified four return trajectories: functioning but incomplete; ambivalent or gradual return requiring active reorganization; return supported by communal and social continuity and use of personal resources; and ongoing erosion and unresolved damage. Discussion These findings demonstrate that return is not restoration but a reconfiguration of person-environment fit, place identity, belonging, and security in later life. For older adults, this transition involved rebuilding environmental familiarity, security, belonging, and agency rather than simply resuming pre-displacement life. The study highlights social infrastructure as critical for post-return adaptation, underscoring the need for policies recognizing the return process as a significant transition requiring continued communal support.

archiveRecords.title: Transportation Use, Trip Taking, and Trip Purposes Among Older Adults Not in the Labor Force: Evidence From the 2022 National Household Travel Survey
archiveRecords.abstract: Transportation needs may differ by labor-force participation status, yet little is known about travel behavior among older adults not in the labor force.  To examine alternative transportation use, trip taking, and trip purposes among older adults not in the labor force.  Data came from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey ( N = 3,474; aged ≥65; not in the labor force). Logistic regression models examined factors associated with transportation mode, taking any trip on the assigned reporting day, and trip purposes.  Nearly 87% drove, 5%–7% used rideshare/taxi, public transit, or bicycles, and one-third walked for transportation. Transportation use and trip-taking varied by socioeconomic characteristics, living arrangements, and digital engagement. Drivers, transportation walkers, and college graduates were more likely to travel. Social/recreational trips were more common among those living alone and among college graduates.  Improving transportation accessibility, affordability, and digital literacy may support late-life mobility and community participation.

archiveRecords.title: Perceived Care Among Rural Left-Behind Older Adults in China: A Network Analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: Rural-to-urban migration separates many rural older adults from adult children and changes how care is received and experienced. Rural left-behind older adults remain in their rural places of origin after family members migrate for work.  This study examined conditional associations among reported care items and compared care networks by number of children and gender.  Cross-sectional data were obtained from 836 rural left-behind older adults aged 55 to 95 who completed the 14-item CSS-RLE. EBIC-LASSO Gaussian graphical models estimated item-level networks, expected influence summarized net signed connectivity, and network comparison tests assessed subgroup differences.  Village care and visits had the highest expected influence in the overall, male, and three-or-more-child networks. Holiday gifts from offspring ranked highest in the one- and two-child networks, whereas living expenses from children ranked highest in the female network. Network structure differed between one-child and larger-family groups and between men and women.
