archiveRecords.title: Reducing Stress in Caregivers of People With Dementia in Psychiatric Care: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of an Emotion-Focused Group Intervention
archiveRecords.abstract: Caregivers of people with dementia (CPwD) are at higher risk for psychological stress and mental health issues.  This study evaluated the effectiveness of a brief, four-session group intervention combining socio-medical education, mindfulness and emotion-focused support in reducing stress and improving psychological outcomes in an acute psychiatric hospital setting.  A within-subject waiting-period control design with repeated measures was conducted with N = 52 CPwD. Assessments were performed at baseline, pre-intervention, post-intervention and follow-up. Changes across phases were analyzed using subsequent contrast analyses.  Following the intervention, perceived stress decreased significantly ( p = .038) and general functioning improved ( p = .002) at follow-up. No significant changes were found for depressive symptoms or subjective well-being. The study protocol was designed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the joint Ethics Committee of the medical faculty at the Ludwig-Maximilians-University of Munich (project number 22-0995).

archiveRecords.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

archiveRecords.title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary : (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content.  revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. However, older adults recalled as many episodic details as younger participants. There was no difference as a function of the recipient's age. Overall, these  underscore the value of studying memory in everyday social contexts.

archiveRecords.title: Rethinking Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Severe Alzheimer's Disease: From Intentional Explanation to an Ecological, Body–Environment Framework
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: In contemporary dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are often understood as expressions of the person's intentions or needs. This paper examines the limits of understanding BPSD as “expressions of intention” in severe Alzheimer's disease. It argues that while desires may still be preserved, the formation and maintenance of beliefs—an essential constituent of intentions in the standard desire–belief model—are likely to be severely compromised. As a result, many behavioral and perceptual symptoms closely related to basic activities of daily living cannot be adequately explained within an intention-based framework. As a complementary framework to existing dementia care theories, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of BPSD as arising from the interaction between embodied procedural memory and environmental affordances. Many BPSD are better understood not as expressions of intention, but as the outcome of situational and non-selective reactivation of fragments of relatively preserved procedural memory in response to the structure of the immediate environment. This reconceptualization extends the focus of care practice beyond the interpretation of the presumed meanings or intentions underlying BPSD and highlights the importance of modifying care environments in ways that appropriately support or constrain the reactivation of procedural memory.

archiveRecords.title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.  Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.  EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.  We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.

archiveRecords.title: ‘Keeping me sharp”: Self-perceived effects of grandparenthood on cognition: An exploratory thematic analysis
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: The experience of grandparenthood holds the potential for novel and engaging social interactions and activities, which may protect against cognitive decline. The present study outlines how individuals believe grandparenthood has impacted their cognitive abilities in late life.  We asked 127 grandparents (87 grandmothers and 40 grandfathers) how they thought grandparenthood had impacted their mental ability (memory, concentration, and cognitive ability). An exploratory thematic analysis utilizing a codebook approach was conducted on the participant responses.  Analysis revealed four major themes among the responses: “grandparenthood as a continuous experience that promotes healthy cognitive functioning”, “shifting perspectives”, “limited interaction”, and “the negative impacts of grandparenthood.” Discussion A majority of grandparents expressed the belief that interacting with their grandchildren is beneficial to their cognition. However, some participants qualified grandparenthood as a stressful experience that has negatively impacted their cognitive health. These findings support previous literature showing both cognitive benefits associated with grandparental caregiving and negative cognitive outcomes that may result from the stress of caregiving.

archiveRecords.title: Latent Structures of Social Determinants of Health in Later Life: A Comparison of U.S.-Born and Immigrants
archiveRecords.abstract: This study examined whether the latent structure of social determinants of health (SDOH) differs by nativity and how they relate to health outcomes in later life.  Using 2016–2018 HRS data, exploratory factor analyses by nativity were conducted, followed by nativity-stratified regressions linking SDOH factors to health outcomes.  Four comparable factors emerged in both groups: neighborhood environment, interpersonal stressors, socioeconomic resources, and family support. Loading patterns showed modest nativity differences: among immigrants, social isolation aligned more strongly with family support than socioeconomic resources and perceived discrimination loaded weakly on interpersonal stressors. Interpersonal stressors were associated with poorer mental and cognitive health in both groups; socioeconomic resources were associated with better health outcomes but more weakly among immigrants. Associations of neighborhood environment and family support with health varied by nativity. Discussion Findings indicate substantial commonality in SDOH structures alongside suggestive nativity-related differences, warranting replication in larger immigrant samples.

archiveRecords.title: Control Beliefs and Emotional Aspects of Psychological Frailty Among Couples in Later Life
archiveRecords.abstract: This study investigated the associations between control beliefs and the emotional aspects of psychological frailty (i.e., depression, anxiety, and loneliness) among older married couples.  Multivariate Actor-Partner Interdependence Models were used to analyze data from 538 couples aged 65 or older, drawn from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study.  Individuals’ own control beliefs were consistently associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, and loneliness for both spouses. A partner effect emerged for loneliness, with wives’ control beliefs associated with lower levels of loneliness in their husbands, but this was not significant after adjusting for marital support and strain. Discussion These findings identify control beliefs as a consistent individual-level protective factor. Interventions to improve emotional well-being in older couples should prioritize strengthening personal control beliefs. Dyadic processes merit further investigation, particularly for outcomes such as loneliness that are closely embedded in the relational context.

archiveRecords.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

archiveRecords.title: Does the Pilot Long-Term Care Insurance Work as Expected in China? Examining its Impact on Hospital Utilizations, Medical Expenses, and Health
archiveRecords.abstract: This study investigates the impact of long-term care insurance (LTCI) on older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Using national representative data from four waves of CHARLS (2011, 2013, 2015, 2018), we find that LTCI decreases older adults’ monthly outpatient visits but is associated with an increase in both annual inpatient stays and inpatient medical expenses. Further evidence suggests that older adults covered by the pilot LTCI program have better health status compared to their counterparts in non-pilot cities. Overall, findings offer empirical support for the role of the LTCI program in Chinese older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Findings of China’s LTCI may offer insights for other countries with a large aging population but with no feasible LTCI framework.

archiveRecords.title: Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) and Cognition: A Scoping Review
archiveRecords.abstract: To map the evidence of disparities in cognition across different social determinants of health (SDOH), examine how SDOH are measured in the context of research on cognitive outcomes and identify knowledge gaps. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched. We included peer-reviewed studies of adults that examined SDOH as primary exposures in relation to cognitive outcomes, and described a SDOH framework or definition in the context of cognition. Non-human studies, case reports, case series, editorials, protocols, and -only records were excluded. Ninety-one records were included. Most of the included studies were conducted in the US and the most frequently used framework was the Healthy People (2030) framework. Among studies examining a single SDOH indicator, the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) was the most used measure. Most of the existing research failed to explain the concept of SDOH and lacked a framework to guide the inclusion and interpretation of SDOH indicators. SDOH measures were heterogeneous across studies, with many examining only a single indicator and limited use of multidimensional approaches. This heterogeneity made findings challenging to compare. More research is needed on multidimensional SDOH and cognition in various racial/ethnic groups and less-studied geographic and cultural contexts, under explicit SDOH frameworks.

archiveRecords.title: Deprescribing Fall Risk–Increasing Drugs in Older Adults: Implementation Challenges and a Conceptual Framework from the DeFRID Trial and Global Evidence
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Deprescribing fall risk–increasing drugs (FRIDs) is essential for reducing polypharmacy and falls in older adults, yet randomized controlled trials (RCTs) face unique implementation challenges. The DeFRID study is an ongoing multi-center RCT evaluating an ARMOR-based deprescribing intervention versus usual care in adults aged ≥60 years prescribed FRIDs. The  of this review are threefold: (1) to describe practical challenges encountered during a multi-center deprescribing RCT in India; (2) to propose a conceptual framework for categorizing these barriers; and (3) to contextualize DeFRID's experience within the broader deprescribing research landscape.  We conducted a narrative review with systematic scoping elements, synthesizing global RCT evidence from PubMed, OpenAlex, and Google Scholar (inception–December 2025) with DeFRID process evaluation data. DeFRID barriers and facilitators were identified via mixed- (clinician KAP questionnaire and qualitative interviews), team meetings, retention logs, and Phase II RCT implementation data, thematically categorized, then compared with global RCT challenges.  DeFRID implementation revealed four challenge categories: ethical–clinical difficulties establishing equipoise for FRID withdrawal; operational barriers to recruitment and retention; methodological complexities in fall outcome ascertainment; and context-specific constraints unique to the Indian LMIC setting—limited deprescribing guidelines, polypharmacy normalization, fragmented care coordination, and hierarchical decision-making. Global RCTs revealed substantial implementation challenges: low clinician adherence, short follow-up periods, restrictive eligibility excluding frail or cognitively impaired older adults, and resource-intensive interventions limiting scalability.  Deprescribing FRIDs in older adults is impeded by ethical, operational, methodological, and provider-patient challenges, necessitating multilevel strategies integrating training, shared decision-making, context-specific guidelines, and stakeholder engagement for scalable implementation.

archiveRecords.title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of  impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.  This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.  We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.  Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and F 1 -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns.  A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.

archiveRecords.title: Blind giving predicts longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility in later life
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Financial fraud is a common and consequential threat among older adults, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 4% to 17% annually. Although cognitive decline has been widely studied as a risk factor, less is known about behavioral characteristics that may predict changes in scam susceptibility. In the present study, we examined whether blind giving predicted trajectories of scam susceptibility across a two-year period and whether this association differed as a function of age. Research Design and  One hundred and sixteen cognitively unimpaired older adults (aged 51 to 83; 72% female) completed a behavioral economic measure of blind giving at baseline and a self-report measure of scam susceptibility annually across three visits.  Linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant interaction between time, blind giving, and age (p = .022), such that greater baseline blind giving was associated with increasing scam susceptibility over time among relatively older participants, whereas scam susceptibility remained stable across levels of blind giving among relatively younger participants. Blind giving was not associated with scam susceptibility at baseline (p = .515), and the longitudinal association persisted after separately adjusting for global cognition, socioeconomic status, and race (all ps ≤ .026).  Greater blind giving predicted longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility over a two-year period, with this pattern observed specifically in advanced age. These findings suggest that prosocial tendencies may become maladaptive in later life, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk individuals to inform prevention efforts in aging populations.

archiveRecords.title: Vulnerability intersections: an integrative conceptual framework for understanding vulnerability in AI-assisted care for older adults
archiveRecords.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.

archiveRecords.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

archiveRecords.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
archiveRecords.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

archiveRecords.title: Heat stress and coping strategies among older adults in three Sunbelt cities in the United States
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Prevailing scientific evidence suggests that extreme heat poses a substantial threat to the health and well-being of older adults in the Sunbelt cities of the United States. However, prior research has not adequately addressed the specific socio-demographic, health-related vulnerabilities, and coping-strategic factors influencing heat stress among older urban populations.  Informed by the Socio-Ecological Model, this study adopts a retrospective cohort study design to investigate the predictors and experiences of heat stress among older adults. Data from older adults in Los Angeles, Houston, and Phoenix were analyzed using thematic and multiple binary logistic regression analyses.  The  reveal that much older adults (aged 80 +) were less likely to experience heat stress compared to their relatively younger counterparts. Also, marital status, income, respiratory diseases, physical activity, taking cool showers, and city of residence were significantly associated with a higher risk of suffering heat stress. The qualitative  uncovered individual-level behavioural adjustment as an effective coping mechanism during extreme heat events.  These  underscore the complex interplay of behavioral, socio-demographic, and health-related factors influencing heat stress among older adults. The study recommends that urban health strategies prioritize these demographics, enhancing support systems and coping mechanisms to reduce vulnerability to heat stress among older urban populations.

archiveRecords.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.

archiveRecords.title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort
archiveRecords.abstract: Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.  This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.  This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.  At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.  Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

archiveRecords.title: Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Low vitamin D and B12 levels are linked to low self-reported sleep quality and conditions comorbid with sleep disturbances in older adults. We examined the associations between serum vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep indices in middle-aged and older adults.  We studied 460 participants aged 40 and older (70.9 ± 12.0 [SD] years; 52.8% female; 22.2% Black) in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Predictors included total serum vitamin D and B12, sleep outcomes included total sleep time (TST, minutes), sleep efficiency (SE, %), sleep onset latency (minutes), wake after sleep onset (WASO, minutes), and average wake bout length (WBL, minutes). We examined race and sex as effect modifiers of associations between vitamins and sleep.  Higher vitamin D concentration was associated with longer TST (B = 23.63 minutes, 95% CI, 9.62-37.64) and shorter WBL (B = −0.29 minutes, 95% CI, −0.50 to −0.09). Vitamin D deficiency was associated with shorter TST (B= −23.03 minutes, 95% CI, −42.05 to −4.01). The associations between vitamin D and sleep were stronger among Black participants. Higher B12 was associated with shorter WASO in women but longer WASO in men. B12 insufficiency/deficiency was associated with longer TST in men but shorter TST in women.  Higher vitamin D levels are associated with longer and less disturbed sleep in middle-aged and older adults. Future studies are needed to understand if maintaining optimal vitamin D levels improve sleep quality and promote better sleep-associated health outcomes.

archiveRecords.title: Planetary health diet adherence and frailty in older adults: evidence from the Seniors-ENRICA cohorts
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Frailty is a major determinant of disability and adverse outcomes in older adults. The Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a plant-based dietary pattern promoting environmental sustainability, has been associated with lower mortality and reduced chronic disease risk. We examined the association between adherence to the Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) and frailty over time using repeated frailty assessments.  Data came from two cohorts of community-dwelling older adults: Seniors-ENRICA-1 (2008-2015; ≥60 years; n = 3289) and Seniors-ENRICA-2 (2015-2023; ≥65 years; n = 3273). Baseline diet was assessed using a validated diet history, and adherence to the PHD was assessed using the PHDI (0-140), based on 15 food groups. Frailty was defined by the Fried phenotype (≥3 criteria of exhaustion, low physical activity, slow gait, muscle weakness, and unintentional weight loss). Generalized estimating equation (GEE) models estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for frailty across PHDI tertiles, adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors.  Higher PHDI adherence was consistently associated with lower odds of frailty over time. Comparing highest versus lowest tertiles, multivariable-adjusted ORs (95% CI) were 0.62 (0.42, 0.92) in Seniors-ENRICA-1, 0.40 (0.24, 0.65) in Seniors-ENRICA-2, and 0.52 (0.38, 0.70) in the pooled analyses. Higher PHDI adherence was primarily associated with lower odds of low physical activity, while vegetables and fruits showed the strongest independent associations among individual PHDI components.  Greater PHDI adherence is associated with lower odds of frailty in older Spanish adults, supporting the potential role of sustainable, plant-based dietary patterns for healthy aging.

archiveRecords.title: Replicating the RISE-APS Elder Abuse and Self-Neglect Intervention Model in new contexts: A pre-implementation analysis
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Elder abuse and self-neglect (EASN) remain pervasive phenomena, yet intervention research is limited. Adult Protective Services (APS) plays a central role, but statutory timelines and resource constraints make long-term follow-up difficult. RISE was developed to fill this systems gap as a complement to APS, extending support beyond the investigative phase. Initial implementation of the RISE-APS model at the state level in Maine demonstrated feasibility, acceptability, and improvement in case outcomes. Building on these findings, the present study examines the pre-implementation phase of replicating this model in three new U.S. sites serving different communities to identify implementation determinants likely to shape integration. Research Design and  We conducted six focus groups with 25 managers from APS and partnering community-based organizations housing RISE in three U.S. states. Transcripts underwent reflexive thematic analysis guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR).  Participants noted strong philosophical compatibility between RISE and existing practices. However, structural constraints, including bureaucratic bottlenecks and APS staffing instability, could impede delivery. The warm handoff was viewed as central to engagement, yet sometimes unrealistic given resource constraints or limited time available to build APS-client rapport. Furthermore, while broad service networks may ease initial integration, dedicated partnership maintenance is required to sustain referral flow.  Findings highlight the organizational conditions and partnership infrastructure necessary to support replication of the RISE-APS model. Feasibility relies not only on philosophical alignment but on adapting workflows to withstand turnover, resource limitations, and structural constraints across varying service systems.

archiveRecords.title: Re-Examining Age-Friendly Communities for Older People with Insecure Housing Histories
archiveRecords.abstract: In many countries, population aging and increasing rates of housing security among older people are unfolding simultaneously. While the World Health Organization's Age-Friendly Cities and Communities (AFCC) framework is largely considered the leading framework for developing age-supportive communities, it does not adequately account for the ways in which a community may be inclusive, supportive, or age-friendly for older people with lived experience of housing insecurity. This paper began with a question: What would an age-friendly community look like for older people with experiences of housing insecurity? Drawing on the Aging in the Right Place (AIRP) framework, a rights-based conceptual model of six indicators developed through community-based participatory research, this paper re-examines and extends each of the WHO AFCC framework's eight domains: housing, transportation, social participation, respect and social inclusion, civic participation, communication and information, community support and health services, and outdoor spaces and buildings. This paper argues that age-friendly approaches must recognize housing as a human right and housing security as a cornerstone of age-friendly communities, requiring protections including rent control, eviction prevention, and incentives for non-market housing development. Recommendations are offered for municipalities seeking to embed AIRP and rights-based perspectives into age-friendly strategies and evaluation.

archiveRecords.title: Scaling Caregiver Health and Wellbeing Coaching: A Mixed Methods Evaluation of Implementation and Sustainment in the Veterans Health Administration
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Effective and sustainable support for family caregivers is a growing priority, yet practical guidance for scaling promising coaching interventions into routine practice is limited. The  of this evaluation was to identify organizational determinants, barriers, facilitators, and adaptations affecting national implementation of the Caregiver Health and Wellbeing Coaching (CHWC) program in the Veterans Health Administration. Research Design and  An explanatory, sequential mixed‑ design included surveys of CHWC staff (n = 53) and qualitative interviews (n = 14), guided by the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, its Outcomes Addendum, and the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications‑Enhanced.  Successful implementation—defined as program launch and delivery to at least one caregiver at each site—and successful sustainment—defined as ongoing or expanding delivery to new and returning caregivers—were associated with thorough planning, leadership engagement, and flexible delivery. Barriers included staff turnover, complex documentation, and challenges recruiting caregivers. Facilitators and process improvements were rapidly integrated into program operations.  Findings can inform strategies to scale caregiver support programs that underpin sustainable aging and long-term care systems.

archiveRecords.title: Exploring Experiences of Disempowerment in Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Study
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Disempowerment in the context of chronic illness refers to the state of dissatisfaction with diminishing opportunities to control personal lives, potentially leading to disengagement in health management and negative health outcomes. However, the experiences and perceptions of disempowerment in chronic illness among older adults are not fully understood. This study aims to explore the experiences and perceptions of disempowerment in older adults with chronic illness. Research Design and  Qualitative description was employed. From January to March 2025, individual face-to-face semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 Cantonese-speaking older adults with chronic illness. Template analysis was used.  Three themes emerged regarding the experiences of disempowerment: (1) confusion and uncertainty amid unexpected changes and unclear information, (2) struggles to manage their health in the way they would like, and (3) difficulty in living the life they had before or had hoped for. Negative feelings towards the experiences were also identified with indirect expression to others. The causes included: (1) irreversibly declining health and intrinsic capacity, (2) unmet expectations, and (3) age discrimination. The consequences involved: (1) disengaging the context of disempowerment by suppressing negative emotions, distancing themselves from care partners, and trying to overcome the situation, followed by (2) accepting or despairing over time.  This study revealed the experiences and perceptions, causes and consequences of disempowerment in older adults with chronic illness. The tendency to indirectly express or suppress the negative feelings underscores a need for tailored strategies to better assess and address disempowerment in this population.

archiveRecords.title: Impact of a Geriatric Co-management Service on Surgical Cancer Care for Older Adults
archiveRecords.abstract: In 2011, Brown University Health’s Division of Geriatrics started its inaugural geriatric co-management service to improve older adult (OA) care for patients with hip fractures. Its success in care and cost reduction prompted the health system to expand geriatric co-management. Meanwhile, oncology surgeons treat increasingly older and frailer patients due to improved therapies and survival. The literature established what we saw here: increased mortality and complications in frail OA and failure of strategies like Enhanced Recovery After Surgery and Prehabilitation. In 2021, the division launched an oncologic surgery co-management program. Explicit to its launch, hospital sponsors required a 2-year study for benchmarks and quality metrics with a primary outcome of reducing mortality and delirium. QI metrics were developed through PowerBI dashboards using hospital and EMR data, analyzing 4,359 cases, which measured length of stay (LOS), readmissions, mortality, and disposition, from July 2018 to August 2024. We compared outcomes between the pilot (Geri) and those with no geriatric involvement (UC) using 1:1 propensity score matching. Bivariate analyses used chi-square and Student’s t-tests for descriptive comparisons and multivariate linear or logistic regression analyses for outcome rates and adjusted when appropriate. The matched sample consisted of 309 cases in each group. 14% were underrepresented minorities. The Geri group had a lower odds ratio (OR) for hospice or in-hospital mortality (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.12–0.61, p = 0.0016), as well as significantly lower odds of delirium, measured by a positive CAM (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.11–0.73, p = 0.0086). ICU admission was lower in the geri group, although not statistically significant (18 vs 25, p = 0.0690). Overall hospital length of stay was longer in the geri group (8.2 ± 15.4 vs. 6.2 ± 5.6 days, p = 0.0350). Geri patients were less likely to be discharged home (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33–0.77) but were more likely to be discharged to a skilled nursing facility (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.43–3.53) or inpatient rehabilitation facility (OR 8.52, 95% CI 1.04–69.6). : Geriatric co-management in surgical oncology significantly reduced mortality and delirium as measured by CAM among OA, demonstrating meaningful improvements in patient outcomes. Although LOS increased and home discharges decreased, these  may indicate more appropriate discharge planning for this patient population. Geriatric co-management represents a critical, evidence-based component of surgical oncology care for OA. This study adds to the growing evidence supporting the role of Geriatric Medicine in improving the quality of care for OA.

archiveRecords.title: The role of lifestyle medicine in shaping and supporting successful aging
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Within gerontology, various theoretical perspectives on what it means to age successfully have emerged over recent decades and garnered empirical support. Similarly, within medicine and related healthcare fields, research and practice have focused on healthy living in terms of physical health, mental health, and well-being. In recent years, the practice of Lifestyle Medicine (nutrition, physical activity, stress management, restorative sleep, social connection, and avoidance of risky substances) has emerged to describe the role of such lifestyle factors in health.  The present article proposes a pathway to integrate lifestyle medicine with successful aging. We take a holistic approach to develop a model that merges the foundational pillars of lifestyle medicine with the principles of successful aging.  This new approach to exploring the linkages between the principles of lifestyle medicine and the essential components of successful aging highlights how proactive behavioral health strategies related to nutrition, exercise, sleep, stress, and substances could play a role in fostering optimal aging in cognitive and physical functioning and disease prevention, thereby potentially yielding more positive outcomes for aging well.

archiveRecords.title: Cigarette and e-cigarette tax effects on the oldest generation of smokers in the United States
archiveRecords.abstract: and  As cigarette smoking continues to decline among youth and young adults, smoking rates among older U.S. adults remain unchanged. Historically, cigarette and, more recently, e-cigarette tax policies influenced smoking behavior in younger smokers. This study examined how older smokers respond to tax changes to inform public health strategies. Research Design and  Our data combined a panel of state cigarette and standardized e-cigarette tax rates with individual-level survey microdata. Our sample included adults aged ≥65, with and without a history of smoking. We estimated two-way fixed-effects population-weighted regression models of current smoking and past-year quit attempts. Exploratory subgroup analyses tested for heterogeneity by education and income level.  Among 3,117,382 adults, 48% had a history of smoking; of whom 18% currently smoked. A $1.00 cigarette tax increase was associated with current smoking: est. = -0.56 percentage points (pp) (CI: -0.85, -0.27). A $0.10 increase in e-cigarette tax (open) was associated with current smoking (+0.28 pp; CI: 0.01, 0.55). Approaching tax parity by one dollar was associated with a 0.48-pp (CI: 0.20, 0.76) increase in current smoking. While varied by socioeconomic status, there was no association between cigarette/e-cigarette taxes and quit attempts.  For older U.S. adults, cigarette taxes were associated with lower smoking, whereas e-cigarette taxes were associated with higher smoking. The type of e-cigarette tax appears important for tobacco control in older smokers. Policies increasing the relative cost of e-cigarettes may perpetuate smoking rates in older populations at the highest risk of smoking-related harm.

archiveRecords.title: Study design and results of the Wave VI Add Health Cognitive Assessment, Physical, and Sensory Function (Add CAPS) protocol
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: The goal of the Add Health Cognitive Assessment, Physical, and Sensory Function (Add CAPS) protocol was to establish a comprehensive, nationally representative assessment of cognitive, physical, and sensory function in early midlife to support longitudinal and life course Alzheimer’s disease risk research. We developed the Add CAPS, a comprehensive and multidimensional assessment battery in Wave VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health).  We describe protocol implementation and examine the distribution of cognitive, physical, and sensory measures by age, sex, and educational attainment in Add Health Wave VI.  Among participants who completed the survey, response rates were approximately 85% for digital cognitive assessments and 94% for interviewer-administered cognitive, physical, and hearing measures. Participants with complete Add CAPS data had a mean age of 44.2 years. Cognitive performance varied by age, education, and sex. Younger participants and those with higher educational attainment had better cognitive performance scores across assessments. Participants who were male, older, and had lower educational attainment had poorer hearing. There were no age differences in grip strength, but it did vary by educational attainment. Survey-reported cognitive and physical challenges were common. Discussion The Add CAPS Protocol fills a critical gap by providing robust measures of cognitive, physical, and sensory function earlier in the adult life course than most nationally representative aging studies. These data will support future research on aging trajectories and health in the U.S. population.

archiveRecords.title: Novel place-based socio-contextual measures in Add Health for aging researchers: characteristics and methodological considerations
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: We introduce comprehensive, multilevel, time-varying contextual indicators linked to the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), describe Black–White differences in their distributions and trends across the early life course, and provide methodological considerations for using these new data.  Contextual indicators spanning housing and credit market, political, criminal-legal, cultural climate, and historical domains at various geographic levels were compiled from external data sources and merged to Add Health respondents’ state, county, census tract, and block group locations across Waves I–V (1994–2018), capturing exposures from adolescence (ages 12–20) through early midlife (ages 33–42). Descriptive statistics for each indicator—overall and by race (Black and White)—are presented alongside temporal trends.  Substantial and persistent Black–White disparities were observed across domains and waves. Relative to White respondents, Black respondents were more likely to reside in counties characterized by higher eviction rates, greater racialized economic segregation, elevated housing cost burden, higher incarceration rates, and more hate crime incidents. Black respondents also lived in states with greater historical lynching violence. Methodological considerations presented include data source-level characteristics (e.g., data collection procedures and coverage) and measure-specific considerations. Discussion By linking comprehensive place-based socio-contextual measures to Add Health’s rich biological, demographic, behavioral, and psychosocial data spanning critical developmental periods, and a new battery of cognitive, physical, and sensory function in midlife, researchers can identify life course pathways of aging inequalities and inform interventions to reduce trends and disparities in healthy aging in American society.

archiveRecords.title: Feeling younger or older? How life events reshape subjective age among Chinese older adults
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Subjective age is a construct that displays considerable individual variability. This study, conducted within the Chinese context, investigates how major life events affect older adults’ subjective age, measured by felt age and look age, and the moderating effects of chronological age and community services for older adults.  We used a nationally representative sample of older adults aged 60 and over from three waves (collected in 2018, 2020, and 2023) of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey. Fixed-effects models were employed to examine how negative events (e.g., serious illness or death of a relative/friend) and positive events (e.g., a child’s marriage or childbearing) impact subjective age. Random-effects models were conducted for robustness checks.  The findings indicate that experiencing negative events is associated with an older subjective age by approximately 1.3% or 1 year. In contrast, witnessing positive events reduces their felt age and look age by roughly 0.9% or 0.6 years and 1.2% or 0.9 years, respectively. The negative impact of adverse events on subjective age intensifies with chronological age, whereas the rejuvenating effect of positive events attenuates. The availability of community services for older adults significantly reduces the impact of both negative and positive life events. Discussion The  highlight the complex relationship between life events and subjective age, suggesting that supportive environments can buffer older adults from the psychological effects of life transitions.

archiveRecords.title: Mode effects for Add Health in transition from in-person to mixed mode
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: As longitudinal panel surveys face escalating costs, many are transitioning from traditional in-person interviews to mixed-mode designs. While essential for fiscal sustainability, this shift creates a methodological challenge: distinguishing genuine longitudinal change from measurement effects introduced by the change in mode. This study evaluated the impact of this transition within the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) as the cohort entered midlife.  Utilizing Wave VI data and a randomized split-sample design (in which the eligible sample was randomly divided between a new web-first mixed-mode protocol [Sample 1] and an in-person control replicating the legacy survey protocol [Sample 2]), the study estimated the differential mode effect, capturing cross-sectional differences between the two designs. Subsequently, a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) was applied across Waves III–VI to decompose these design effects into mode-specific measurement error and residual nonresponse components.  Concerns regarding systemic declines in data quality were largely unfounded; the mixed-mode design outperformed the traditional in-person design in measurement accuracy. However, significant mode effects were identified for some items, particularly sensitive health outcomes and stigmatized behaviors, driven by distinct combinations of measurement error and differential nonresponse. Discussion Because these differences can inadvertently mimic or obscure actual aging trends, researchers should screen variables for mode sensitivity and incorporate appropriate adjustments, such as a mode or design indicator, inverse propensity weighting, or HMM-based decomposition, in longitudinal analyses, ensuring that “signals” of aging are not obscured by survey redesign.

archiveRecords.title: Asymmetric behavioral responses to changes in subjective survival expectations: Implications for health investment in later life
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Subjective survival probability (SSP) is a key predictor of economic and health decisions in later life, yet existing research assumes that gains and losses in survival expectations have symmetric behavioral effects. This study examines how within-person changes in SSP are associated with health-promoting behaviors among middle-aged and older adults in South Korea.  Using ten waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2006-2024), we estimate individual fixed-effects models on an analytic sample of 65,069 person-wave observations from 10,878 individuals aged 45 and older. We extend the standard symmetric model by adopting an asymmetric fixed-effects framework, which decomposes cumulative SSP increases and decreases into separate parameters.  The symmetric model shows that a one-unit increase in SSP (on a 0-10 scale) is associated with a 0.69 percentage-point increase in regular exercise, after controlling for self-rated health, chronic diseases, functional limitations, and socioeconomic characteristics. The asymmetric decomposition reveals two distinct patterns: exercise responds exclusively to SSP losses (loss-only), while paid health checkups respond only to SSP gains (gain-only). Formal symmetry tests reject equal absolute effects for both outcomes (p Discussion These findings provide evidence that associations between changing survival expectations and health behaviors may be asymmetric. The domain-specific nature of these asymmetries—loss-only disengagement in exercise and gain-only investment in preventive care—suggests that interventions targeting middle-aged and older adults may benefit from considering potentially different mechanisms linking survival expectations to behavior across outcome domains.

archiveRecords.title: Intergenerational differences and similarities in economic well-being, family context, health, and life experiences among older adult parents and their middle-aged children: data from the Add Health and Add Health Parent Studies
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: We examined the strength of intergenerational associations between midlife adults in Add Health and their Baby Boomer parents from the Add Health Parent Study (AHPS) across numerous substantive domains.  Using linked data from AHPS Phase 1 (2015–2017), a subset of parents of Add Health respondents, with new Add Health Wave VI data, we estimated intergenerational correlations between each cohort’s socioeconomic status (e.g., income, economic insecurity, and educational attainment); family context (e.g., union formation, time/money transfers, and psychological traits); health (e.g., mental, physical, and behavioral); and life experiences (e.g., social integration). We harmonized measures across the two generations and estimated either Pearson (r) or polychoric (ρ) correlations depending on the level of measurement. Intergenerational correlations were further contrasted by sex, the biological relationship of the parent-child dyad, and educational attainment.  The largest correlations were found within socioeconomic and health domains, with significant correlations found for food insecurity (ρ = 0.52), educational attainment (r = 0.42), diabetes (ρ = 0.41), and obesity (ρ = 0.37). We found more significant and larger correlations for biological parent-child dyads and parent-daughter dyads. Few educational grades in intergenerational correlations were significant (e.g., health behavior and social integration). Discussion Intergenerational correlations are stronger when there is a known shared genetic component in outcomes such as health and health behavior, but shared environments also play an important role for socioeconomic outcomes. Intergenerational similarities in advantage for the higher educated and disadvantage for the less educated are evident. Small sample sizes precluded analysis by race/ethnicity; however, AHPS Phase 2 data (2026–2027) will fill that research gap.

archiveRecords.title: Laboratory methods and quality assurance in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health Waves V and VI
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Gerontological and population health sciences increasingly emphasize life-course, biosocial frameworks linking social environments to biological aging and disease processes, for which high-quality biological data are essential. We report on the collection, assay, and quality of aging-related biomarkers in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) Waves V and VI.  Staff collected blood specimens during in-home health exams, processed them locally, and shipped them to the lab for further processing, assay completion, and archiving. Analytes assessed cardiovascular disease risk, glucose homeostasis, lipids, renal function, hepatic injury, inflammation, immune system processes, and neurodegeneration. Inter-assay coefficients of variation (CVs) were estimated for sample sets. In 2% of participants, a duplicate specimen was collected within 2 weeks and assays repeated; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were calculated to assess short-term reliability.  Wave V collected blood from 92% of 5,381 participants who completed the exam (mean age 38); Wave VI collected blood from 91% of 6,073 participants (mean age 44). Reliability was excellent (ICC ≥ 0.75) and highest for hemoglobin A1c at Waves V–VI and GFAP and HSV and SARS-CoV-2 serologies at Wave VI. Reliability was fair to good (ICC 0.40 to Discussion High-quality biological data from Add Health Waves V and VI greatly expand the study’s capacity to support life-course, biosocial research.

archiveRecords.title: Add Health becomes an aging study: conceptualization, history and Wave VI design, response, and descriptive health data
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: This paper describes the history and previous research contributions of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) and provides an overview of the recently completed Wave VI (average age 44 years) design and content. We provide a comparison of basic Wave VI data with two major U.S. cross-sectional health studies. We then report descriptive distributions for several survey-based health measures in Wave VI, both for the overall cohort as well as for subgroups. Finally, we discuss ways that Add Health data can be used to make important contributions to the study of health and aging in the U.S. population.  Wave VI utilized a mixed-mode (web and in-person) survey design, with follow-up home examinations to collect biological data. Using weighted Wave VI survey data, we provide descriptive distributions of selected early midlife health measures by race/ethnicity, educational attainment, and sex.  Wave VI yielded 11,979 surveys, 6,073 home examinations, and thousands of contextual, environmental, and administrative variables. Self-reported survey data demonstrate the cohort’s relatively poor health, including nearly one-half with a body mass index above 30 kg/m2 and 17% reporting current depression. There are wide disparities by race/ethnicity and educational attainment in every assessed health outcome. Discussion Wave VI of Add Health broke new ground in transforming a study of U.S. adolescents and young adults into a study of early midlife adults. These rich longitudinal, multi-level (i.e., social, biological, and contextual), nationally representative data are a key resource for understanding health and aging in American society.

archiveRecords.title: Internalizing active aging norms: Self-attributed responsibility as a mediator linking prescriptive views on aging to late-life preparation
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
authors: M Clara P de Paula Couto
archiveRecords.abstract: Older adults face prescriptive expectations about aging, including active aging norms emphasizing physical activity, social engagement, and autonomy. While previous research has linked active aging norms to health-related and social behaviors, no studies to date have examined whether and how these norms are related to proactive, future-oriented behaviors such as late-life preparation. Drawing on theories of norm internalization, this study examines self-attributed responsibility for aging preparation as a mediator linking active aging norms to late-life preparation.  Data were drawn from the Ageing as Future project and included 1,003 participants aged 34 to 90 years (M = 58.82 years; 52% female). Late-life preparation was assessed using two complementary indicators: a count-based checklist of concrete preparatory behaviors and a continuous scale of perceived preparatory engagement. Mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS models, with Poisson regression-based mediation applied to the behavioral count outcome.  Across both indicators, stronger endorsement of active aging norms was associated with greater engagement in late-life preparation. These associations were partially mediated by perceived responsibility, indicating that individuals endorsing active aging norms more strongly were more likely to perceive preparation as their own responsibility, which was itself associated with higher preparatory engagement. Discussion The findings suggest that active aging norms are associated with late-life preparation in part through a greater sense of personal obligation to manage one’s own aging process, highlighting the role of norm internalization and perceived responsibility in translating prescriptive views of aging into proactive behavior.

archiveRecords.title: Midlife in crisis? Life course pathways to health at midlife across U.S. cohorts
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Recent trends of increasing midlife morbidity and mortality and widening educational disparities in the United States are concerning. This study documented the age pattern and educational disparities in health in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) cohort as they enter midlife, and situates the cohort relative to preceding, similar, and following cohorts in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).  Using data from Add Health and NHANES on 6 birth cohorts observed from adolescence to middle age, we characterized age patterns in general health, mental health, health behaviors, and chronic conditions within and across cohorts. We documented disparities by educational attainment, focusing on those with and without a 4-year college degree, and how such disparities emerge and evolve across the life course.  Analysis showed that general health, mental health, and chronic disease deteriorated for the Add Health cohort as they aged into midlife, while health behaviors improved. Compared to the NHANES cohorts, the Add Health cohort had worse health than older cohorts, generally worse health compared to the same birth cohort, with some exceptions, and mixed health compared to younger cohorts. Educational gradients were relatively stable across age, with some evidence of increases, while educational gradients generally increased across cohorts. Discussion The worsening health of the Add Health cohort with age and relative to previous cohorts has important implications for aging, as this currently midlife cohort of U.S. adults will enter old age in worse health than their predecessors.

archiveRecords.title: Family structure and transitions into and out of homeboundness: Evidence from the National Health and Aging Trends Study, 2011–2024
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Homebound status refers to needing assistance or an assistive device to leave home, being normally unable to leave home, or experiencing leaving home as a major effort. This study examines transitions into and out of homeboundness and whether family structure is associated with these transitions, with attention to gender differences.  Using National Health and Aging Trends Study data from 2011–2024, transition probabilities across four states—independent, homebound, nursing home residence, and deceased—were estimated using an unadjusted continuous-time homogeneous Markov model. Multinomial logistic regression models then assessed associations between family structure and subsequent transitions, including gender interactions.  Among respondents who were independent, 84.6% remained independent, and 12.2% became homebound by the next wave. Among those who were homebound, 23.6% returned to independence, 60.1% remained homebound, 2.4% entered nursing home residence, and 13.9% died. Family structure may shape pathways into homeboundness, institutional care, and death, with implications for aging in place.

archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: U.S.-based Latino older adult populations face disproportionate barriers to accessing behavioral health services. We examined associations between multifaceted mental illness stigma and help-seeking from different sources of behavioral health supports among understudied Latino older adults with behavioral health problems.  Data come from a cross-sectional survey that included U.S.-based Latino residents ages 50-86 (N=274; 2021). The survey measured mental illness biopsychosocial causal beliefs, treatment efficacy beliefs, and social rejection beliefs as multiple facets of mental illness stigma that may influence mental and physical health help-seeking behaviors from four sources: traditional media, online/digital media, family/friends, and healthcare providers. Linear regression models examined associations between each stigma component and each help-seeking outcome, adjusting for personal/family factors in the full sample of Latino older adults and among a subsample reporting a self/familial behavioral health problem (n=173). archiveRecords.title: Social disconnection and cognitive aging across the life course: coordinated longitudinal analysis of three national cohort studies
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: This study aims to better understand the effect of social disconnection on cognitive aging regarding its life course variation, temporal dynamics, and multidimensionality.  We conducted coordinated data analysis of three large U.S. population-based longitudinal cohort panels (Add Health I–VI, MIDUS 1–3, and HRS 2006–2020) consisting of 18,553 individuals aged 11+. We harmonized measures of longitudinal patterns of social isolation and loneliness (never/transient/persistent), episodic memory (word recalls), and working memory (backward digit span and serial 7’s) across datasets. We estimated growth curve models to assess prospective associations of social isolation and loneliness with subsequent memory trajectories from adolescence to old adulthood.  We found strong detrimental effects of social isolation in both young and older adulthood and loneliness in older adulthood on memory function. Longer (particularly persistent) exposures to isolation and loneliness predicted poorer memory test scores. These effects were attenuated but largely remained significant after adjusting for sociodemographic, behavioral, and health risk factors. Social isolation and loneliness show weaker and less consistent associations with the rate of memory decline across the life course samples. Discussion Comparative life course research helped to elucidate the complex relationship between social disconnection and memory change and inform the timing and duration of cognitive impacts of  and subjective social disconnection. Interventions to promote healthy aging should focus on reducing the chronicity of isolation starting early in life and feelings of loneliness in later life. Future research should include additional longitudinal data to further investigate links between cognition, social disconnection, and underlying mechanisms.

archiveRecords.title: The ethno-racial patterning of depression and loneliness: new evidence from a diverse cohort of U.S. midlife adults
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Mental health is a central concern for aging and well-being over the life course. This study examined ethno-racial patterns of depressive symptoms and loneliness among a diverse cohort of U.S. midlife adults to illuminate why some individuals age more successfully than others. Drawing on the Stress Process Model, we investigated whether these patterns persist after accounting for socioeconomic and relational stressors and social support resources.  We used new Wave VI data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health). Descriptive statistics and negative binomial regression were employed to document ethno-racial variation in depressive symptoms and loneliness among this cohort of midlife U.S. adults (N = 11,435; ages 39–50).  Multiracial adults initially reported slightly higher depressive symptoms and loneliness relative to White adults, but these differences were attenuated with adjustment for stressors and social support. Black adults exhibited poorer mental health than White adults descriptively, but better outcomes after adjusting for stressors and social support. Hispanic adults reported lower levels of depressive symptoms and loneliness than White adults net of sociodemographic covariates. Asian adults demonstrated no statistically significant differences from White adults. Discussion Ethno-racial groups each display unique mental health patterns in midlife, possibly reflecting differences in how ethno-racial groups perceive and cultivate resources in response to stressors and adverse structural conditions. Future studies should continue to investigate the complex set of factors which shape the mental well-being and aging of the U.S. population.

archiveRecords.title: Effects of an Online Training Program on Quality of Life and Caregiver Burden in Dementia Informal Caregivers
archiveRecords.abstract: Informal caregivers of people living with dementia experience high caregiver burden (CB) and reduced quality of life (QoL), yet evidence on caregiver training remains limited.  To evaluate the effects of an online training program on caregivers’ QoL and CB.  A quasi-experimental pre–post study was conducted. Caregivers completed the WHOQOL-BREF and Zarit Scale at baseline and after a four-week training program.  Sixty-four caregivers completed the program; 42.1% reported clinically significant burden at baseline. Following the intervention, improvements in overall QoL ( p = 0.001) and reductions in CB ( p = 0.031) were observed among caregivers. These changes were greater among caregivers with baseline burden. Higher educational attainment was associated with increased odds of CB (OR = 1.243, 95% CI: 1.053–1.468).  Online caregiver training was associated with improved caregiver well-being and lower CB, supporting its potential integration into dementia care. However, the absence of a control group limits causal inference.

archiveRecords.title: “I Wanted to Get Back Out There”: In-depth Interviews With Older Adults and Family Caregivers About Moving Out of Nursing Homes Using Medicaid’s Money Follows the Person Program and How Dementia Influences Transitions
archiveRecords.abstract: Medicaid’s Money Follows the Person (MFP) Program enables nursing home residents to return to community living, yet people living with dementia (PLWD) less often transition to the community through MFP, for unclear reasons. To understand mechanisms underlying this disparity, we conducted in-depth interviews with 44 older adults in Connecticut eligible for MFP and 44 family caregivers (41% PLWD/PLWD family members). Desire to move, program awareness, ability to self-advocate, personal care needs, family support, housing and home and community-based services (HCBS) resources all influenced moves. PLWD less often desired to move, typically required more assistance to move, were less able to self-advocate and manage logistics, had higher personal care needs, needed more family/informal support, and had additional safety and supervision needs. Better support for PLWD is needed in transition and HCBS programs as the population grows, nursing homes beds decrease, and the desire to live in the community persists.
