archiveRecords.title: Rural and Urban Differences in the Trends in Supply of Home Care Workers From 2015 to 2024
archiveRecords.abstract: Given the rapidly aging population in the United States and preferences to age-in-place, demand for direct care workers in the home will increase. Yet, it is unclear whether labor supply will meet demand, particularly in rural areas.  To describe differences in home care worker supply and demand by rurality and temporal trends between 2015 and 2024.  Repeated cross-sectional description of the supply of care workers serving adults 65 and older with functional impairments in the United States using 2015-2024 American Community Survey data.  From 2015 to 2024, the national supply of home care workers increased by 6.0% (95% CI: [2.6%, 9.4%]). Relative supply in metropolitan areas increased 7.3% (95% CI: [3.6%, 11.0%]) and decreased in rural areas by −10.3% (95% CI: [-19.7%, −1.0%]). While potential demand for care increased in both rural and metropolitan areas over this period, the number of care workers increased only in urban areas.

archiveRecords.title: Sex-specific multimorbidity clusters and all-cause mortality among community-dwelling older adults: findings from the ASPREE cohort
archiveRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
archiveRecords.abstract: Multimorbidity is common in older adults, but sex differences in chronic condition clustering remain unclear. This study explored multimorbidity clusters and their associations with all-cause mortality among community-dwelling adults aged 70 years and over.  This was a secondary analysis of data from 16 095 Australian ASPREE participants aged ≥70 years without prior dementia or cardiovascular disease. Fifteen baseline chronic conditions were grouped using latent class analysis (LCA). Observed-to-expected (O/E) ratios characterized conditions over-represented within clusters, and Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations with all-cause mortality.  Among 16 095 participants (mean age 75.3 years), 88.3% had multimorbidity at baseline; 4217 deaths occurred over a median follow-up of 10.85 years. Five clusters were identified overall: hypertension and dyslipidemia (52.1%), gout and metabolic (14.4%), depressive symptoms, osteoporosis, and frailty (10.0%), anemia and kidney disease (10.2%), and hypotension, thyroid disorder, and past cancer (13.3%). Sex-stratified analyses revealed 3 clusters in males and 4 in females. The frailty, depressive symptoms and osteoporosis cluster was associated with higher mortality in both sexes (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1.56 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.40-1.73] in males; 1.68 [1.49-1.89] in females). Higher mortality was also observed for the metabolic, gout and kidney disease cluster in males (aHR 1.63 [1.47-1.81]) and the gout, anemia and kidney disease cluster in females (aHR 1.96 [1.74-2.21]).  Distinct multimorbidity clusters were identified overall and in sex-stratified analyses. These hypothesis-generating findings suggest the potential clinical utility of multimorbidity clusters to identify individuals at increased risk of death, but further research is needed.

archiveRecords.title: Rethinking the Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Healthy Older Adults: The Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) Exergames
archiveRecords.abstract: Though exergames attract considerable research interest as tools for preserving cognitive function in older adults, a decade of meta-analytic evidence reveals a persistent gap between theoretical promise and empirical demonstration: exergames rarely outperform conventional motor-cognitive training and do not generate the sustained engagement that preventive benefit requires. These  reflect limitations that are structural: the field focused predominantly on clinical populations rather than primary prevention; training concepts borrowed from rehabilitation protocols rather than grounded in the specific neuroplastic mechanisms of the exergaming medium; and virtual environments that are digitally sophisticated but culturally and esthetically neutral, systematically excluding the stimulation that converging evidence from neuroaesthetics, cultural epidemiology, and narrative neuroscience identifies as a core active ingredient of brain health promotion. To address these limitations simultaneously, this viewpoint introduces Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) exergames, defined as “virtual reality solutions in which motor-cognitive interactions are embedded in artistic content, cultural heritage, or historically situated narrative to exploit optimal neurobiological substrates of the intervention.” Drawing on an integrated theoretical framework, we develop mutually reinforcing mechanistic pillars: multimodal sensorimotor engagement within ecologically valid immersive environments; semantic and narrative activation of memory systems; emotional and autobiographical resonance as a dopaminergic driver of learning consolidation and sustained participation; and the re-engineering of physical effort evaluation from aversive to appetitive through aesthetic pleasure and narrative absorption. A fundamental implication is that in MAGIC exergames, motivation is not engineered through gamification mechanics—it is released by the intrinsic value of inhabiting a culturally meaningful world. We further argue MAGIC exergames correspond to a specific use that is, Cultural Snacking, which consists of the serialization of MAGIC content into brief, narratively open daily episodes of 5 to 10 minutes, designed for 3 to 5 daily consumptions across varied contexts. This dosing architecture is compatible with the motivational profile of healthy older adults who do not identify as patients or trainees. The paper opens perspectives with a design and research agenda structured around three priorities: characterizing MAGIC exergames by the type of motor-cognitive interactions they deliver rather than by the technology platform; conducting mechanistic neuroimaging investigations targeting the specific biomarkers of neuroplastic benefit that creative cultural engagement is expected to produce; and building the intersectoral innovation ecosystem that brings cultural institutions, digital health teams, and older adults together as co-designers. Without waiting for MAGIC-specific trials, we invite the digital medicine, public health, and silver economy communities to recognize that museums, heritage sites, and cultural institutions are potentially the most ecologically valid, intrinsically motivating, and cost-effective substrates for a new generation of brain health exergames that are as meaningful as they are effective. The scientific, institutional, and economic conditions for this convergence already exist.

archiveRecords.title: Knowledge Performance, User Experience, and Cybersickness With Immersive Virtual Reality for Tai Chi Movement-Encoding in Older Adults: Randomized Comparison Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used for embodied training, but its practical value for older adults depends on whether the experiential benefits can be achieved without unacceptable discomfort or overstated claims about motor learning.  This randomized study compared head-mounted immersive VR with standardized, content-matched 2D video instruction for Tai Chi movement-encoding in community-dwelling older adults.  A total of 106 older adults were randomized to immersive VR (n=56) or video instruction (n=50). The primary analysis included 92 participants with complete age, pretest, and posttest data (VR: n=45; Video: n=47). The primary outcome was a 5-item movement-encoding knowledge score (range 0‐20), analyzed using analysis of covariance, with posttest score as the dependent variable and group, pretest score, and age as predictors. Secondary outcomes were intrinsic motivation, game experience, and learning engagement; safety, tolerability, and feasibility were assessed using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, Game Experience Questionnaire, Utrecht Work Engagement Scale–Short Form, participant flow, and Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire. VR system telemetry was analyzed descriptively as an exploratory process outcome.  Adjusted posttest movement-encoding performance did not differ between VR and video instruction (adjusted difference −0.27, 95% CI −2.25 to 1.72; P =.79; partial η 2 =0.001). The Game Experience Questionnaire  favored VR for competence (Video: mean 3.36, SD 1.21; VR: mean 4.15, SD 0.92; q =0.009), flow (Video: mean 3.77, SD 1.26; VR: mean 4.46, SD 0.76; q =0.014), and lower tension (Video: mean 1.76, SD 1.04; VR: mean 1.27, SD 0.63; q =0.037), whereas challenge did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction ( q =0.073). In the VR Group, recognition accuracy was associated with posttest movement-encoding score (n=44; r =0.317, P =.04), but pose accuracy was not (n=44; r =0.129, P =.41). The Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire scores were low among valid VR participants (total score mean 3.77, SD 11.12), and 36 out of 46 (78%) participants reported zero symptoms.  With a strong active control, immersive VR did not produce higher short-term Tai Chi movement-encoding performance than video instruction. Among participants who completed the VR session, the immediate game-experience profile was more favorable. These findings indicate that VR may offer experiential benefits, while also highlighting the need to manage cybersickness and technical exclusions and to distinguish movement knowledge from actual motor execution.

archiveRecords.title: Social Determinants and Oral Health Among Indigenous and Non-Indigenous Older Adults in La Araucanía, Chile: Cross-Sectional Study
archiveRecords.abstract: Social disparities in oral health persist, disproportionately affecting Indigenous populations.  This study aims to compare oral health status, dental care access, treatment needs, and social determinants between Mapuche and non-Mapuche older adults in the La Araucanía Region of Chile, within a hybrid dental care model, and to explore whether ethnicity is associated with these outcomes, guided by the World Health Organization (WHO) Commission on Social Determinants of Health (CSDH) framework.  We conducted a cross-sectional exploratory analytic study using data from 480 adults aged 60 years or older who received dental care through a hybrid teledentistry and mobile clinic model (Geriatric Dental Specialties Tele-Platform [TEGO]) in 4 municipalities of La Araucanía. The analytic sample was restricted to community-dwelling, functionally independent older adults. Outcomes included oral health status (nonfunctional dentition, edentulism, cavitated caries, and periodontitis), dental care access (fixed prosthetic rehabilitation and unmet denture need), and dental treatment needs (restorative and prosthetic). Structural (sex, age, education, rurality, and ethnicity) and intermediary determinants (behavioral, biological, psychosocial, and health system access) were analyzed following the WHO-CSDH framework. Bivariate analyses compared outcomes between Mapuche and non-Mapuche participants. Multivariable logistic regression models examined associations between determinants and outcomes.  A total of 471 older adults (mean age 72.8, SD 7.7 years) were included; 76.9% (362/471) had nonfunctional dentition, 18% (85/471) were edentulous, 25.6% (98/383) had cavitated caries, and 46% (154/335) had periodontitis. In bivariate analyses, Mapuche participants showed lower educational attainment, higher rural residence, poorer oral health, more behavioral risk factors (eg, infrequent toothbrushing and higher sugar intake), greater restorative needs, and reduced access to complex dental care compared with non-Indigenous peers. In multivariable analyses, female sex was associated with increased odds of edentulism but lower odds of periodontitis. Lower education was associated with nonfunctional dentition (odds ratio [OR] 4.28, 95% CI 2.34-7.88; P  Oral health inequalities among older adults in La Araucanía were associated with both structural and behavioral determinants. Although Mapuche participants exhibited poorer oral health, higher restorative needs, and reduced access to complex dental care in bivariate analyses, ethnicity remained associated only with cavitated caries and periodontitis in adjusted models. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating social determinants into oral health planning for underserved older adults and highlight the potential utility of data generated through digitally supported territorial care models for informing equity-oriented oral health strategies.

archiveRecords.title: Healthcare Provider Experiences Delivering Dementia Care in Indigenous Communities: Challenges and Recommendations
archiveRecords.abstract: and  Little is known regarding the effects of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) in in American Indian and First Nation (AI/FN) communities in the US and Canada. Yet, research suggests FN populations in Canada experience 34% higher dementia rates and over half of US-based Indigenous adults demonstrate incident cognitive impairment, including dementia due to AD and/or cerebrovascular disease. Already higher than the general population, rates will increase as Indigenous populations age. The Indigenous Cultural Understandings of ADRD-Research and Engagement (ICARE) project was established to understand lived-experiences of dementia in AI/FN communities around the Great Lakes. We report themes describing practitioner experiences providing dementia care in selected US and Canadian Indigenous communities. Research Design and  Healthcare practitioners (n = 14) providing care in Indigenous communities were interviewed by community-based researchers using semi-structured guides exploring a range of topics. Thematic analysis was used to identify challenges and recommendations to improve care. Trustworthiness checks included reflexivity, consensus, prolonged engagement, member checking and audit.  Thematic analysis yielded six superordinate themes. Provider-perceived challenges included: 1) Limited Resources for Providing Dementia Care, 2) Need for Caregiver-focused Preparation and Support, 3) Communication and Relationship Gaps, 4) Low-levels of Community Dementia-related Awareness, Education and Engagement. Provider recommendations were characterized as: 5) Increase Dementia-related Awareness, Education and Engagement, 6) Invest in Dementia Caregiver Support and Community Strengths.  Findings were contextualized with post-colonial and relational care frameworks. Providers described relevant challenges and provided culturally safe and equitable strategies to improve dementia care outcomes.

archiveRecords.title: Clinical and Geriatric Profiles of Centenarians Living in Long-Term Care Facilities in Martinique, a Validated Blue Zone, and Neighboring Guadeloupe (French Caribbean Islands)
archiveRecords.abstract: Martinique has recently been described as one of the world’s five “Blue Zones” of longevity, while the status of Guadeloupe remains to be established. This study described the observed proportion and clinical and geriatric profiles of centenarians living in sampled long-term care settings in Martinique and Guadeloupe. Data from two observational cohorts of nursing home ( n = 332) and foster family residents ( n = 107) were pooled. Among 439 participants, 13 (3.0%) were centenarians (mean age 102.1 ± 2.4 years; 76.9% women). Compared with younger residents (mean age 80.8 ± 9.8 years), centenarians had similar prevalences of major comorbidities and polypharmacy, but greater functional impairment and poorer physical performance. One-year mortality was higher among centenarians (58.3% vs. 21.4%; p = 0.002). In long-term care settings, exceptional longevity was characterized by greater functional impairment and mortality without a greater burden of major chronic diseases.

archiveRecords.title: Caregiver Perspectives on Alzheimer’s Care in the Turkish Sociocultural Context
archiveRecords.abstract: In the context of global demographic change, the number of patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and other forms of dementia is steadily increasing. These individuals require ongoing care but often struggle to communicate their needs and preferences regarding quality care. This study re-examines existing qualitative data to explore perceptions of “quality care” for patients with AD within the Turkish sociocultural context. Building on a primary study of caregivers’ definitions of quality care, it employs a secondary analysis approach to generate new insights without collecting additional data. The dataset includes face-to-face, semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 15 formal and informal caregivers, including family members, professional caregivers, and managers from care institutions across four provinces in Türkiye. Analysis reveals that patients with AD often experience discomfort when their bodies are exposed or touched, particularly in ways that infringe upon their sense of privacy. Caregivers emphasised that protecting privacy relies on understanding the individual’s life story, values, and preferences, highlighting the role of relational familiarity in delivering care. Many participants described forming close, family-like bonds, often adopting kinship roles to provide personalised support. These dynamics were also shaped by gender norms, with caregiving commonly framed through a mother-child lens, reflecting societal expectations that women assume primary caregiving responsibilities. The findings show how privacy, emotional closeness, and gender roles intersect to shape caregiving practices. These findings suggest that care quality for patients with AD in Türkiye may be enhanced by approaches that attend to cultural and relational dimensions, recognise caregiver support needs, and incorporate culturally attuned practices — though further research across diverse settings is needed to assess the broader applicability of these insights. These insights contribute to the international discourse on dementia care by showing how culturally specific practices can guide globally relevant approaches to quality care.

archiveRecords.title: Domain-Specific Associations of Physical Activity With Phase Angle and Extracellular Water–to–Total Body Water Ratio in Middle-Aged or Older Adults: Cross-Sectional Study
archiveRecords.abstract: The phase angle (PhA) and extracellular water (ECW)–to–total body water (TBW) ratio serve as indicators of cell membrane integrity and body fluid balance in older adults.  This study examined the domain-specific associations of physical activity (PA) with PhA and the ECW-to-TBW ratio.  A nationally representative sample of 5211 adults aged 50 years and older was analyzed. Weekly amounts of moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) in leisure-time, occupational, and transport-related domains were assessed using the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire. A bioelectrical impedance analyzer was used to measure PhA (°) and the ECW-to-TBW ratio (%). Linear regression analyses were conducted.  For leisure-time PA, compared with 0 min/week, participating in 150 to 299 min/week and ≥300 min/week of MVPA was associated with 0.08 (95% CI 0.02-0.14) and 0.13 (95% CI 0.06-0.20) degrees higher PhA, respectively. Additionally, compared with 0 min/week, engaging in 150 to 299 min/week and ≥300 min/week of MVPA was associated with –0.11 (95% CI –0.19 to –0.03) and –0.15 (95% CI –0.22 to –0.07) percentage points lower ECW-to-TBW ratio, respectively. For transport-related PA, compared with 0 min/week, engaging in ≥300 min/week of MVPA was negatively associated with the ECW-to-TBW ratio (β=–0.07, 95% CI –0.14 to –0.01). Occupational PA showed no clear associations with PhA or the ECW-to-TBW ratio.  While the observed associations were modest, the associations of PA with both PhA and the ECW-to-TBW ratio differed across PA domains. Specifically, leisure-time PA was positively associated with PhA and inversely associated with the ECW-to-TBW ratio. These findings highlight the potential role of leisure-time PA in improving bioelectrical markers of cellular health and fluid distribution.

archiveRecords.title: Positioning Care Robots Within Filial Responsibility: Perspectives of Chinese Only Children
archiveRecords.abstract: The adoption of care robots for older adult care is often framed as a question of whether older adults will accept the technology. This paper argues that, in family-based care for older adults at home, an equally important question is how adult children position care robots within intergenerational care relationships and their responsibility for ageing parents. Using Q methodology with 42 Chinese only children, by-person factor analysis identified four profiles: the Worried Controller, who may prioritise safety over parental autonomy; the Modern Filial, who sees tailored robots as a contemporary expression of filial piety; the Presence Keeper, who resists technologies that substitute for family presence; and the Filial Complementarity Conditionalist, who sees robots as supplementary to filial and emphasises broader policy and service conditions. These profiles show how participants balance filial obligation, caregiving pressure, parental autonomy, family presence, and wider conditions surrounding care-robot use.

archiveRecords.title: Clinical Group Assignment in Home Health Care for Medicare Beneficiaries With ADRD: A 2019 Pre-PDGM Simulation
archiveRecords.abstract: The Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM) assigns home health episodes to clinical groups using primary diagnosis codes. The implications of this approach for beneficiaries with ADRD, whose condition is rarely coded as primary, are unclear.  To compare simulated PDGM clinical group assignment between ADRD-highly likely and ADRD-unlikely episodes.  Using national 2019 Medicare fee-for-service data, we simulated clinical group assignment and compared primary diagnosis profiles before and after 1:1 propensity score matching.  Nine in ten ADRD-highly likely episodes carried a non-ADRD primary diagnosis. After matching on demographics, comorbidity, and functional and cognitive status, clinical group assignment differences between cohorts attenuated but persisted. Most strikingly, ADRD-highly likely episodes were nearly 12 times as frequently assigned to Behavioral Health, the group with the lowest average payment weight, and comprised 92.1% of all matched Behavioral Health episodes. Within clinical groups, primary diagnosis profiles differed between cohorts, suggesting distinct care needs.

archiveRecords.title: Linking Online Learning Time to Social Participation Among Older Adults: Urban-Rural Differences in the Online Learning Performance and Efficacy Pathways
archiveRecords.abstract: Lifelong learning is known to promote social participation among older adults. However, in the digital age, it remains unclear whether online learning yields a positive effect and what the mechanisms are.  A total of 1,013 older adults aged 60 years and above completed the online learning efficacy scale, the online learning performance checklist, and the social participation checklist. Participants also self-reported their online learning time.  Online learning time was positively associated with social participation. The association was mediated by online learning efficacy and by a sequential pathway from online learning performance to online learning efficacy. These mediating effects were stronger among rural older adults than among urban older adults.  Active digital engagement among older adults may promote social participation, with particularly strong benefits for rural older adults. To promote active aging, future policies should incorporate internet-based learning programs into social participation interventions in rural areas.

archiveRecords.title: Social Capital and Life Satisfaction Among Older Adults in South Korea: The Role of AI Literacy
archiveRecords.abstract: Bonding (close, homogeneous ties) and bridging (weaker, heterogeneous ties) social capital are associated with older adults’ life satisfaction, but the indirect role of AI literacy remains unclear.  To examine direct and indirect associations among bonding and bridging social capital, AI literacy, and life satisfaction among Korean older adults.  Data from 1,250 adults aged ≥65 years in the 2024 Digital Divide Survey were analyzed using structural equation modeling and 5,000 bootstrap resamples.  Both social capital forms and AI literacy were positively associated with life satisfaction. Bridging social capital was positively associated with AI literacy, whereas bonding social capital was negatively associated. Their indirect associations were 0.063 (95% CI 0.040–0.090, P Discussion Bonding and bridging ties may shape older adults’ AI learning differently, suggesting that social context matters for AI literacy and life satisfaction.

archiveRecords.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Longitudinal Changes in Intrinsic Capacity in Older Chinese Adults: The Role of Social Support
archiveRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
archiveRecords.abstract: The links between adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), intrinsic capacity (IC) trajectories in older adults and the role of social support remain unclear.  Using data from 3,897 Chinese adults aged 60 + years in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. IC was assessed at Waves 1 and 3. ACEs were from the Life Event Survey. Mediation analyses were performed.  ACEs were associated with lower baseline IC but not with IC changes over time. Psychological capacity declines were associated with total ACEs (−0.024, 95% CI: −0.040, −0.008) and threat-related ACEs (−0.030, 95% CI: −0.052, −0.007). Threat-related ACEs showed a stronger association with lower baseline IC among those not living with children, and deprivation-related ACEs were linked to greater sensory decline (−0.054, 95% CI: −0.096, −0.012) only in this group. Social support did not mediate these associations.  ACEs are linked to domain-specific IC declines, modified by living arrangement.

reviewRecords.title: Association between inappropriate medications and comprehensive geriatric assessment outcomes: a cross-sectional study using PRISCUS, STOPP, and Beers criteria
reviewRecords.abstract: Aim Different criteria were developed to identify drugs with a negative benefit/risk ratio in older adults, so-called potentially inappropriate medication (PIM). We investigated the correlation between the number of PIMs identified using PRISCUS 2.0, STOPP version 3, and Beers criteria and the functional and nutritional status of Turkish geriatric patients, as assessed by comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) tools.  This retrospective cross-sectional analysis was conducted in geriatric outpatients over the past 10 months. Data were collected on age, clinical conditions, medication, and CGA test . To identify independent factors associated with PIM use and to adjust for potential confounding, logistic regression analyses were performed. PIM use was analysed as a binary outcome (no PIM versus at least one PIM), and no imputation was performed. Two logistic regression models were fitted in 362 patients with complete data, without (Model 1) and with (Model 2) the number of drugs.  Among 397 participants, 58.7% ( n = 233) of patients received at least one PIM when combining all three criteria (PIM-ALL). Multivariable analyses showed that the number of medications and functional status (Katz Activities of Daily Living) were most strongly associated with PIM use. In the fully adjusted model (Model 2, n = 362), each additional medication was associated with 55% higher odds of PIM use (OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.40–1.73), while a higher Katz ADL score was associated with lower odds (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.60–0.87).  There is relevant variability among PIM tools and in their association with CGA test . Advanced, systematic, and easily implementable methodologies are required to address these shortcomings. Clinical trial registration This study does not involve a clinical trial and thus was not registered.

reviewRecords.title: Supporting Diversity in Health and Aging Research and Education: Recommendations from a Multidisciplinary Gerontological Symposium
reviewRecords.abstract: Increasing attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) have left many researchers and educators in aging scrambling on how best to navigate this political landscape in their research and teaching. In response, the Gerontological Society of America (GSA)’s Public Policy Advisory Panel convened a multidisciplinary panel discussion of experts from the six GSA member groups and three advisory panels in November 2025 to discuss the current state of the research and education, particularly as it relates to diversity in health and aging; current efforts by researchers and educators to adapt and respond to these efforts; and future actionable recommendations on how to continue to support DEI principles in all phases of health and aging research and education. Several common themes emerged across disciplines (collaboration, education, mentorship, and research) that led to four key recommendations: (1) cultivate authentic community relationships and collaboration; (2) intentionally engage historically excluded populations; (3) innovate; and (4) invoke national and state professional and competency standards. Ultimately, this multidisciplinary convening and its ensuing recommendations provide gerontological researchers and educators with both context and guidance for navigating recent attacks on DEI and contribute to a broader conversation on this important topic.

reviewRecords.title: Prevalence of frailty syndrome among patients with severe aortic stenosis qualified for TAVI
reviewRecords.abstract: Frailty syndrome is a common comorbidity in elderly patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS), significantly influencing outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Early identification of frailty and its determinants is essential for optimizing care and improving quality of life.  This cross-sectional, observational study included 113 Polish patients qualified for TAVI between January and September 2024. Frailty was assessed using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI). Quality of life, mental health, and social support were evaluated with TASQ, HADS, and MSPSS questionnaires. Logistic regression was used to identify predictors of frailty.  Frailty syndrome was present in 82.3% of patients. Higher frailty levels were associated with worse NYHA class, unhealthy lifestyle, and increased emotional burden. Depression and anxiety were significantly correlated with frailty, especially its psychological domain. Logistic regression revealed that NYHA class, emotional impact (TASQ), and unhealthy lifestyle were independent predictors of frailty. Social support negatively correlated with social frailty scores, suggesting a protective effect.  Frailty is highly prevalent among patients with severe AS undergoing TAVI. Comprehensive preprocedural assessment should include physical, emotional, and social factors. Targeted interventions - particularly prehabilitation and psychosocial support - may help address modifiable components of frailty in this population. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

reviewRecords.title: Multilingual Dementia Training for Paid Caregivers: A RE-AIM Mixed-Methods Evaluation
reviewRecords.abstract: and  This study evaluated the IHSS+ ADRD Training Project, a multilingual intervention for caregivers serving individuals living with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) through California’s In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) program, using the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) framework. Research Design and  A quasi-experimental, mixed- evaluation was conducted from July 2019 to June 2024 across Alameda and Los Angeles counties. By applying the RE-AIM framework, Reach and Effectiveness dimensions were assessed through surveys completed by 488 caregivers in English (n = 297), Spanish (n = 102), and Chinese (n = 89) at pre-training, post-training, and 3-month follow-up. Caregivers were diverse among English speakers (38% Black/African American, 23% Hispanic/Latino, and 20% Asian), averaged 49.9 years old, and were predominantly women (88%). Quantitative measures assessed dementia knowledge, self-efficacy, distress, and depression. Qualitative interviews with stakeholders (n = 11) and open-ended caregiver survey responses explored Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance dimensions  RE-AIM findings demonstrated: Reach across diverse caregiver populations in multilingual formats; Effectiveness with significant improvements in dementia knowledge and self-efficacy sustained at 3-month follow-up, plus 88-99% satisfaction; Adoption facilitated by union partnership; Implementation successfully transitioned to virtual delivery during COVID-19 despite technology barriers; and Maintenance supported by increased caregiver confidence, self-care awareness, and stress management skills, though sustainability required ongoing funding.  Language-concordant training produced meaningful, sustained improvements across a diverse paid caregiver workforce, demonstrating its value as an equity strategy in home care workforce development. While virtual delivery was feasible and cost-effective, long-term success depends on securing dedicated funding and reliable technology infrastructure.

reviewRecords.title: Patterns of Social Participation Among Community-Dwelling People With Dementia in Japan: Individual and Neighborhood Correlates
reviewRecords.abstract: Social participation supports quality of life among people with dementia, yet participation patterns and their correlates remain poorly understood.  To identify patterns of leisure activities, community group participation, and social contact and their individual and neighborhood correlates.  We analyzed cross-sectional data from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study–Home Care linked with Long-Term Care Insurance records ( n = 1,604; aged ≥65 years with dementia). Fourteen participation-related indicators were analyzed using latent class analysis. Correlates were examined using bias-adjusted multinomial logistic regression adjusted for sex and age.  Three classes were identified: Broad (10.1%), Relationship-based (21.9%), and Limited (68.0%). Compared with Limited participation, both other classes were associated with younger age, living alone, greater functional independence, lower dementia severity, and more favorable perceived walkability and availability of parks or walking paths.  Findings suggest that participation support should consider individual characteristics and perceived characteristics of the neighborhood physical environment.

reviewRecords.title: Naturalistic Driving Engineered Trajectories Forecast Future Cognitive Decline
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Early population-based screening for Alzheimer’s disease remains limited by the scalability and accessibility of conventional biomarker testing. We tested whether passive naturalistic driving changes predict progression from cognitively normal status to sustained mild cognitive impairment.  Season-adjusted monthly driving data from 298 older adults, including 25 progressors, were summarized into within-person trajectory features capturing drift and instability in cornering and destination diversity relative to a six-month baseline. A GEE logistic regression was evaluated under leave-one-out cross-validation with a paired-consecutive flagging rule. Landmark survival analyses at 12 and 24 months assessed prognostic value. Five held-out clinical subgroups (n = 82 evaluable), plasma pTau217, MoCA trajectories, and depression scores provided independent post hoc validation.  The model detected 19/25 progressors (AUC=0.752, 95%CI: 0.627–0.863; 76% sensitivity; 75% specificity) with an 18-month median lead time before sustained CDR conversion. Adding static baseline driving features reduced discrimination (AUC=0.702), supporting that within-person driving change, not absolute level, carries a predictive signal. Driving markers stratified risk at 12 months (HR = 6.02, 95%CI: 2.35–15.41) and 24 months (HR = 13.38, 95%CI: 3.03–59.04). Signals converged or were directionally consistent with higher pTau217 among detected progressors and clinically ambiguous single-endpoint cases, whereas flagged stable participants showed MoCA decline without pTau217 enrichment. Depressive symptoms did not explain the driving signal (Spearman rho=0.05, p=0.53). The sustained conversion rate (12.3/1,000 person-years) matched epidemiological expectations. Discussion Scalable driving-trajectory features can detect preclinical functional decline with clinically meaningful lead time, without demographic, genetic, or cognitive data, and may serve as an  neurobehavioral screening tool.

reviewRecords.title: Grounded in Experience: Designing the Financial Empowerment Scale Through Community Dialogues
reviewRecords.abstract: Financial fraud and exploitation (FFE) are associated with billions of dollars lost annually and have significant adverse effects on older adults.  Given the challenges and complexities of FFE identification and response, this study aimed to identify domains associated with elder FFE risk from a multidisciplinary perspective.  This qualitative study interviewed experts within the field through six qualitative focus groups conducted in 2024. A thematic analysis approach was used to identify themes.  Five domains were identified encompassing intersecting factors associated with elder FFE: cognitive health, individual behaviors, social health, financial well-being, and health and environment considerations. These findings demonstrate nuanced FFE risk considerations and the need to approach assessment models from a multidisciplinary, accessible perspective to enhance financial empowerment in older adulthood. Findings will be used to inform development of a financial tool to assess potential risk for FFE among older adults.

reviewRecords.title: Mentoring Undergraduates in Aging and Disparities Research: Hopkins USTAR
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: The Johns Hopkins Undergraduate Summer Training and Research Program (Hopkins USTAR) was a 2-year program funded by the National Institute on Aging R25 Advancing Diversity in Aging Research through Undergraduate Education. Hopkins USTAR was designed to provide undergraduate students primarily from underrepresented backgrounds in biomedical and behavioral science with interdisciplinary research training in aging and health disparities research. From 2023 to 2025, a total of 15 undergraduate students participated in faculty-mentored research projects, professional development, research education, and national research conferences. Program evaluation  included pre- and post-program surveys and interviews.  suggest that the Hopkins USTAR program significantly increased aspects of participants’ research self-efficacy and strengthened perceived science identity. Despite the early termination of Hopkins USTAR, the program's short-term outcomes indicate modest success in fostering positive feelings about science and preparing participants for graduate school. Continued follow-up to assess long-term program outcomes will be important to measure impact.

reviewRecords.title: Crossing the Digital Divide: Understanding Older Adults’ Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Qualitative Study
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence is redefining the relationship between older adults and digital technologies. Existing studies have largely explained the digital divide among older adults through traditional digital media such as smartphones and mobile payment, while insufficient attention has been paid to how conversational artificial intelligence changes older adults’ entry thresholds, sustained-use motivations, and risk-judgment mechanisms. This study adopts a multimethod qualitative design, with semistructured interviews as the primary method and digital scenario-based tasks as a complementary method. From January to February 2026, the study was conducted in Chedun Town and Xinqiao Town, Songjiang District, Shanghai, with 40 participants aged 60 and above who had internet-use experience and showed a pronounced tendency toward high-frequency smartphone use. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Interview transcripts, task-observation records, screenshots of AI conversations, and field notes were triangulated; an initial coding manual, double review, and consensus discussion were used to enhance analytic credibility. The study finds that generative artificial intelligence shifts the technological threshold from procedural operation to need articulation and result evaluation, enabling some older adults to compensate for limitations in traditional interface operation through life experience and language-expression skills. Older adults’ sustained use is not driven simply by efficiency, but is closely related to emotional anchoring in later life, experience organization, relationship maintenance, and concrete task handling. Community support, peer learning, and intergenerational assistance constitute important mediating mechanisms through which older adults move from initial experimentation to stable use. Whether older adults truly cross the digital divide depends on whether they can develop the capacities of source verification, contextual delimitation, and boundary judgment. Based on these findings, the study proposes a “conditional crossing” mechanism for older adults’ acceptance of AI technologies and argues that age-friendly governance should move beyond interface simplification toward capability enhancement and risk support.

reviewRecords.title: Diagnostic performance of calculated serum osmolarity versus clinical impression for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients
reviewRecords.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and agreement of calculated serum osmolarity for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients, using clinical impression of dehydration as the reference standard, and to examine glucose levels across concordant and discordant classification groups. Design and setting This prospective, observational study was conducted in a geriatric acute care unit. Participants The study included 455 older hospitalized patients with a mean age of 82.2 ± 6.8 years and 70% were female. Measurements Clinical impression of dehydration (dehydration vs. no dehydration [normal hydration + hyperhydration]) was judged and recorded by the attending physician within 24 h of admission. Calculated serum osmolarity was derived from routine laboratory values and classified as high (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) or normal (  Clinically, 23% of patients were classified as dehydrated. High calculated osmolarity occurred in 38%. Using the ≥ 295 mOsmol/l cut-off, sensitivity was 48.6% and specificity 65.1%; positive and negative predictive values were 29.7% and 80.7%, respectively, and accuracy was 61.3%. Agreement beyond chance was poor (κ = 0.112). reviewRecords.title: Incentives for Access: Changes in Admissions and Care Delivery for Metastatic Cancer Patients in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities, After the Patient-Driven Payment Model
reviewRecords.abstract: Cancer patients experience suboptimal care in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs). Medicare’s Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) incentivized SNFs to admit complex patients, potentially promoting admissions without appropriate changes in care delivery.  To evaluate changes in SNF admissions, rehabilitation therapy volume, and chemotherapy/radiation around admission or discharge, following PDPM and COVID-19.  Adjusted interrupted time series examining 1,125,782 hospital stays from metastatic cancer patients, using 100% Traditional Medicare claims (2018–2021).  PDPM was associated with increased SNF admissions (0.47 pp/month; 95% CI: [0.17, 0.76]) and an immediate reduction in therapy volume (−24.95 minutes per day, 95% CI: [−26.40, −23.48]). Chemotherapy use remained low, but increased by 21% at PDPM implementation, without subsequent slope change (RR: 1.21; 95% CI: [1.01, 1.46]); radiation was unchanged. COVID-19 reversed admission gains. SNF admissions for metastatic cancer patients increased without sustained changes in cancer-relevant care delivery, warranting investigation of health outcomes and outcome-driven policy.

reviewRecords.title: Toward Standardization of Intrinsic Capacity Assessment: A Methodological Comparison of the Responsiveness of Composite Scoring Methods
reviewRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used as an intervention outcome; however, IC composites lack a standardized scoring method, hindering comparisons across trials. To determine whether the scoring method influenced the detection of intervention effects, we applied multiple composite scoring approaches to the same data and compared their responsiveness to a 12-week exercise intervention in older adults at risk of mild cognitive impairment. : Pre- and post-intervention IC data were obtained from 59 community-dwelling older adults assigned to resistance training (n=34) or stretching and flexibility (n=25). The five-domain IC composite was computed repeatedly using alternative scoring approaches: z-score (concurrent and baseline-anchored variants), percentage of maximum possible (POMP), binary classification (0/1), and a three-category ordinal scale. Responsiveness was quantified using the standardized response mean (SRM). : Responsiveness ranged from negligible to large for identical data, indicating that the intervention effect depended on the scoring method. The ordinal and POMP composites were the most responsive (SRM 0.74–0.88 and 0.50–0.76). Within the z-score composite, responsiveness depended entirely on the standardization anchor: the concurrent specification was insensitive (SRM ≈ 0), whereas baseline-anchoring showed moderate responsiveness (0.62–0.71). The binary scoring was the least sensitive, showing a ceiling effect. : Ordinal three-category scoring was the most responsive, suggesting that approaches combining a fixed reference with a category-based structure are well suited for detecting change in IC. This finding requires confirmation against external criteria for IC, such as its predictive validity for adverse health outcomes, along with domain weighting and instrument selection.

reviewRecords.title: Location, Location, Location: How Community Distress Shapes Physical and Mental Health Outcomes for Caregiving Grandparents
reviewRecords.abstract: The health of caregiving grandparents is a critical area of research. Financial strain is a well-established predictor of health and a common issue for caregiving grandparents.  We sought to understand how community context influences this relationship between financial strain and health. Specifically, we examined two dimensions of community context: community distress and perceived access to key resources for caregiving.  Using a sample of caregiving grandparents ( N = 439), we first conducted Latent Class Analysis to identify distinct profiles of resource access. We then used moderated mediation analyses to test whether financial well-being mediated the relationship between community distress and health, and whether this indirect effect varied by resource access profile.  We found the relation between community distress and health through financial well-being varies depending on the grandparents’ perceived resource access. This research points to the importance of community context in the lives of grandparent caregivers.

reviewRecords.title: Transportation Use, Trip Taking, and Trip Purposes Among Older Adults Not in the Labor Force: Evidence From the 2022 National Household Travel Survey
reviewRecords.abstract: Transportation needs may differ by labor-force participation status, yet little is known about travel behavior among older adults not in the labor force.  To examine alternative transportation use, trip taking, and trip purposes among older adults not in the labor force.  Data came from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey ( N = 3,474; aged ≥65; not in the labor force). Logistic regression models examined factors associated with transportation mode, taking any trip on the assigned reporting day, and trip purposes.  Nearly 87% drove, 5%–7% used rideshare/taxi, public transit, or bicycles, and one-third walked for transportation. Transportation use and trip-taking varied by socioeconomic characteristics, living arrangements, and digital engagement. Drivers, transportation walkers, and college graduates were more likely to travel. Social/recreational trips were more common among those living alone and among college graduates.  Improving transportation accessibility, affordability, and digital literacy may support late-life mobility and community participation.

reviewRecords.title: Perceived Care Among Rural Left-Behind Older Adults in China: A Network Analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: Rural-to-urban migration separates many rural older adults from adult children and changes how care is received and experienced. Rural left-behind older adults remain in their rural places of origin after family members migrate for work.  This study examined conditional associations among reported care items and compared care networks by number of children and gender.  Cross-sectional data were obtained from 836 rural left-behind older adults aged 55 to 95 who completed the 14-item CSS-RLE. EBIC-LASSO Gaussian graphical models estimated item-level networks, expected influence summarized net signed connectivity, and network comparison tests assessed subgroup differences.  Village care and visits had the highest expected influence in the overall, male, and three-or-more-child networks. Holiday gifts from offspring ranked highest in the one- and two-child networks, whereas living expenses from children ranked highest in the female network. Network structure differed between one-child and larger-family groups and between men and women.

reviewRecords.title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.

reviewRecords.title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie
reviewRecords.journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
reviewRecords.abstract: This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary : (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content.  revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. However, older adults recalled as many episodic details as younger participants. There was no difference as a function of the recipient's age. Overall, these  underscore the value of studying memory in everyday social contexts.

reviewRecords.title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.  Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.  EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.  We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.

reviewRecords.title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.

reviewRecords.title: Vulnerability intersections: an integrative conceptual framework for understanding vulnerability in AI-assisted care for older adults
reviewRecords.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.

reviewRecords.title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The  of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.  We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.  Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians. Discussion Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

reviewRecords.title: Multimorbidity, Polypharmacy, and Neighborhood Disadvantage as Determinants of Cognitive Performance in the ARCHES Cohort
reviewRecords.abstract: African American adults experience a disproportionate burden of dementia, shaped by structural and clinical factors that remain unclear.  To quantify associations between multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and cognition in the context of neighborhood disadvantage.  This study is a cross-sectional analysis of 348 African American adults aged 45–92 years (mean 64.3 years; 73.6% female) from the Aging Research Characterizing Health Exposome via Social drivers (ARCHES) cohort. Comorbidity burden was assessed using a modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), polypharmacy as ≥5 medications, and neighborhood disadvantage using the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Linear regression estimated associations with a Preclinical Alzheimer’s Cognitive Composite (PACC). The polypharmacy model included modified CCI as a covariate, and effect modification by ADI was assessed using an interaction term between polypharmacy and ADI.  Higher modified CCI was associated with lower cognitive performance (B = −0.071; 95% CI: −0.130, −0.012). Polypharmacy was not independently associated with cognition after modified CCI adjustment (B = −0.081; β = −0.057; p = 0.257). No significant ADI interaction was found (p = 0.064).

reviewRecords.title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.

reviewRecords.title: Replicating the RISE-APS Elder Abuse and Self-Neglect Intervention Model in new contexts: A pre-implementation analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Elder abuse and self-neglect (EASN) remain pervasive phenomena, yet intervention research is limited. Adult Protective Services (APS) plays a central role, but statutory timelines and resource constraints make long-term follow-up difficult. RISE was developed to fill this systems gap as a complement to APS, extending support beyond the investigative phase. Initial implementation of the RISE-APS model at the state level in Maine demonstrated feasibility, acceptability, and improvement in case outcomes. Building on these findings, the present study examines the pre-implementation phase of replicating this model in three new U.S. sites serving different communities to identify implementation determinants likely to shape integration. Research Design and  We conducted six focus groups with 25 managers from APS and partnering community-based organizations housing RISE in three U.S. states. Transcripts underwent reflexive thematic analysis guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR).  Participants noted strong philosophical compatibility between RISE and existing practices. However, structural constraints, including bureaucratic bottlenecks and APS staffing instability, could impede delivery. The warm handoff was viewed as central to engagement, yet sometimes unrealistic given resource constraints or limited time available to build APS-client rapport. Furthermore, while broad service networks may ease initial integration, dedicated partnership maintenance is required to sustain referral flow.  Findings highlight the organizational conditions and partnership infrastructure necessary to support replication of the RISE-APS model. Feasibility relies not only on philosophical alignment but on adapting workflows to withstand turnover, resource limitations, and structural constraints across varying service systems.

reviewRecords.title: Exploring Experiences of Disempowerment in Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Study
reviewRecords.abstract: and  Disempowerment in the context of chronic illness refers to the state of dissatisfaction with diminishing opportunities to control personal lives, potentially leading to disengagement in health management and negative health outcomes. However, the experiences and perceptions of disempowerment in chronic illness among older adults are not fully understood. This study aims to explore the experiences and perceptions of disempowerment in older adults with chronic illness. Research Design and  Qualitative description was employed. From January to March 2025, individual face-to-face semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 Cantonese-speaking older adults with chronic illness. Template analysis was used.  Three themes emerged regarding the experiences of disempowerment: (1) confusion and uncertainty amid unexpected changes and unclear information, (2) struggles to manage their health in the way they would like, and (3) difficulty in living the life they had before or had hoped for. Negative feelings towards the experiences were also identified with indirect expression to others. The causes included: (1) irreversibly declining health and intrinsic capacity, (2) unmet expectations, and (3) age discrimination. The consequences involved: (1) disengaging the context of disempowerment by suppressing negative emotions, distancing themselves from care partners, and trying to overcome the situation, followed by (2) accepting or despairing over time.  This study revealed the experiences and perceptions, causes and consequences of disempowerment in older adults with chronic illness. The tendency to indirectly express or suppress the negative feelings underscores a need for tailored strategies to better assess and address disempowerment in this population.

reviewRecords.title: Impact of a Geriatric Co-management Service on Surgical Cancer Care for Older Adults
reviewRecords.abstract: In 2011, Brown University Health’s Division of Geriatrics started its inaugural geriatric co-management service to improve older adult (OA) care for patients with hip fractures. Its success in care and cost reduction prompted the health system to expand geriatric co-management. Meanwhile, oncology surgeons treat increasingly older and frailer patients due to improved therapies and survival. The literature established what we saw here: increased mortality and complications in frail OA and failure of strategies like Enhanced Recovery After Surgery and Prehabilitation. In 2021, the division launched an oncologic surgery co-management program. Explicit to its launch, hospital sponsors required a 2-year study for benchmarks and quality metrics with a primary outcome of reducing mortality and delirium. QI metrics were developed through PowerBI dashboards using hospital and EMR data, analyzing 4,359 cases, which measured length of stay (LOS), readmissions, mortality, and disposition, from July 2018 to August 2024. We compared outcomes between the pilot (Geri) and those with no geriatric involvement (UC) using 1:1 propensity score matching. Bivariate analyses used chi-square and Student’s t-tests for descriptive comparisons and multivariate linear or logistic regression analyses for outcome rates and adjusted when appropriate. The matched sample consisted of 309 cases in each group. 14% were underrepresented minorities. The Geri group had a lower odds ratio (OR) for hospice or in-hospital mortality (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.12–0.61, p = 0.0016), as well as significantly lower odds of delirium, measured by a positive CAM (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.11–0.73, p = 0.0086). ICU admission was lower in the geri group, although not statistically significant (18 vs 25, p = 0.0690). Overall hospital length of stay was longer in the geri group (8.2 ± 15.4 vs. 6.2 ± 5.6 days, p = 0.0350). Geri patients were less likely to be discharged home (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33–0.77) but were more likely to be discharged to a skilled nursing facility (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.43–3.53) or inpatient rehabilitation facility (OR 8.52, 95% CI 1.04–69.6). : Geriatric co-management in surgical oncology significantly reduced mortality and delirium as measured by CAM among OA, demonstrating meaningful improvements in patient outcomes. Although LOS increased and home discharges decreased, these  may indicate more appropriate discharge planning for this patient population. Geriatric co-management represents a critical, evidence-based component of surgical oncology care for OA. This study adds to the growing evidence supporting the role of Geriatric Medicine in improving the quality of care for OA.

reviewRecords.title: The role of lifestyle medicine in shaping and supporting successful aging
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Within gerontology, various theoretical perspectives on what it means to age successfully have emerged over recent decades and garnered empirical support. Similarly, within medicine and related healthcare fields, research and practice have focused on healthy living in terms of physical health, mental health, and well-being. In recent years, the practice of Lifestyle Medicine (nutrition, physical activity, stress management, restorative sleep, social connection, and avoidance of risky substances) has emerged to describe the role of such lifestyle factors in health.  The present article proposes a pathway to integrate lifestyle medicine with successful aging. We take a holistic approach to develop a model that merges the foundational pillars of lifestyle medicine with the principles of successful aging.  This new approach to exploring the linkages between the principles of lifestyle medicine and the essential components of successful aging highlights how proactive behavioral health strategies related to nutrition, exercise, sleep, stress, and substances could play a role in fostering optimal aging in cognitive and physical functioning and disease prevention, thereby potentially yielding more positive outcomes for aging well.

reviewRecords.title: Cigarette and e-cigarette tax effects on the oldest generation of smokers in the United States
reviewRecords.abstract: and  As cigarette smoking continues to decline among youth and young adults, smoking rates among older U.S. adults remain unchanged. Historically, cigarette and, more recently, e-cigarette tax policies influenced smoking behavior in younger smokers. This study examined how older smokers respond to tax changes to inform public health strategies. Research Design and  Our data combined a panel of state cigarette and standardized e-cigarette tax rates with individual-level survey microdata. Our sample included adults aged ≥65, with and without a history of smoking. We estimated two-way fixed-effects population-weighted regression models of current smoking and past-year quit attempts. Exploratory subgroup analyses tested for heterogeneity by education and income level.  Among 3,117,382 adults, 48% had a history of smoking; of whom 18% currently smoked. A $1.00 cigarette tax increase was associated with current smoking: est. = -0.56 percentage points (pp) (CI: -0.85, -0.27). A $0.10 increase in e-cigarette tax (open) was associated with current smoking (+0.28 pp; CI: 0.01, 0.55). Approaching tax parity by one dollar was associated with a 0.48-pp (CI: 0.20, 0.76) increase in current smoking. While varied by socioeconomic status, there was no association between cigarette/e-cigarette taxes and quit attempts.  For older U.S. adults, cigarette taxes were associated with lower smoking, whereas e-cigarette taxes were associated with higher smoking. The type of e-cigarette tax appears important for tobacco control in older smokers. Policies increasing the relative cost of e-cigarettes may perpetuate smoking rates in older populations at the highest risk of smoking-related harm.

reviewRecords.title: Study design and results of the Wave VI Add Health Cognitive Assessment, Physical, and Sensory Function (Add CAPS) protocol
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: The goal of the Add Health Cognitive Assessment, Physical, and Sensory Function (Add CAPS) protocol was to establish a comprehensive, nationally representative assessment of cognitive, physical, and sensory function in early midlife to support longitudinal and life course Alzheimer’s disease risk research. We developed the Add CAPS, a comprehensive and multidimensional assessment battery in Wave VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health).  We describe protocol implementation and examine the distribution of cognitive, physical, and sensory measures by age, sex, and educational attainment in Add Health Wave VI.  Among participants who completed the survey, response rates were approximately 85% for digital cognitive assessments and 94% for interviewer-administered cognitive, physical, and hearing measures. Participants with complete Add CAPS data had a mean age of 44.2 years. Cognitive performance varied by age, education, and sex. Younger participants and those with higher educational attainment had better cognitive performance scores across assessments. Participants who were male, older, and had lower educational attainment had poorer hearing. There were no age differences in grip strength, but it did vary by educational attainment. Survey-reported cognitive and physical challenges were common. Discussion The Add CAPS Protocol fills a critical gap by providing robust measures of cognitive, physical, and sensory function earlier in the adult life course than most nationally representative aging studies. These data will support future research on aging trajectories and health in the U.S. population.

reviewRecords.title: Mode effects for Add Health in transition from in-person to mixed mode
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: As longitudinal panel surveys face escalating costs, many are transitioning from traditional in-person interviews to mixed-mode designs. While essential for fiscal sustainability, this shift creates a methodological challenge: distinguishing genuine longitudinal change from measurement effects introduced by the change in mode. This study evaluated the impact of this transition within the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) as the cohort entered midlife.  Utilizing Wave VI data and a randomized split-sample design (in which the eligible sample was randomly divided between a new web-first mixed-mode protocol [Sample 1] and an in-person control replicating the legacy survey protocol [Sample 2]), the study estimated the differential mode effect, capturing cross-sectional differences between the two designs. Subsequently, a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) was applied across Waves III–VI to decompose these design effects into mode-specific measurement error and residual nonresponse components.  Concerns regarding systemic declines in data quality were largely unfounded; the mixed-mode design outperformed the traditional in-person design in measurement accuracy. However, significant mode effects were identified for some items, particularly sensitive health outcomes and stigmatized behaviors, driven by distinct combinations of measurement error and differential nonresponse. Discussion Because these differences can inadvertently mimic or obscure actual aging trends, researchers should screen variables for mode sensitivity and incorporate appropriate adjustments, such as a mode or design indicator, inverse propensity weighting, or HMM-based decomposition, in longitudinal analyses, ensuring that “signals” of aging are not obscured by survey redesign.

reviewRecords.title: Midlife in crisis? Life course pathways to health at midlife across U.S. cohorts
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Recent trends of increasing midlife morbidity and mortality and widening educational disparities in the United States are concerning. This study documented the age pattern and educational disparities in health in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) cohort as they enter midlife, and situates the cohort relative to preceding, similar, and following cohorts in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).  Using data from Add Health and NHANES on 6 birth cohorts observed from adolescence to middle age, we characterized age patterns in general health, mental health, health behaviors, and chronic conditions within and across cohorts. We documented disparities by educational attainment, focusing on those with and without a 4-year college degree, and how such disparities emerge and evolve across the life course.  Analysis showed that general health, mental health, and chronic disease deteriorated for the Add Health cohort as they aged into midlife, while health behaviors improved. Compared to the NHANES cohorts, the Add Health cohort had worse health than older cohorts, generally worse health compared to the same birth cohort, with some exceptions, and mixed health compared to younger cohorts. Educational gradients were relatively stable across age, with some evidence of increases, while educational gradients generally increased across cohorts. Discussion The worsening health of the Add Health cohort with age and relative to previous cohorts has important implications for aging, as this currently midlife cohort of U.S. adults will enter old age in worse health than their predecessors.
