reviewRecords.title: Multifaceted mental illness stigma and help-seeking behaviors among Latino older adults experiencing behavioral health problems
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: U.S.-based Latino older adult populations face disproportionate barriers to accessing behavioral health services. We examined associations between multifaceted mental illness stigma and help-seeking from different sources of behavioral health supports among understudied Latino older adults with behavioral health problems.  Data come from a cross-sectional survey that included U.S.-based Latino residents ages 50-86 (N=274; 2021). The survey measured mental illness biopsychosocial causal beliefs, treatment efficacy beliefs, and social rejection beliefs as multiple facets of mental illness stigma that may influence mental and physical health help-seeking behaviors from four sources: traditional media, online/digital media, family/friends, and healthcare providers. Linear regression models examined associations between each stigma component and each help-seeking outcome, adjusting for personal/family factors in the full sample of Latino older adults and among a subsample reporting a self/familial behavioral health problem (n=173).  Among Latino older adults with self/familial behavioral health problems, higher biopsychosocial causal beliefs were associated with increased mental and physical health help-seeking from healthcare providers (p Discussion Multifaceted anti-stigma interventions for multi-generational Latino families may be an opportune strategy for increasing help-seeking for behavioral health problems among Latino older adults.

reviewRecords.title: Social disconnection and cognitive aging across the life course: coordinated longitudinal analysis of three national cohort studies
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: This study aims to better understand the effect of social disconnection on cognitive aging regarding its life course variation, temporal dynamics, and multidimensionality.  We conducted coordinated data analysis of three large U.S. population-based longitudinal cohort panels (Add Health I–VI, MIDUS 1–3, and HRS 2006–2020) consisting of 18,553 individuals aged 11+. We harmonized measures of longitudinal patterns of social isolation and loneliness (never/transient/persistent), episodic memory (word recalls), and working memory (backward digit span and serial 7’s) across datasets. We estimated growth curve models to assess prospective associations of social isolation and loneliness with subsequent memory trajectories from adolescence to old adulthood.  We found strong detrimental effects of social isolation in both young and older adulthood and loneliness in older adulthood on memory function. Longer (particularly persistent) exposures to isolation and loneliness predicted poorer memory test scores. These effects were attenuated but largely remained significant after adjusting for sociodemographic, behavioral, and health risk factors. Social isolation and loneliness show weaker and less consistent associations with the rate of memory decline across the life course samples. Discussion Comparative life course research helped to elucidate the complex relationship between social disconnection and memory change and inform the timing and duration of cognitive impacts of  and subjective social disconnection. Interventions to promote healthy aging should focus on reducing the chronicity of isolation starting early in life and feelings of loneliness in later life. Future research should include additional longitudinal data to further investigate links between cognition, social disconnection, and underlying mechanisms.

reviewRecords.title: Sex-specific multimorbidity clusters and all-cause mortality among community-dwelling older adults: findings from the ASPREE cohort
reviewRecords.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
reviewRecords.abstract: Multimorbidity is common in older adults, but sex differences in chronic condition clustering remain unclear. This study explored multimorbidity clusters and their associations with all-cause mortality among community-dwelling adults aged 70 years and over.  This was a secondary analysis of data from 16 095 Australian ASPREE participants aged ≥70 years without prior dementia or cardiovascular disease. Fifteen baseline chronic conditions were grouped using latent class analysis (LCA). Observed-to-expected (O/E) ratios characterized conditions over-represented within clusters, and Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations with all-cause mortality.  Among 16 095 participants (mean age 75.3 years), 88.3% had multimorbidity at baseline; 4217 deaths occurred over a median follow-up of 10.85 years. Five clusters were identified overall: hypertension and dyslipidemia (52.1%), gout and metabolic (14.4%), depressive symptoms, osteoporosis, and frailty (10.0%), anemia and kidney disease (10.2%), and hypotension, thyroid disorder, and past cancer (13.3%). Sex-stratified analyses revealed 3 clusters in males and 4 in females. The frailty, depressive symptoms and osteoporosis cluster was associated with higher mortality in both sexes (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1.56 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.40-1.73] in males; 1.68 [1.49-1.89] in females). Higher mortality was also observed for the metabolic, gout and kidney disease cluster in males (aHR 1.63 [1.47-1.81]) and the gout, anemia and kidney disease cluster in females (aHR 1.96 [1.74-2.21]).  Distinct multimorbidity clusters were identified overall and in sex-stratified analyses. These hypothesis-generating findings suggest the potential clinical utility of multimorbidity clusters to identify individuals at increased risk of death, but further research is needed.

reviewRecords.title: Rethinking the Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Healthy Older Adults: The Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) Exergames
reviewRecords.abstract: Though exergames attract considerable research interest as tools for preserving cognitive function in older adults, a decade of meta-analytic evidence reveals a persistent gap between theoretical promise and empirical demonstration: exergames rarely outperform conventional motor-cognitive training and do not generate the sustained engagement that preventive benefit requires. These  reflect limitations that are structural: the field focused predominantly on clinical populations rather than primary prevention; training concepts borrowed from rehabilitation protocols rather than grounded in the specific neuroplastic mechanisms of the exergaming medium; and virtual environments that are digitally sophisticated but culturally and esthetically neutral, systematically excluding the stimulation that converging evidence from neuroaesthetics, cultural epidemiology, and narrative neuroscience identifies as a core active ingredient of brain health promotion. To address these limitations simultaneously, this viewpoint introduces Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) exergames, defined as “virtual reality solutions in which motor-cognitive interactions are embedded in artistic content, cultural heritage, or historically situated narrative to exploit optimal neurobiological substrates of the intervention.” Drawing on an integrated theoretical framework, we develop mutually reinforcing mechanistic pillars: multimodal sensorimotor engagement within ecologically valid immersive environments; semantic and narrative activation of memory systems; emotional and autobiographical resonance as a dopaminergic driver of learning consolidation and sustained participation; and the re-engineering of physical effort evaluation from aversive to appetitive through aesthetic pleasure and narrative absorption. A fundamental implication is that in MAGIC exergames, motivation is not engineered through gamification mechanics—it is released by the intrinsic value of inhabiting a culturally meaningful world. We further argue MAGIC exergames correspond to a specific use that is, Cultural Snacking, which consists of the serialization of MAGIC content into brief, narratively open daily episodes of 5 to 10 minutes, designed for 3 to 5 daily consumptions across varied contexts. This dosing architecture is compatible with the motivational profile of healthy older adults who do not identify as patients or trainees. The paper opens perspectives with a design and research agenda structured around three priorities: characterizing MAGIC exergames by the type of motor-cognitive interactions they deliver rather than by the technology platform; conducting mechanistic neuroimaging investigations targeting the specific biomarkers of neuroplastic benefit that creative cultural engagement is expected to produce; and building the intersectoral innovation ecosystem that brings cultural institutions, digital health teams, and older adults together as co-designers. Without waiting for MAGIC-specific trials, we invite the digital medicine, public health, and silver economy communities to recognize that museums, heritage sites, and cultural institutions are potentially the most ecologically valid, intrinsically motivating, and cost-effective substrates for a new generation of brain health exergames that are as meaningful as they are effective. The scientific, institutional, and economic conditions for this convergence already exist.

reviewRecords.title: Effectiveness of Psychoeducational Interventions for Informal Caregivers of People With Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
reviewRecords.abstract: Informal caregivers of people with dementia experience substantial psychological burden, affecting caregiver well-being and care sustainability.  To evaluate the effectiveness of psychoeducational interventions in reducing caregiver burden among informal caregivers of people with dementia.  A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials were conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Searches were conducted across major databases. Eligible interventions combined structured dementia education with skills-based training. Caregiver burden, measured using the Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI) or validated adaptations, was the primary outcome. A random-effects model (REML) was used.
